quiz.prompt: Your friend is fractal wood-burning with a salvaged microwave transformer, suddenly freezes, and cannot let go of the probe. First move?

options.label: Grab them by the dry cotton hoodie and yank them backward
options.feedback: At 2,000–15,000 V, dry clothing and wooden dowels break down fast—you just volunteered to become Resistor #2 in the same circuit.

options.label: Kick the workbench away with your sneaker
options.feedback: High voltage arcs across damp garage floors and thin rubber soles. Stepping closer before killing power is how double fatalities happen.

options.label: Cut the main breaker or wall power first—then call 911, start CPR, and get an AED
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Never touch the victim or bench until power is confirmed dead at the source.

quiz.prompt: A heavy-duty commercial truck tire ran flat for a mile and needs air back up to 105 PSI. Where should you stand?

options.label: Crouched directly facing the sidewall so you can watch the bulge
options.feedback: You just parked your sternum 50 cm from a potential 265 PSI zipper-failure blast cone.

options.label: Inside a steel restraining cage? No—put the TIRE in a steel cage, use a clip-on chuck, and stand ≥2.5 m away along the tread line
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! And if a commercial tire was driven flat, scrap/inspect it internally before ever re-inflating.

options.label: Lean over the top of the tire holding a short manual gauge
options.feedback: If steel sidewall cords unzip under pressure, the air wave throws nearby bodies across the bay.

quiz.prompt: You need to transport dry ice, but your SUV has no cargo compartment separate from the passenger cabin. What is the safer choice?

options.label: Tape the cooler lid shut airtight so the CO₂ stays inside
options.feedback: Never seal a dry ice container airtight. Gas buildup can rupture the container.

options.label: Do not carry it in that SUV. Use a vehicle with a separate, ventilated cargo compartment.
options.feedback: Open windows and fresh-air mode do not make a shared cabin safe. Keep dry ice out of passenger airspace and use packaging that allows gas to escape.

options.label: Turn on cabin A/C recirculation so it stays cool and sublimates slower
options.feedback: Recirculation does not bring in outside air. Do not transport dry ice in the occupied cabin.

quiz.prompt: You accidentally graze your thumb with a 3,000-PSI paint sprayer. It leaves a tiny 2-mm dot that barely bleeds and barely hurts. Next move?

options.label: Wash it with soap, slap a Band-Aid on it, and check it in the morning
options.feedback: The classic amputation trap. High-pressure injection blows solvent deep down tendon sheaths while numb nerves hide the compartment pressure.

options.label: Squeeze the puncture hard to milk the paint back out
options.feedback: Squeezing drives injected fluid deeper along fascial planes and worsens tissue necrosis.

options.label: Go straight to an ER with hand-surgery capability NOW and bring the exact material/SDS label
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Early surgical decompression & washout is the difference between keeping a hand and losing it.

quiz.prompt: A pneumatic nail gun kicks back and leaves a tiny puncture dead-center over your sternum. Your blood pressure is 120/70, pain is zero, and even a quick bedside ultrasound looks clean. Next move?

options.label: Yank any protruding nail head out with pliers and drive yourself to urgent care
options.feedback: Pulling an embedded nail can unplug a sealed vessel or tear adjacent ones—and bouncing a cardiac-box projectile over potholes in a pickup truck is bold theater with terrible odds.

options.label: Pack gauze into the puncture, tape plastic over it, and relax since vitals look normal
options.feedback: Normal 120/70 vitals and a negative quick ultrasound cannot clear a trans-sternal nail riding beside the heart in paracardiac fat, and packing a chest puncture only makes trauma surgeons weep.

options.label: Disconnect the nail gun, leave the nail untouched, hold still, call 911, and get a 3D CT
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Inside the cardiac box, only 3D cross-sectional CT rules out an occult projectile—never your pain scale or a quick bedside scan.

quiz.prompt: Three days after a backyard cookout, you develop sharp, localized abdominal pain—but zero fever, normal bowel movements, and a clear plain abdominal X-ray. What crucial sentence must you tell the ER doctor?

options.label: “It’s probably just mild food poisoning, I’ll take Pepto and go home.”
options.feedback: Grill-brush wire perforations are frequently walled off by omentum—normal stool and zero free air do not rule out an abscess.

options.label: “We ate off a grill cleaned with a wire bristle brush—could we check thin-slice CT for a stray bristle?”
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Plain X-rays routinely miss thin stainless grill bristles; thin-slice CT catches them.

options.label: “I would have tasted metal if I swallowed a wire.”
options.feedback: Almost no documented wire-bristle ingestion victims ever felt or tasted the wire going down.

quiz.prompt: After heavy use of OTC benzocaine toothache gel, a patient turns dusky gray and reads SpO₂ 86% despite high-flow oxygen. What test actually proves what is happening?

options.label: Switch to a brand-new finger pulse oximeter on the other hand
options.feedback: Every standard 2-wavelength finger probe hits the exact same ~85% optical plateau in methemoglobinemia.

options.label: Multi-wavelength co-oximetry (which measures MetHb% directly) followed by IV methylene blue
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Co-oximetry breaks the 85% lie and IV methylene blue reverses it in ~15 minutes.

options.label: Wait 30 minutes on 100% oxygen to let the lung saturation climb
options.feedback: Dissolved oxygen is already sky-high, but oxidized Fe³⁺ hemoglobin cannot release oxygen to tissues until chemically reduced.

quiz.prompt: You wear reusable monthly contacts—sometimes in the shower—and now one eye is intensely painful, blurry, and light-sensitive despite steroid drops calming the redness. What should you do?

options.label: Keep using the steroid drops since the redness faded, and give your lenses a fresh tap-water rinse.
options.feedback: Corticosteroid drops act like a polite curtain over Acanthamoeba keratitis—muting surface redness while double-walled amoebic cysts dig deeper—and tap water is the delivery truck that brought the parasite.

options.label: Pry out the lens even if it feels stuck, scrub the case in the sink, and drive yourself to clinic.
options.feedback: Forcing a stuck lens tears an inflamed cornea, scrubbing the case erases the exact lab specimen ophthalmologists need, and driving yourself with impaired vision compounds an eye crisis.

options.label: Remove the lens gently only if unstuck, seal lenses and case for lab testing, and get a ride to eye care.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Delivering the sealed lenses, case, and a complete list of every prior drop—especially steroids—lets an ophthalmologist catch Acanthamoeba before it wrecks the cornea.

quiz.prompt: Sudden sharp one-sided pelvic pain and shoulder-tip pain hit someone who could be pregnant. Yesterday’s serum beta-hCG fell to 10 mIU/mL, there is zero external bleeding, and a fresh home urine strip shows one negative line. What now?

options.label: Lie down, call 911 instead of driving, and flag the pregnancy possibility and falling hCG
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! A ruptured ectopic tube can hemorrhage into the abdomen below a urine test’s detection floor—and falling hCG never cancels a rupture.

options.label: Take a second urine strip, press deep on the belly, and sleep it off with heat
options.feedback: A second urine stick only repeats the same detection-floor blind spot, while poking the abdomen and sleeping on an internal bleed lets blood pressure crater silently.

options.label: Drive yourself to urgent care since there’s no vaginal bleeding to worry about
options.feedback: Intraperitoneal hemoperitoneum hides cleanly inside the abdomen—and dropping blood pressure behind the wheel turns one surgical emergency into a highway wreck.

quiz.prompt: A healthy-looking baby has been chewing a 'natural' artisan teething bracelet from a local fair, and a routine capillary finger-prick lead screen comes back at or above 3.5 µg/dL. What is your next step?

options.label: Remove the bracelet, seal it with vendor info for public health, and get a confirmatory venous blood draw.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Unmarked metal spacer beads can hide 17,000 ppm lead alongside choking hazards, and a venous confirmation draw launches certified source tracing and proper pediatric follow-up.

options.label: Clear the bracelet with a home lead-swab kit and order online chelation drops while keeping it on.
options.feedback: Home swab tests cannot reliably clear infant jewelry, unregulated internet chelation drops are dangerous, and keeping beaded jewelry on a baby preserves both lead ingestion and strangulation hazards.

options.label: Blame vintage house paint alone and dry-scrape any chipped trim around the nursery yourself.

quiz.prompt: Your toddler had access to colorful sensory water beads. Nobody saw him swallow one, he looks totally fine right now, and later a plain X-ray shows no beads while he is still passing gas. Safe move?

options.label: Induce vomiting or push extra glasses of water right away to flush any tiny bead safely through
options.feedback: Water is rocket fuel for a superabsorbent polymer—extra liquid expands it toward a watertight ileal plug, while vomiting risks choking or esophageal impaction.

options.label: Wait for vomiting or pain since nobody witnessed a swallow and a plain X-ray would have spotted a swallowed toy
options.feedback: Water beads are acid-proof, radiolucent ghosts on plain X-ray that silently swell inside the small bowel—and passing gas early never rules out an evolving obstruction.

options.label: Get immediate medical care, call Poison Help (1-800-222-1222) or 911 for choking, and purge the beads
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Never wait for symptoms or trust a clear plain X-ray after suspected water-bead access—early evaluation beats emergency bowel surgery every time.

options.label: Yes—normal eye pressure means no deep structural injury
options.feedback: Pressure, pupil shape, acuity, and internal anatomy answer completely different questions. This patient had 20/800 vision, a torn iris root, and blood inside the eye at 15–17 mmHg.

options.label: No—any blurred vision, irregular pupil, or internal blood demands immediate ophthalmology evaluation regardless of normal pressure
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Never rub or press the eye; shield it loosely and get urgent specialist slit-lamp evaluation.

options.label: Put an ice pack firmly over the eyelid and sleep it off
options.feedback: Pressing directly on a traumatized globe can worsen internal bleeding or rupture an occult injury.

quiz.prompt: Your dog may have chewed on a yard sago palm (cycad) and starts vomiting—yet an initial belly X-ray is clean, ammonia is normal, and liver enzyme ALT is barely over the line. What's the verified move?

options.label: Spend time combing the garden to count missing seeds, then induce vomiting or give activated charcoal at home before calling the clinic.
options.feedback: Delaying departure to count yard seeds burns critical minutes, and DIY vomiting or charcoal—especially in a wobbly or mentally altered dog—risks aspiration while cycad neuro-vascular toxicity advances.

options.label: Call a vet or pet poison line at first suspected contact, skip home vomiting and charcoal, share clean facts, and keep rechecks.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Clean X-rays and mild early liver enzymes can mask cycad-driven brain edema, 230 mmHg pressure, and plummeting platelets—so rapid vet care and follow-up rechecks catch delayed crashes.

options.label: Breathe easy once early liver labs look barely elevated, and skip follow-up visits if neurological signs start improving by Day 3.
options.feedback: Cycad toxicosis plays dirty with timelines: even when early ALT barely budges or Day 3 neurology looks brighter, delayed coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and ocular hemorrhage can still be building.

quiz.prompt: A relative wearing a prescribed fentanyl pain patch becomes unresponsive in a 106°F hot bath. Paramedics peel the patch off and revive them with Narcan. Why is refusing ER transport still lethal?

options.label: The bathwater soaked through the skin and diluted their sodium
options.feedback: The culprit isn’t water—it’s the huge reservoir of fentanyl that heat already drove deep into the dermis.

options.label: Narcan wears off in 30–90 minutes while the saturated skin depot keeps pumping fentanyl into the bloodstream for up to 17 hours
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Peeling the patch stops NEW transfer, not the drug already parked inside the skin.

options.label: Because fentanyl patches explode when removed wet
options.feedback: No explosion—just silent re-narcotization once short-acting naloxone fades.

options.label: Chase it with a crust of dry bread and fizzy soda to cushion the point and push it safely through.
options.feedback: Fizzy soda won't dissolve lumber, and dry bread recruits gastric peristalsis to drive a sharp toothpick straight out of the stomach wall into liver segment 3 while the mucosa seals behind it.

options.label: Eat nothing, drink nothing, avoid inducing vomiting, and get urgent hospital assessment right away—even while pain-free.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Staying strictly nothing-by-mouth and seeking urgent hospital care lets clinicians address a sharp swallowed foreign body before silent migration seeds a septic liver abscess.

options.label: Induce vomiting immediately before it leaves your stomach, or wait two weeks to see if real belly tenderness develops.
options.feedback: Vomiting turns the esophagus into a return-trip pincushion, while waiting out a quiet belly gives a migrating toothpick time to build a liver abscess behind normal vitals and a clear X-ray.

options.label: Dig into painful lumps with tweezers to pull stray grass seeds out first
options.feedback: Backward-barbed grass awns act like one-way ratchets—digging or snapping an embedded tip leaves the marching barb behind to seed infection deep inside the chest.

options.label: Call the vet ER directly, keep transport calm, and let your dog hold his upright posture

quiz.prompt: A week after quitting a potent Class 1 topical steroid cream cold turkey, someone battling pneumonia develops repeated vomiting, profound weakness, and dizziness—yet stays awake, talking, with normal sodium and potassium. What do you do?

options.label: Skip the ambulance—it was only a skin cream, they are still lucid, and normal sodium and potassium rule out adrenal crisis.
options.feedback: High-potency topical steroids absorb straight past the skin to mute the HPA axis, and secondary adrenal crisis loves flashing normal electrolytes right while septic shock collapses vascular tone.

options.label: Call 911 immediately, grab the steroid tubes, and announce the stopped potent cream to paramedics and triage.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Flagging a recently stopped potent topical steroid lets emergency clinicians treat occult cortisol failure and septic shock immediately instead of waiting on lab panels.

options.label: Restart the skin cream at home—or use a prescribed emergency injection kit—and cancel the ER visit once they seem steadier.
options.feedback: Rubbing lotion back onto skin cannot rescue failing vascular tone, and even a prescribed sick-day injection never cancels the ambulance because underlying pneumonia and septic shock still require ICU care.

quiz.prompt: You take an SGLT2 inhibitor (-flozin) strictly for heart failure—not diabetes. After an injury leaves you barely eating, nausea and deep breathlessness hit, yet your finger-stick glucose reads a boring 124. What now?

options.label: Blame a stomach bug—non-diabetics with a 124 glucose can’t be in ketoacidosis
options.feedback: SGLT2 inhibitors dump glucose into urine on purpose, keeping your meter serenely normal while starvation lipolysis floods your blood with acid—euglycemic ketoacidosis wears a flawless disguise.

options.label: Chug pitchers of water and juice at home to flush the nausea and bump sugar up
options.feedback: Rapid DIY fluid loading in heart failure can trigger flash pulmonary edema, and home juice will not switch off high-anion-gap ketonemia.

options.label: Get urgent ER care now, name your SGLT2 pill immediately, and ask for a blood ketone check
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! On any -flozin pill, a boring blood sugar never rules out ketoacidosis—flag the drug immediately and ask for blood beta-hydroxybutyrate testing plus written sick-day hold rules.

quiz.prompt: Right after aortic valve replacement (AVR), a patient with a thick ventricular septum suffers a sudden, plunging blood-pressure crash—and standard inotropes only make the shock deepen. What is the life-saving pivot?

options.label: Grab TEE, cut dobutamine and epinephrine now, add IV volume, slow the rate with esmolol, and add phenylephrine.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Cutting inotropes halts a dynamic post-AVR 'suicide LV' from clamping its own outflow shut, while volume, rate control, and phenylephrine reopen the exit.

options.label: Escalate epinephrine and dobutamine aggressively to force the thick-walled ventricle to pump through the drop.
options.feedback: Whipping a thick-septum heart with more inotropes turns its own hyperdynamic muscle into an outflow vise—accelerating the exact 'suicide LV' collapse you are fighting.

options.label: Reassure the room that the coronary arteries are wide open and the new valve works fine, then watch the pressure trend passively.
options.feedback: Wide-open coronaries and a spotless prosthesis offer zero protection when dynamic left-ventricular outflow collapse is strangling cardiac output beat by beat.

quiz.prompt: A coworker bracing an old two-prong, metal-cased tool on damp concrete collapses motionless. Their skin has zero burns, and the tool passed an unplugged continuity check that morning. What do you do first?

options.label: Grab them off the wet floor to start CPR immediately—zero skin burns on low voltage means the tool isn't live.
options.feedback: Water acts as a heat sink that erases thermal Joule burns while collapsing skin resistance—grabbing someone on wet concrete hands 60 Hz AC a second victim.

options.label: Treat it as a routine fainting spell rather than cardiac arrest because the unplugged multimeter cleared the tool.
options.feedback: Dynamic faults can energize an ungrounded Class 0 metal housing only under live trigger load, driving low-voltage AC across the chest into ventricular fibrillation without leaving a single scorch mark.

options.label: Kill the breaker or pull the plug safely while dry first, then call 911 and start CPR with an AED immediately.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Killing the circuit keeps rescuers alive, and immediate hard-and-fast CPR plus an AED directly treats the ventricular fibrillation hiding under unblemished wet skin.

options.label: Sit the stung person upright to help them breathe, and consult a faith healer first before driving to a hospital for a mosquito-sized nick.
options.feedback: Sitting a vasodilated collapse victim upright drains blood from the heart, and detours to a faith healer burn the narrow window before painless krait venom demands mechanical ventilation and antivenom.

options.label: Inject 0.3–0.5 mg IM epinephrine into the outer thigh, call 911, and lie flat with legs up—or race straight to an ER for krait bites.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Immediate outer-thigh epinephrine (plus baseline serum tryptase screening afterward) beats hive-free mast-cell shock, just as rapid ER ventilation beats silent neurotoxic venom.

quiz.prompt: Stepping out of the bathroom, you spot blood spurting steadily from a tiny 2–4 mm pinhole on an ankle varicose vein. What stops this bleed?

options.label: Walk quickly down the hall to grab thick bath towels and wrap the entire lower leg tightly.
options.feedback: Standing upright turns your veins into a full-height water tower, every step fires the calf pump, and bulky bath towels spread pressure far too thin to clamp a pressurized 2–4 mm pinhole.

options.label: Lie flat right there, hoist the leg above your heart, press one firm finger onto the dot, and call 911.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Lying flat and hoisting the leg kills the hydrostatic column instantly, and one steady finger clamped directly onto that tiny hole halts exsanguination until paramedics arrive.

options.label: Sit upright in a chair, dab the ankle with a towel, and lift your hand every few seconds to check clotting.
options.feedback: Sitting leaves gravity powering the bleed, and lifting your hand to peek rips off any fragile clot before that high-pressure pinhole can seal.

quiz.prompt: After getting a plaster cast for an injury whose X-ray came back clean, the pain inside the cast turns ferocious and keeps escalating despite rest. What is the right call?

options.label: Take a stronger painkiller, wrap the edges tighter to calm the throbbing, and sleep it off until your follow-up.
options.feedback: Painkillers just unplug the smoke alarm while plaster hides avascular fascial necrosis or compartment syndrome—overnight, S. pyogenes can escalate straight into septic shock.

options.label: Skip the ER since the X-ray was normal and the visible skin looks clean, and wait overnight to see if swelling settles.
options.feedback: A clean X-ray and spotless toes reveal nothing about the sealed plaster chamber underneath; waiting out escalating cast pain lets a surgical emergency sprint past salvage.

options.label: Go straight to the ER immediately so clinicians can split or bivalve the cast and inspect the bare skin underneath.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Escalating pain under any splint or plaster cast is an urgent 'open the box' mandate—only bare-skin inspection catches compartment syndrome or necrotizing fasciitis in time.

quiz.prompt: After giving birth, a severe headache ignores over-the-counter painkillers and escalates into projectile vomiting, vision changes, and a first seizure—even though discharge blood pressure was normal and an earlier plain head CT came back clear. What do you do?

options.label: Call 911/999, cushion their head with nothing in their mouth while timing the seizure, and lead with the birth date and anesthesia.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Postpartum cerebral venous sinus thrombosis routinely hides behind normal blood pressure and a clear plain CT, so flagging the recent birth speeds clinicians straight to dedicated venous imaging.

options.label: Drive to a clinic once the seizure stops—normal blood pressure, no fever or facial droop, and a clear head CT already ruled out emergencies.
options.feedback: A plain head CT is famously blind to clotted brain veins; driving yourself risks another seizure on the highway while venous outflow obstruction pushes intracranial pressure higher.

options.label: Slip a spoon between their teeth so they can't swallow their tongue, then give water and extra painkillers once they stir so they can sleep off the migraine.
options.feedback: You physically cannot swallow your tongue—putting objects in the mouth causes injury, giving liquids before full alertness risks aspiration, and sleeping off escalating postpartum pain misses a clotted venous sinus.

options.label: Press under your left ribs to check for tenderness, sip water to settle the dry retching, and sleep it off since your Monospot was negative.
options.feedback: Palpating a fragile mono spleen can widen a capsular tear into massive internal bleeding, sipping liquids invites aspiration if your stomach is twisted shut, and a negative Monospot never clears EBV.

options.label: Stop moving, take nothing by mouth, call 911/999 instead of driving yourself, and name any recent viral illness or hiatus hernia out loud at triage.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Left shoulder-tip pain can be splenic blood irritating the phrenic nerve, while violent dry retching flags a strangulating gastric volvulus—both surgical emergencies you never sleep off.

options.label: Treat the mild 4-out-of-10 shoulder ache as a pulled muscle since your vitals look fine, and assume an arbitrary 30-day calendar window clears you after mono.
options.feedback: Calm early vitals happily conceal internal hemoperitoneum until circulation falls off a cliff, and an arbitrary 30-day calendar countdown is no substitute for real clinician clearance.

options.label: Relax and monitor overnight—it is over-the-counter hair foam and you already wiped the puddle dry.

options.label: Wrestle the cat into a thorough bath and syringe in milk or water to dilute whatever was licked.
options.feedback: Uninstructed bathing stresses a cat barreling toward cardiovascular collapse, and forcing milk, water, or vomiting by mouth risks aspiration without reversing systemic vasodilation.

options.label: Calculate a ‘safe’ grape count by weight—or massage and walk off a tight puppy belly

options.label: Call the vet ER on speaker right now—zero home grape math, belly pressing, or peroxide

options.label: Let them sleep off the alcohol on the couch—without even a surface bruise, the blow clearly didn't reach the heart.

options.label: Get emergency care immediately and treat it as cardiac trauma until bedside FAST ultrasound rules out tamponade.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Unconsciousness minutes after a chest blow is mechanical cardiac trauma until ultrasound proves the pericardium is clear, regardless of alcohol or unbruised skin.

quiz.prompt: Within 12 hours of a crash and long-bone fracture, sudden chest pain and dyspnea hit—yet SpO₂ reads 97% and leg ultrasounds are clean. Meanwhile, at a roadside wreck, bystanders want to tug off a downed rider's helmet. What's verified?

options.label: Push for Troponin I, D-dimer, and urgent CTPA despite 97% SpO₂—and remove a helmet only with two-rescuer inline C-spine control.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Hyperacute day-one lung clots can strike within 12 hours without a leg DVT or low SpO₂, and solo helmet tugging can turn a hidden skull-base ring fracture lethal.

options.label: Relax about a pulmonary clot since oxygen is 97% and leg veins look clear, and pull the rider's helmet off solo right away if the scalp isn't cut.
options.feedback: An uncut scalp inside a helmet can still conceal a circumferential skull-base fracture, and normal pulse oximetry plus negative leg ultrasounds do not rule out hyperacute pulmonary thrombosis.

options.label: Ride the lap belt comfortably over the soft abdomen instead of the hip bones, and stay near your disabled car on the highway so tow trucks spot you.
options.feedback: A lap strap perched above the pelvic bones becomes a fulcrum capable of tearing the aorta at L1—and lingering roadside ignores that a 77 km/h lorry needs roughly 83–87 meters to stop.

quiz.prompt: A brand-new nasogastric feeding tube is prepped for its first formula infusion, and an air puff produces a textbook 'whoosh' through the stethoscope over the upper abdomen. Should the feed begin?

options.label: Yes—a clear stethoscope whoosh confirms gastric placement, so waiting for radiology just delays nutrition.
options.feedback: Air whooshing into a lung or pleural space impersonates a stomach effortlessly through a stethoscope—which is how 350 mL of tube formula ends up mimicking chyle inside the chest.

options.label: Hold the feed completely and confirm subdiaphragmatic tip placement on X-ray before a single drop goes in.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Abolishing the stethoscope whoosh test in favor of X-ray tip confirmation keeps enteral nutrition in the stomach instead of turning the pleural space into an empyema.

options.label: Run a slow test drip of formula first, and order an X-ray only if the patient coughs or the external tube feels loose.
options.feedback: A slow test drip still pours nutrient broth straight into a misplaced pleural tract, and trusting bedside feel over imaging is exactly how 'minimally invasive' tubes turn deadly.

quiz.prompt: You find someone pinned neck-deep under the dropped lid of an ottoman storage bed—or wedged head-first inside an empty, fresh-air farm tank. Gravity and bad hinge geometry are running the clock; what is your first move?

options.label: Pull straight out by their ankles or shoulders immediately so you don't waste seconds moving furniture or tipping the tank.
options.feedback: Gravity loves a straight tug-of-war: hauling on ankles usually fails in a narrow hatch, and dragging a pinned neck out from under an unlifted mattress lid worsens fulcrum vascular and thoracic crushing.

options.label: Call 911 and remove the mechanical load first—lever and prop the bed lid up from the foot end, or tip the tank horizontally onto its side.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Offloading the diaphragm or lifting the fulcrum off the neck breaks mechanical asphyxia before inverted venous overload and chest compression shut down breathing.

options.label: Take a breath and pace yourself—the tank is completely empty with fresh air, and an ordinary household mattress lid isn't a fast hazard.
options.feedback: Fresh air does zero good when your own organs splint your diaphragm upside down or a hinged mattress frame acts like a Class 5 lever across your neck and chest.

options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Naming plain water or diluted formula right away—with zero shame—sends ER clinicians straight to electrolytes instead of losing critical minutes chasing meningitis.

options.label: Restrain the baby's limbs, put a finger in their mouth to guard the airway, and skip mentioning the bottled water since the label looked made for babies.
options.feedback: A smiling infant printed on a water bottle adds zero electrolytes; restraining limbs or placing fingers in the mouth risks injury, and leaving water out of the feeding history blinds the ER to brain swelling.

quiz.prompt: Mid-run after eating noodles, sudden itching, wheezing, and lightheadedness strike—even though you've eaten wheat your whole life and don't have a single hive on your skin. What's your first move?

options.label: Stop exercising immediately, inject prescribed epinephrine into the outer thigh, call 911, and lie flat instead of standing or walking.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Exercise-amplified anaphylaxis doesn't wait for hives before dropping blood pressure, and staying supine prevents fatal empty ventricle syndrome while epinephrine reverses mast-cell shock.

options.label: Take Benadryl or a quick inhaler puff, walk off the dizziness, and drive yourself to urgent care if vomiting doesn't make you feel better.
options.feedback: Oral antihistamines and inhalers cannot halt systemic vasodilatory shock, and standing up—or getting behind the wheel—invites fainting and empty ventricle arrest.

options.label: Rule out a food allergy since you've safely eaten noodles for years, and just rely on a 4–6 hour wait window before your next solo workout.
options.feedback: Wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis only detonates when wheat meets cofactors like exertion, NSAIDs, or alcohol—and a 4–6 hour gap is no universal cure without an allergist workup and prescribed epinephrine.

quiz.prompt: Your dog gulps down a discarded lamb rib and starts drooling and gagging—yet his gums are pink, he's breathing calmly, and routine blood work would look squeaky clean. What's the play?

options.label: Call a veterinarian or pet ER immediately—skipping peroxide and bread—and log the exact bone type, approximate size, and time swallowed.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Clean blood tests and calm breathing easily hide a thoracic esophageal impaction crushing mucosal capillaries, so moving straight to X-ray and endoscopy prevents necrosis and stricture.

options.label: Give hydrogen peroxide to bring the rib back up right away, or push it down into the stomach with soft bread.
options.feedback: Spasming a wedged 120-mm rib backward can tear straight through the chest esophagus, and packing bread behind it just cements the blockage tighter.

options.label: Wait to see if it passes naturally since he's breathing comfortably, and switch strictly to raw bones next time for safety.
options.feedback: Waiting hands trapped bone pressure the hours it needs to necrose the esophageal wall—and WSAVA warns that both cooked and raw bones carry real fracture and impaction risks.

quiz.prompt: At a crowded indoor pool, a child goes unresponsive in the water and is pulled onto the deck not breathing normally. Plenty of people are hovering, and someone runs off hunting for an AED. What do you do right this second?

options.label: Jump in untrained to grab them, then pause on the deck to hunt for a wrist pulse and wait for the AED before touching their chest.
options.feedback: Untrained water entries invite panicked victims to climb straight on top of you—and hunting for a pulse or delaying CPR for an AED burns precious oxygen during hypoxic arrest.

options.label: Reach or throw from the deck, point at one bystander to call 911, start CPR with rescue breaths immediately, and go to the ER.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Per AHA 2025, drowning is hypoxic arrest needing rescue breaths with compressions—and a restored deck pulse isn't clearance when aspirated water can collapse lungs hours later.

options.label: Assume the crowd of instructors is watching closely, and once a pulse returns on the deck, warm them up in towels and watch a lingering cough at home.
options.feedback: Diffusion of responsibility makes a crowd of watchers act like zero watchers—and a deck pulse can conceal extreme acidosis (pH 6.67) and delayed post-aspiration lung failure needing ER care.

quiz.prompt: Days after adding a standard trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole ear antibiotic to daily heart and kidney prescriptions—without double-dosing anything—severe muscle weakness, faintness, and odd heartbeats hit. What's your next move?

options.label: Sleep off the lingering ear-infection fatigue, check a smartwatch pulse later, and offer orange juice or a banana for quick energy if drowsiness sets in.
options.feedback: Trimethoprim layered onto heart/kidney blockers can trigger BRASH syndrome—driving potassium to 8.6 mmol/L and complete heart block—and forcing juice or bananas on a drowsy person adds aspiration risk to an arrhythmia crisis.

options.label: Stop your daily heart pills unilaterally, drive yourself to urgent care, and chart the interaction as an antibiotic allergy.
options.feedback: Driving into complete AV block risks fainting behind the wheel, quitting heart meds solo destabilizes care, and logging a drug synergy as a fake allergy hides the real mechanism.

options.label: Call 911/999 now without hunting for bottles, give nothing by mouth if drowsy, and report the new antibiotic plus kidney history.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Naming the new trimethoprim prescription beside heart/kidney meds points paramedics and ER clinicians straight at hyperkalemic BRASH syndrome before shock deepens.

quiz.prompt: Someone is pinned across the chest under an unstable vehicle or tilted stone slab. They aren't visibly bleeding out, and they're making occasional irregular gasping sounds. What's your move in the first 60 seconds?

options.label: Crawl under the tilted load with coworkers and an improvised jack to lift it before calling 911—there's no heavy bleeding, so you have a few minutes.
options.feedback: External thoracic compression locks the breathing bellows shut with zero visible blood loss, and DIY jacks or bare-handed lifts under an unstable load invite secondary shifts that crush rescuers too.

options.label: Call 911/999 immediately with heavy-rescue access details, hold everyone out of the unstable crush zone, and treat irregular gasping as cardiac arrest if safely reachable.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Entrapment itself is the 911 trigger—holding the perimeter prevents second victims, and recognizing irregular gasps as non-breathing starts dispatcher-guided CPR and AED deployment fast.

options.label: Hold off on CPR because irregular gasping proves they're still breathing, and guess the exact load weight and hidden injuries so dispatch moves faster.
options.feedback: Irregular gasps are agonal breaths, not ventilation—and guessing unseen details misleads heavy rescue, whereas reporting only what you see from safety keeps response accurate.

quiz.prompt: After an oral sodium phosphate bowel prep, a dog whose morning calcium tested completely normal develops tremors, blank staring, and labored breathing hours before the scheduled procedure. What do you do?

options.label: Call the supervising vet or animal ER immediately without waiting for the appointment, bring the original labeled box and dose times, and keep water out of his throat.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Oral phosphate binds ionized calcium in real time—especially with underlying kidney disease—sparking tetany, a 106.1°F tremor furnace, and acute hypernatremia morning labs could never predict.

options.label: Syringe water and crushed antacids into his mouth to calm the fasting shakes, then wait for the morning procedure since today's calcium was normal.
options.feedback: Forcing water into a tremoring, dull dog causes instant aspiration pneumonia, kitchen-chemistry antacids won't safely fix ionized-calcium collapse, and waiting for morning wastes crucial hours.

options.label: Induce vomiting to clear leftover bowel prep, or double-dose later if he throws up, treating it as rough colonoscopy diarrhea.
options.feedback: Inducing vomiting in a neurologically dull pet risks aspiration, double-dosing piles more phosphate and sodium onto the fire, and tremors with blank staring are metabolic toxicity—not routine prep diarrhea.

quiz.prompt: A toddler has severe unexplained belly pain and vomiting, yet an abdominal ultrasound looks clean; meanwhile, an adult with severe constipation leaks watery diarrhea, and another gets leg-buckling positional headaches. Which instinct keeps everybody off the table?

options.label: Ask about a two-view plain X-ray for the toddler, skip anti-diarrheals in severe constipation, and get brain imaging before any spinal tap for positional drop-attack headaches.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Bowel gas blinds ultrasound to swallowed batteries or magnets, watery diarrhea masks fatal impaction, and scanning before a lumbar puncture prevents hydrocephalic brainstem herniation.

options.label: Trust the clean ultrasound to rule out swallowed metal, give anti-diarrheals since watery stool proves the bowel isn't blocked, and request an immediate spinal tap for the headache.
options.feedback: Three classic traps in one breath: bowel gas hides metal from ultrasound, anti-diarrheals worsen fatal fecal impaction, and a spinal tap with a third-ventricle colloid cyst invites medullary arrest.

options.label: Sleep off unproductive dry retching with upper-belly pain, and assume cold-room confusion can wait because the chart already lists thyroid medication.
options.feedback: Violent dry retching with upper-belly pain screams closed-loop gastric volvulus, and a thyroid pill printed on a chart never proves someone isn't sliding into myxedema coma.

quiz.prompt: Someone accidentally swallows radiator antifreeze, still feels only mildly tipsy, and later turns up with a 26.4 mmol/L bedside blood-gas lactate—yet urine doesn't glow under a black light. What saves their kidneys?

options.label: Wait at home while they still feel normal, and if they reach the ER, treat the 26.4 mmol/L lactate as septic shock since a dark Wood's lamp urine test rules out antifreeze.
options.feedback: Bedside L-lactate oxidase electrodes mistake antifreeze's metabolite glycolate for lactate, while a dark black-light urine check proves nothing—leaving oxalate free to shred proximal renal tubules.

options.label: Hold off on any antidote until external gas-chromatography reference labs confirm antifreeze levels—especially if vapor-pressure testing didn't flag it.
options.feedback: Reference gas-chromatography assays take hours and vapor-pressure tests miss ethylene glycol; waiting lets liver ADH1B keep minting acid and birefringent calcium oxalate crystals.

options.label: Call 911 and Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) even while they feel fine, bring the jug, and name ethylene glycol for immediate IV fomepizole.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Naming ethylene glycol early gets IV fomepizole locking down ADH1B immediately and prompts clinicians to compare bedside ABG lactate against core-lab LDH lactate and freezing-point osmometry.

quiz.prompt: Shortly after sipping a homemade cured herbal root soup, sudden vomiting hits alongside a bizarre 'ice-water-ants' tingling and numbness across your skin. What happens in the next 60 seconds?

options.label: Wait to see if your stomach settles—traditional kitchen simmering neutralizes root toxins, so tingling is probably just a spicy broth.
options.feedback: Standard kitchen cooking cannot reliably detoxify monkshood (wolfsbane), where just 2 to 5 mg of aconitine can kill an adult and push the heart into collapse within 45 minutes.

options.label: Call 911 at the first tingle, bag the leftover soup or root, and say 'possible monkshood/aconitine' while still conscious so the ER doesn't anchor on digoxin.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Aconitine locks cardiac NaV1.5 floodgates wide open into bidirectional ventricular tachycardia that impersonates digoxin on an ECG—except DigiFab won't touch it.

options.label: Skip mentioning the homemade root soup at triage so nobody gets blamed; the ICU cardiac monitor alone will tell doctors which antidote to give.
options.feedback: Monkshood's bidirectional ventricular tachycardia looks like textbook digoxin toxicity on the monitor—hiding the herbal brew wastes lethal minutes chasing DigiFab while cardiogenic shock closes in.

options.feedback: Repeated pure dextrose boluses fuel an even bigger rebound insulin surge without octreotide, and blind IV bicarbonate pushes diffuse CO₂ inward and worsen severe metformin acidosis instead of dialysis evaluation.

options.label: Ask your clinician about holding metformin on dehydrating sick days, and insist on 24+ hours of ER monitoring after any sulfonylurea save.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Holding metformin protects dehydrated kidneys from mitochondrial shutdown, and bringing the exact sulfonylurea bottle secures prolonged observation (and octreotide if rebounds strike).

options.feedback: Double trap: doxylamine rhabdomyolysis peaks AFTER mental confusion clears, and OTC sleep aids routinely trip rapid urine false positives for methadone, opiates, and PCP.

options.label: Bring the exact box, flag dark urine for serial CK and kidney labs, and get LC-MS/MS confirmation
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Delayed muscle rupture and myoglobinuric kidney stress decouple from normal initial labs—serial rechecks catch the surge while LC-MS/MS clears the false methadone flag.

options.label: Assume any familiar nighttime sleep-aid brand contains gentle melatonin instead of an anticholinergic
options.feedback: Nighttime pharmacy brands swap active ingredients between melatonin, diphenhydramine, and doxylamine—always bring clinicians the exact package.

quiz.prompt: Someone who chewed concentrated gas-station 7-OH kratom tablets collapses with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing—yet the quick ER opiate screen comes back completely negative. What saves them?

options.label: Skip naloxone because the opiate screen is negative and a legal herbal chew sold at the register can’t cause true opioid apnea
options.feedback: Concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine tablets flood brainstem µ-opioid receptors while dodging morphine-ring immunoassay antibodies—the same tests that still falsely flag poppy-seed bagels.

options.label: Discharge them once naloxone restores breathing—the antidote clears every cardiac and drug-interaction hazard from kratom
options.feedback: Naloxone reverses brainstem apnea but does nothing to unblock cardiac hERG channels—leaving QTc prolongation, Type-1 Brugada arrhythmias, and CYP2D6 buildup active.

options.label: Call 911, give naloxone despite the negative screen, share all meds, and demand 12-lead ECG monitoring
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Naloxone rescues breathing while 12-lead telemetry guards against hERG arrhythmias and full med disclosure catches 2-to-5-fold CYP2D6/CYP3A4 pileups.

quiz.prompt: Midway through an awake shoulder nerve block, syringe aspiration was completely blood-free—yet suddenly your lips tingle, your ears ring, and your tongue tastes like cold copper pennies. What happens next?

options.label: Stay polite and ‘tough it out’ for a minute—a blood-free syringe aspiration proves the bupivacaine stayed out of your bloodstream
options.feedback: Blood-free aspiration fails routinely, and copper taste plus ringing ears are your 45-second warning bells before bupivacaine locks cardiac NaV1.5 channels into wide-QRS arrest.

options.label: Shout immediately so the team stops injecting and runs ASRA LAST rescue with 100% O₂ and 20% Intralipid
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Speaking up immediately buys the seconds needed for soybean-oil lipid rescue, midazolam, and epinephrine capped at ≤1 µg/kg—not standard ACLS.

options.label: If cardiac arrest strikes anyway, run standard ACLS with full 1-mg epinephrine boluses, lidocaine, and propofol for seizures
options.feedback: Standard ACLS backfires in bupivacaine LAST: ASRA protocol explicitly forbids propofol, lidocaine, and vasopressin and caps epinephrine at ≤1 µg/kg while rushing 20% Intralipid.

quiz.prompt: Power is out, your portable generator is running outside the cracked garage door, and two people inside wake up dizzy and nauseated. Your plug-in CO alarm is silent and a fingertip pulse oximeter reads 99%—what is your next move?

options.label: Trust the 99% finger clip and silent plug-in alarm, sip water, and head back to bed.
options.feedback: A plug-in CO alarm is a silent plastic paperweight during a power outage, and a standard 2-wavelength pulse oximeter mistakes carboxyhemoglobin for oxygen. It will cheerfully beam 99% while carbon monoxide locks onto hemoglobin 200–250× tighter than O₂.

options.label: Stay inside for ten minutes cracking windows and hunting for where exhaust is sneaking in.
options.feedback: Playing detective inside an aerodynamic wind-wake trap just extends the dose of an invisible, odorless gas. You cannot out-ventilate active generator exhaust by cracking windows while staying indoors.

options.label: Evacuate to fresh air right now, call 911 from the yard, and report the generator.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Fresh air breaks the exposure immediately, and telling 911 about the generator ensures firefighters enter with SCBA and gas meters while the ER runs multi-wavelength CO-oximetry.

quiz.prompt: Hours after eating homemade pesto from foraged wild garlic, severe vomiting and diarrhea hit hard. After day one the stomach misery starts to ease—what do you do?

options.label: Go straight to the ER with bagged leftover leaves and pesto, calling Poison Control en route.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Early gastric decontamination and fast botanical ID of the uneaten leaves are your narrow window before colchicine shuts down cell division across multiple organs.

options.label: Sniff the remaining leaves on your garlicky fingers to confirm the plant and sleep off the stomach flu.
options.feedback: Once wild-garlic oil coats your hands, even odorless autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale) smells like dinner. Treating that lull like ordinary stomach flu gives colchicine time to bind α/β-tubulin and arrest mitotic spindles.

options.label: Toss the leftover pesto so nobody else eats it, sip electrolytes, and ride out the recovery at home.
options.feedback: Trashing the leftover leaves destroys the exact forensic evidence toxicologists and botanists need to rule out autumn crocus—and a deceptive reprieve after day one is not recovery.

quiz.prompt: You have taken lisinopril peacefully for ten years, and tonight your throat abruptly tightens, saliva pools, and speech drops to single words. Your lips aren't swollen and your oximeter reads 95%—what now?

options.label: Swallow an oral antihistamine with water and wait to see if the strange food allergy settles.
options.feedback: ACE-inhibitor angioedema is driven by bradykinin, not histamine—so Benadryl is bringing a squirt gun to a deep vascular leak, and forcing water past pooling saliva risks choking.

options.label: Call 911 right now—never drive yourself—and name lisinopril to EMS immediately.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Late-onset bradykinin swelling can strike after a decade without touching your lips, and naming the '-pril' immediately puts hospital anesthesia on standby before the airway shuts.

options.label: Drive yourself to urgent care since your lips look normal and your oxygen still reads 95%.
options.feedback: Deep laryngeal swelling hides behind normal lips and a lagging 95% pulse oximeter until the airway closes abruptly—the worst possible moment to be gripping a steering wheel.

quiz.prompt: A toddler bites a concentrated laundry detergent pod and spits it out. Their mouth looks completely pink with zero visible burns, and they seem calm—what is the right call?

options.label: Keep the original container and call Poison Help (1-800-222-1222) immediately—or 911 for any distress.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Concentrated pods slip straight past an immaculate pink mouth into occult esophageal, airway, and systemic injury, so immediate toxicology guidance beats waiting for visible drama.

options.label: Have them chug glasses of water and induce vomiting right away to clear every drop of detergent.
options.feedback: Forced vomiting sends caustic detergent back up the esophagus for a second burn and straight toward the lungs, and improvised water chugs without poison-center direction can worsen aspiration.

options.label: Wipe their chin and relax—pink lips and an unburned mouth prove they spat out the pod safely.
options.feedback: Detergent packets are built for rapid 'slip-and-slide' mucosal transit, meaning unburned pink lips and even a 97% oximeter can conceal severe lactic acidosis, CNS depression, and sudden airway compromise.

quiz.prompt: Sudden, severe testicular pain and nausea strike—and even after an earlier scan showed blood flow on Color Doppler with a 'normal' resistive index of 0.75, the pain comes roaring back. What do you do?

options.label: Trust the reassuring Color Doppler flow and wait at home to run out a fasting clock before returning.
options.feedback: A cord twisted 720° can still flash central arterial flow on Color Doppler while collapsed venous outflow strangles the organ—and waiting out a DIY fasting clock at home burns surgical salvage time.

options.label: Gently massage and try untwisting the cord yourself, then drive straight to the ER if pain persists.
options.feedback: DIY detorsion is a 50/50 coin toss where guessing wrong cranks 720° straight into 1,080°, and severe scrotal pain can trigger sudden vasovagal fainting right behind the wheel.

options.label: Keep hands off, get a ride straight to the ER now, and state the exact onset time.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Persistent or returning pain overrides a 'normal' Doppler every time, and immediate hands-off surgical triage protects the narrow window to save the testicle.

quiz.prompt: Someone collapses silently beside chemical bottles in an unventilated space. The rotten-egg stench you smelled moments ago has suddenly vanished, and their silver jewelry looks blackened—what is your move?

options.label: Rush inside since the odor cleared, pull them out, and begin mouth-to-mouth resuscitation immediately.
options.feedback: Hydrogen sulfide does not politely clear out—it paralyzes your olfactory nerve right as levels turn lethal, making bare-handed rescuers victim number two and turning mouth-to-mouth into secondary poisoning.

options.label: Stop at the door, move upwind and uphill, call 911 for chemical gas, and wait for SCBA.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Blackened silver plus a vanished rotten-egg smell screams low-pooling H₂S, and staying upwind until SCBA and calibrated gas monitors clear the scene stops one collapse from multiplying.

options.label: Hold your breath to drag them into the breeze—outdoor air neutralizes chemical fumes fast enough.
options.feedback: Heroic breath-holding fails in seconds inside dense low-lying gas pockets, and even an outdoor breeze can harbor lethal localized hydrogen cyanide or H₂S before you reach safety.

quiz.prompt: After heavy drinking, a friend passes out on the couch, won't wake to loud shouting or a firm sternal rub, and is taking slow, gasping breaths with long pauses. What do you do right now?

options.label: Call 911 immediately, skip the recovery position, lay them flat on a hard surface, and start CPR with an AED.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Fewer than 8 breaths a minute or agonal gasps signal failing medullary respiratory pacemakers—not sleep—so immediate EMS and chest compressions beat waiting out still-absorbing stomach alcohol.

options.label: Roll them onto their side under a blanket and let them sleep it off—the recovery position handles heavy drinking.
options.feedback: The recovery position only protects an airway when breathing is steady and normal; if brainstem centers stop driving breaths altogether, a perfectly clear side-lying airway still suffocates.

options.label: Put them under a cold shower, pour black coffee down them, and trigger vomiting to empty the stomach.
options.feedback: Black coffee and cold water cannot reboot medullary respiratory centers, and inducing vomiting after alcohol abolishes the gag reflex turns stomach contents into lethal aspiration.

quiz.prompt: While taking two differently named herbal prescriptions from separate clinics, someone develops severe arm weakness, unrelenting palpitations, and sudden slurred speech. What is the survival move?

options.label: Offer a sports drink and home potassium pills—natural herbal formulas are mild, so it is likely simple dehydration.
options.feedback: Duplicate licorice blocks renal 11β-HSD2 and drains potassium into torsades de pointes and stroke territory, and forcing drinks or kitchen-math potassium into an altered patient risks aspiration and dosing disasters.

options.label: Drive them to clinic yourself once the speech slur fades, leaving the herbal bottles out of the med list.
options.feedback: Self-driving during unstable palpitations or transiently fading stroke signs risks a crash, and omitting herbal prescriptions hides the duplicate glycyrrhetinic-acid root driving the crash.

options.label: Call 911 without self-driving, give nothing by mouth while altered, and bring every prescription, herb, and tea.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Immediate EMS handles sudden arrhythmias or stroke safely, and reconciling every single bottle exposes duplicate licorice roots hiding behind different clinic names.

quiz.prompt: Your puppy bites a live 110 V lamp cord, briefly collapses, and hops right back onto all fours with barely a mark on his mouth. What do you do first?

options.label: Pull the puppy straight off the cord, pry his jaw open to check for burns, and clip on a human oximeter.
options.feedback: Touching a live pet or cord makes you shock victim number two, prying a startled jaw adds stress and injury, and human finger clips cannot reliably read a puppy's oxygen.

options.label: Cut power safely at the breaker or plug first, then call an ER vet right away.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Shutting off power protects you, and immediate ER vet evaluation catches delayed neurogenic pulmonary edema before a catecholamine surge quietly floods both lungs.

options.label: Unplug the lamp, offer a bowl of water and a nap, and only call a vet if mouth burns appear tomorrow.
options.feedback: Standing upright with an unburned lip proves nothing after a 110 V AC zap—CNS catecholamine shunting can drown a puppy's lungs on dry land hours after he seemed to shake it off.

quiz.prompt: You hear a heavy fall inside the shower while someone with epilepsy is bathing, and water is still pouring onto the floor. What is the first-60-seconds rule?

options.label: Wait five minutes before calling 911—that is the seizure rule, and open showers cannot drown you like tubs.
options.feedback: The five-minute seizure timer belongs strictly to dry land: a supine body sealing a single floor drain turns an open shower into a rising drowning pool in seconds.

options.label: Hold their limbs steady until shaking stops, then let them rest in bed once the bathroom goes quiet.
options.feedback: Restraining convulsions causes injury, quiet after shaking does not mean safe breathing, and any seizure involving water demands immediate emergency medical evaluation.

options.label: Call 911 immediately, say 'WATER' first, watch hazards, and check breathing or start CPR.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Water cancels the five-minute seizure timer on the spot, and flagging 'water' while checking breathing immediately keeps a blocked-drain floor pool from becoming fatal.

quiz.prompt: Three drops of '100% natural' tea tree oil were just dabbed onto an 80-gram pet cockatiel's feathers, and within minutes the bird looks dazed and unsteady. What is your move?

options.label: Call an avian vet or animal poison line immediately, bring the exact bottle, and skip DIY soaps or syringed water.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Lipophilic terpenes cross an 80-gram bird's skin and blood-brain barrier in minutes, and immediate avian veterinary care with the exact label beats every household remedy.

options.label: Scrub the feathers right away with household dish soap or carrier oil and syringe water to flush it out.
options.feedback: Uninstructed dish soaps, alcohol, or carrier oils can worsen dermal spread or chill an 80-gram patient, and syringing liquids or inducing vomiting risks oily aspiration into fragile avian air sacs.

options.label: Wait it out in a quiet cage—it is plant-derived, only three drops, and nowhere near a toxic human dose.
options.feedback: Fat-soluble plant defense toxins do not care about amber wellness bottles: three drops on an 80-gram body mass can drive coma, convulsions, and widespread cellular lysis within 30 minutes.

quiz.prompt: Weeks after surviving immune TTP, you feel completely fine and your platelet count has recovered—yet your prescribed therapy is expensive and tempting to stop. What keeps relapse at bay?

options.label: Pause the prescription until bruising returns—recovered platelets and feeling great confirm full remission.
options.feedback: A bounced-back platelet count can sit right on top of stubborn ADAMTS13 inhibitors priming an asymptomatic Day-51 relapse—feeling fine is not immune remission.

options.label: Keep taking prescribed TTP therapy, flag cost barriers early, and track platelets plus ADAMTS13.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Tracking ADAMTS13 activity alongside platelets—and raising cost or pharmacy hurdles with hematology before missing doses—shuts down silent microvascular relapse.

options.label: Skip follow-up unless routine head CT, creatinine, or aPTT turn abnormal, since those flag TTP early.
options.feedback: Immune TTP can rage behind a spotless head CT and normal creatinine or aPTT while shearing red blood cells and packing microvessels with platelet clots.

quiz.prompt: Hours after sharing freshly caught, piping-hot barracuda that tasted spotless, your lips tingle, dizziness hits, and grabbing a glass of ice water burns like fire. What is your move?

options.label: Go straight to an ER, name the reef fish and meal time, warn dining companions, and plan a six-month trigger ban.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Cold-burns-like-fire allodynia is ciguatera's calling card, and prompt ER care handles sudden bradycardia and low pressure while warning everyone who shared the heat-proof platter.

options.label: Treat it as traveler's diarrhea and wash it down with a cold beer—fresh, seared fish cannot cause poisoning.
options.feedback: P-CTX-1 is odorless, tasteless, and completely heat-proof, so ice chests and searing pans touch nothing—and alcohol only dislodges fat-stored toxin to flare nerve symptoms harder.

options.label: Stay home unless companions fall ill too, and drink iced coffee to shake off the lightheadedness.
options.feedback: Lightheadedness after reef predators can signal vagal bradycardia slowing the heart toward 41 bpm, and caffeine is a classic trigger that kicks ciguatoxin nerve firing back into overdrive.

quiz.prompt: Four hours after an excess extended-release bupropion (XL) ingestion, the patient is chatting calmly with a tight 94-millisecond QRS—while a rapid urine screen blames amphetamines. What is the safe call?

options.label: Clear them for discharge since four hours have passed with calm conversation and a normal 94-ms QRS.
options.feedback: Osmotic XL polymer shells run on a slow zero-order fuse: nearly half of delayed bupropion seizures hit out of nowhere between Hours 8 and 24 alongside sudden cardiogenic shock.

options.label: Flag 'XL / extended-release' to override the false amphetamine screen and keep continuous monitoring for 24 hours.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Calling out the XL formulation cuts straight past misleading amphetamine screens and locks in the mandatory 24-hour hospital telemetry watch before delayed seizures or connexin-43 shock arrive.

options.label: Pivot strictly to illicit amphetamine toxicity and sign out once the early screening panels look calm.
options.feedback: Rapid urine immunoassays routinely misread bupropion as amphetamines, and chasing that decoy while leaving early drops telemetry right before active hydroxybupropion surges.

quiz.prompt: After eating a gold foil packet of '100% pure' gas-station Royal Honey, traffic lights suddenly glow neon blue while you are driving and dizziness hits—and you carry nitroglycerin. What do you do?

options.label: Keep driving home and take nitroglycerin if chest tightness hits—pure rainforest honey can't clash with heart meds.
options.feedback: Counterfeit truck-stop vitality sachets routinely pack 60–150 mg of undeclared sildenafil; stacking organic nitrates atop hidden PDE5 blockade triggers runaway cGMP vasodilation and lethal hypotension.

options.label: Pull over briefly to blink away the blue tint, toss the foil packet, and drink grapefruit juice to steady yourself.
options.feedback: Tossing the packet hides a slow-releasing honey depot from ER doctors, and grapefruit juice blocks CYP3A4—cranking circulating sildenafil higher and flooding retinal PDE6 blue cones even harder.

options.label: Pull over safely, lie flat with legs elevated, keep the foil packet, and call 911—warning EMS before any nitrates.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Neon-blue vision is a flashing overdose flare for hidden sildenafil, and warning paramedics upfront prevents a fatal nitrate crash while protecting brain perfusion through viscous honey's prolonged drop.

quiz.prompt: After escaping a closed room filled with smoldering polyurethane couch-cushion smoke, a victim has zero skin burns, nobody smells bitter almonds, and a finger oximeter reads 99%. What is your move?

options.label: Trust the 99% pulse oximeter and lack of bitter-almond odor—have them rest indoors and drink fluids.
options.feedback: Standard finger clips read carboxyhemoglobin as oxygen, half the population cannot smell bitter almonds, and smoldering polyurethane releases cyanide that bolts mitochondrial Complex IV shut behind a smug 99%.

options.label: Stay in fresh air, call 911, report smoldering couch foam, and demand 100% O₂ plus co-oximetry and whole-blood lactate.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Naming nitrogen-rich upholstery smoke flags dual carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning immediately so teams run co-oximetry and arterial lactate instead of trusting a blind finger clip.

options.label: Duck back inside quickly to drag out the smoldering cushions, and go to the ER only if burns or cherry-red veins appear.
options.feedback: Re-entering an enclosed smoke room without professional breathing apparatus risks hydrogen-cyanide collapse in seconds, and severe cellular asphyxiation needs zero skin burns to kill.

quiz.prompt: Your seared tuna loin arrived piping hot and smelled completely fresh, yet mid-meal it tastes sharply metallic and peppery—and your friend across the table starts wheezing and feeling lightheaded. What is your first move?

options.label: Keep eating—the fish was seared piping hot and didn't smell off, so your friend must have a new seafood allergy.
options.feedback: Scombroid histamine doesn't care how aggressively the chef seared the tuna, and it rarely bothers to smell fishy. Bacterial histidine decarboxylation produces heat-stable histamine that laughs at the grill.

options.label: Toss the suspect plates, wait for fresh fillets, and let a clinic blood test prove what happened later.
options.feedback: Ditching the fillet destroys the best forensic evidence because blood histamine fades fast while the rest of that thawed loin keeps dosing the dinner rush. Meanwhile, wheezing and lightheadedness demand emergency airway care, not a menu swap.

options.label: Spit it out, stop the table, call 911 for breathing trouble, and save the fish while alerting the kitchen.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Treat airway trouble or dizziness like anaphylaxis immediately, save a sample of the fish because blood histamine vanishes quickly, and pull that loin off the line before anyone else gets dosed.

quiz.prompt: Someone tumbles off a wobbly ladder onto the top of their head, leaving only a tiny two-inch scalp cut and a smooth-feeling skull—yet they are awake, breathing normally, and feel midline neck stiffness. What do you do?

options.label: Call 911 immediately and keep them completely still as found so EMS can protect the cervical spine for CT imaging.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! A crown impact can wedge-burst the C1 Atlas ring beneath a trivial scalp cut, so keeping a breathing patient motionless until EMS arrives prevents catastrophic spinal shift.

options.label: Help them upright, gently rotate their head side to side to 'clear' the neck, and clean the two-inch cut at home since the skull feels smooth.
options.feedback: A smooth skull hides an occult Jefferson burst fracture plus C2 and C5–C6 breaks completely—and twisting an unstable cervical ring is a disastrous way to test range of motion.

options.label: Build a snug rolled-towel collar around their neck and straighten their head to neutral before driving them to urgent care.
options.feedback: Improvised towel or cardboard collars shift broken bone and raise intracranial pressure—and unless fire, traffic, or failed breathing demands action, forcing an angled head straight makes things worse.

quiz.prompt: Someone just squeezed a tiny 'kitten-sized' drop from a dog's spot-on permethrin flea tube onto a kitten's neck, and now the kitten is twitching and tremoring. What is your immediate move?

options.label: Monitor at home—since it was only a tiny drop scaled down from the dog's dose, the twitching should wear off safely.
options.feedback: Cats are not miniature dogs; deficient feline hepatic glucuronidation leaves permethrin locking voltage-gated sodium channels open until status epilepticus takes over.

options.label: Immediately wrestle the tremoring kitten under the kitchen tap for a thorough dish-soap scrub before calling anyone.
options.feedback: Coat decontamination matters, but wrestling a panicked, tremoring cat into water before vet clearance worsens seizures and aspiration risk—always get explicit vet approval before touching the faucet.

options.label: Call the emergency vet immediately with the signs and exact product, bring the tube, and ask before bathing.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Calling the emergency vet first with the exact permethrin concentration gets anti-seizure triage rolling and tells you whether washing right now is safe.

options.label: Plug your pulse and temperature into an online hospital sepsis chart like NICE NG253 to see if you qualify before calling anyone.
options.feedback: Hospital risk pathways are not DIY reassurance apps; while you self-score on a laptop, dysregulated sepsis lights up leaky E-selectin-activated vessels from the lungs to the brain.

options.label: Take a leftover antibiotic from the cupboard and wait until morning to see if the fever and shivering break.
options.feedback: Leftover pills cannot seal an intestinal perforation or halt systemic vascular leak—waiting to see how morning looks hands multi-organ failure an overnight head start.

options.label: Call 911/999 or get to the ER now, leading immediately with the recent bowel surgery, infection, and newest confusion.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Calling immediately and naming the infection or surgical trigger puts monitored hospital resuscitation and clinician-directed antimicrobials ahead of fulminant septic shock.

quiz.prompt: A crusted scalp sore keeps bleeding, changing, and refusing to heal—and you figure a surface skin spot cannot be lethal if it hasn't spread to internal organs. What is the smartest move?

options.label: Book a prompt clinical exam without trying to self-diagnose, and follow through on any recommended tissue biopsy.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! You are the smoke alarm, not the fire investigator—an early biopsy catches locally invasive squamous cell carcinoma long before it erodes bone or triggers fatal clots.

options.label: Give the bleeding scab another 28 days to heal, since a surface skin lesion without distant spread cannot threaten your life.
options.feedback: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma needs zero distant metastases to kill; left untreated, it can erode full-thickness through the skull and unleash pulmonary embolism or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

options.label: Rely on a visual inspection alone and skip a biopsy if the spot merely looks like an irritated surface scrape.
options.feedback: Naked-eye confidence regularly misfires—per the AAD, visual inspection alone cannot definitively classify a suspicious lesion, and only tissue biopsy unlocks curative early treatment.

quiz.prompt: A child becomes silently entangled by the neck in a low-hung homemade cloth hammock whose soft fabric sits low enough for feet to touch the floor. What is the critical first-60-seconds sequence?

options.label: Slash the cloth free as fast as possible without catching their weight, then offer water and hunt for a neck pulse before dialing.
options.feedback: Cutting a suspended child loose into an uncontrolled fall risks severe head or neck injury, while offering water or hunting for pulses burns precious resuscitation seconds.

options.label: Put emergency dispatch on speaker, support the child's weight while freeing the neck, and start CPR if breathing fails.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Soft low-hung cloth still occludes jugular veins and airways silently—supporting body weight during release and starting immediate CPR when breathing fails protects the brain.

options.label: Skip urgent hospital assessment once untangled if blood pressure looks steady or an early CT scan seems likely to read normal.
options.feedback: Reassuring blood pressure and even two normal early brain CT scans can miss severe hypoxic encephalopathy (down to SpO₂ 47%)—hospital evaluation is mandatory, and the fabric loop must be permanently removed.

quiz.prompt: You cut >90%-silica engineered-quartz countertops in a clean-looking shop, swap respirator filters every week, and haven't coughed once. How do you actually protect your lungs?

options.label: Keep dry-cutting since weekly filter swaps handle the dust, and hold off telling your doctor until a cough starts.
options.feedback: Respirable crystalline silica kills alveolar macrophages in a silent collagen-scarring cycle long before a cough shows up, and a lone dust mask loses badly against dry-cut clouds.

options.label: Blow silica off tools and work clothes at shift's end with compressed air and finish with a brisk dry broom sweep.
options.feedback: Compressed air hoses and dry brooms don't remove respirable silica—they relaunch microscopic quartz needles right back into breathing height for a second lap inside your lungs.

options.label: Demand wet cutting, source ventilation, and HEPA cleanup, wear a fit-tested mask, and name quartz to your doctor.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Putting water on the blade stops silica at the source while naming the exact >90%-silica stone gets medical surveillance started before progressive massive fibrosis steals your breath.

quiz.prompt: Mid-bite of soft food like a banana, an adult at the table suddenly cannot speak, makes zero coughing sound, and grabs their chest. What is your immediate move?

options.label: Put 911 on speaker immediately and alternate 5 sharp back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts—switching to CPR if they become unresponsive.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Complete food airway obstruction is often dead silent ('café coronary'), and rapid 5-and-5 rescue—plus an ER exam even after clearing—breaks the seal safely.

options.label: Assume it is a sudden heart attack rather than choking because banana is soft and choking victims make loud coughing noises.
options.feedback: Soft food seals the vocal cords just as tightly as steak, and complete obstruction silences the cough completely—which is why 'café coronaries' routinely masquerade as heart attacks.

options.label: Do a blind finger sweep down the throat to hook the banana out, and skip the ER once their breathing returns.
options.feedback: A blind finger sweep risks ramming lodged food deeper into the airway, and even successful thrusts require medical evaluation for hidden internal trauma or retained fragments.

quiz.prompt: On an autumn pasture bordered by sycamore maples, a horse develops sudden stiffness, tremors, and a low head carriage—even though he is still munching hay and the seedlings were sprayed last month. What do you do first?

options.label: Wait it out—if he's still eating hay, his urine looks lighter, and those little seedlings were sprayed dead last month, the risk is over.
options.feedback: Dead sprayed sycamore seedlings keep their hypoglycin A intact, and a horse willing to nibble hay can still be pouring 804,101 IU/L of muscle enzyme into its blood from acquired MADD.

options.label: Immediately rush the trembling 500-kg horse up a steep trailer ramp and drive to the clinic before calling anyone.
options.feedback: Forcing failing, dissolving muscles to balance on a steep moving trailer spikes stress and risks collapse—always get equine vet transport instructions before loading.

options.label: Call the equine vet now with the timeline and nearby sycamore trees, ask before trailering, and protect pasture mates.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Immediate equine vet triage avoids trailer collapse on dying muscles and protects every herd mate sharing the same hypoglycin A pasture.

quiz.prompt: Your pet rabbit suddenly turns quiet, hunched, and stops leaving normal droppings—a picture that looks just like routine 'mild gas' or everyday GI stasis. What is your first move?

options.label: Give leftover gut-motility meds and unguided syringe-feeding from a home stasis kit overnight, then call a vet tomorrow.
options.feedback: Dosing motility drugs or force-feeding before a physical vet exam can turn fatal when 'routine stasis' is actually secondary to an obstruction or a twisted, necrotic caudate liver lobe.

options.label: Relax if her temperature is normal at 38.3 °C and early screening shows only mild gas and normal kidney blood labs.
options.feedback: A rabbit can sit at a textbook 38.3 °C with mild gut gas and normal kidney blood values while caudate liver lobe torsion drops hematocrit to 10.7% alongside severe cystic kidney destruction.

options.label: Get same-day exotic vet care for reduced eating or droppings, holding all motility drugs until an exam.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Same-day exotic veterinary assessment backed by exact food and litter-tray counts catches surgical mimics like liver lobe torsion before internal bleeding wins.

quiz.prompt: A splash of hydrofluoric-acid rust remover hits three fingertips, leaving only a pale, unblistered smudge with none of the instant sting of battery acid. What is your immediate survival sequence?

options.label: Give it a quick rinse and carry on—with no blisters, charring, or immediate sting, your skin barrier stopped the splash.
options.feedback: Neutral lipophilic HF (pKa 3.17) slips quietly across intact skin, dissociates 17,000:1 at pH 7.4, turns blood calcium into precipitate, and stretches cardiac QTc straight toward ventricular fibrillation.

options.label: Flush relentlessly with water, call 911 naming hydrofluoric acid, apply calcium gluconate gel, and get ECG monitoring.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Naming HF out loud triggers limb-safe 2.5% calcium gluconate—never peripheral calcium chloride—plus continuous QTc and ionized electrolyte monitoring before silent fluoride stops the heart.

options.label: Skip the water rinse so you don't spread the smudge, wait for blisters before calling anyone, and ask the ER for peripheral calcium chloride.
options.feedback: Delaying copious water flushing leaves unreacted HF soaking deeper into tissue, and peripheral or intra-arterial calcium chloride destroys limbs—calcium gluconate is the safe antidote.

quiz.prompt: Shortly after stirring a single teaspoon of unblended Turkish Black Sea rhododendron honey into boiling herbal tea, cold sweats, nausea, and severe dizziness hit as your pulse crashes toward 38 beats a minute. What do you do?

options.label: Lie flat immediately, call 911, and tell paramedics and ER clinicians out loud about the artisanal rhododendron honey jar.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Lying flat protects brain perfusion through 70/40 hypotension and AV block, and naming the honey guides the ER straight to 0.5–1.0 mg IV atropine instead of a misdirected heart-attack chase.

options.label: Walk it off and brew another hot mug—boiling tea neutralized any plant toxins, and honey from those same mountains was fine last spring.
options.feedback: Boiling water doesn't touch grayanotoxins, unblended batches vary wildly from season to season, and standing up with complete AV block and 70/40 blood pressure puts you on the floor.

options.label: Drive yourself to a clinic and leave out the honey so doctors focus straight on the ST-segment elevation.
options.feedback: Driving during vagal-reflex bradycardia risks sudden syncope behind the wheel, and hiding the honey leaves a 15-nanomolar Bezold-Jarisch fakeout disguised as a blocked coronary artery.
