quiz.prompt: While taking a 'natural' traditional herbal slimming capsule, you develop swelling, nausea, fatigue, and rising blood pressure—though a lab test on today's commercial bottles came back completely negative. What should you do?

options.label: Keep taking the capsules since it is a traditional plant blend and today's commercial bottles tested clean.
options.feedback: Botanical substitutions happen by batch—testing today's clean bottle misses the mislabeled Aristolochia lot you swallowed, which can scar kidneys shut in 90 days and bolt permanent dA-AL-I adducts onto DNA.

options.label: Stop the supplement immediately, bag the exact leftover capsules for lot testing, and get urgent serum creatinine, eGFR, and urinalysis.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Saving the exact pills you consumed is the only way to catch a botanical swap, and urgent kidney labs—plus long-term urologic follow-up if confirmed—guard against fibrosis and urothelial cancer.

options.label: Flush the leftover capsules down the toilet right away to protect everyone at home and drink herbal detox teas to support your kidneys.
options.feedback: Flushing the bottle destroys the sole forensic evidence of an Aristolochia fangchi swap, and chasing rapid interstitial renal fibrosis with unverified detox teas only compounds the risk.

quiz.prompt: Midway through mowing your yard, a sudden sharp sting hits your upper belly. You shut the mower off, lift your shirt, and see spotless skin with zero blood, yet the deep pain stays severe. What is your move?

options.label: Ice the sore spot on the couch and watch overnight for a bruise, since a real metal puncture would leave an obvious bleeding wound.
options.feedback: Elastic skin and fat can snap shut behind a 200-mph wire like self-healing rubber, hiding peritoneal penetration while bowel contamination brews silently.

options.label: Seek immediate emergency medical evaluation and tell triage plainly that you felt a sudden strike or sting while mowing the lawn.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Spotless skin and calm early vitals never outrank sudden severe abdominal pain, and naming the mower triggers targeted imaging before complications start.

options.label: Press a clean magnifying glass and tweezers over the tender patch first to check for a splinter before deciding whether to visit urgent care.
options.feedback: Bathroom tweezers cannot detect a 7-centimeter wire buried beneath muscle and peritoneum, and probing tiny punctures introduces bacteria or dislodges vessel tamponade.

quiz.prompt: Right after a hard sneezing fit, a dark ink-like cloud drops across your right eye. There is zero pain, your eye looks completely normal in the mirror, and it is late evening. What should you do?

options.label: Wait until morning to see if the cloud clears on its own, because true retinal emergencies always cause sharp pain and visible eye redness.
options.feedback: The retina has zero somatic pain receptors, so severe hemorrhage or retinal detachment can unfold completely painlessly behind a spotless cornea.

options.label: Gently massage the closed eyelid and try bearing down once to test whether the shadow moves before driving yourself to an optometrist.
options.feedback: Pressing on the globe or repeating a Valsalva strain risks worsening intraocular bleeding, and driving with acute monocular vision loss endangers everyone on the road.

options.label: Have someone else drive you immediately to an emergency room or urgent eye clinic for dilated specialist assessment, despite the lack of pain.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! A painless dark cloud after a sneeze demands urgent specialist evaluation because neither a normal mirror check nor zero pain rules out retinal injury.

quiz.prompt: One of your two lean nine-month-old guinea pigs develops a cloudy eye and ravenous appetite without extra thirst, while her sister looks spotless. What is the safest first step?

options.label: Schedule prompt exotic veterinary evaluation for the cloudy eye, keep normal high-fiber hay flowing, and avoid DIY fasting or home dosing.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Diabetes in guinea pigs can strike without excess thirst, a clear-eyed sibling can hide worse glucose, and sudden fasting risks lethal GI stasis.

options.label: Cut out hay and pellets for 24 hours to reset blood sugar while watching whether her water bottle starts draining faster than usual.
options.feedback: Withholding food from a hindgut-fermenting guinea pig can trigger fatal gastrointestinal stasis and hepatic lipidosis within 48 hours—far faster than high glucose.

options.label: Relax for a few weeks because young lean guinea pigs rarely get diabetes, and a negative home urine strip rules out dangerous crashes.
options.feedback: Suspected type 1 diabetes strikes young lean guinea pigs without obvious thirst, and negative urine strips cannot detect insulin-driven hypoglycemia or hidden hyperglycemia in a cage-mate.

quiz.prompt: A toddler reaches behind a running home treadmill and pulls back with a postage-stamp-sized red friction burn over two knuckles that is barely bleeding at all. What is your next step?

options.label: Press an ice cube onto the knuckles, dab on soothing home ointment, and bandage it since the tiny, dry scrape spared deeper blood vessels.
options.feedback: Frictional heat cauterizes tiny capillaries to hide deep full-thickness joint damage, while ice chokes off surviving blood supply and ointments trap heat and bacteria.

options.label: Skip ice and home creams, keep any stuck fabric untouched, and take the child promptly for professional medical burn assessment of joint depth.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Postage-stamp 0.3% treadmill burns can expose finger tendons and joint capsules with almost no bleeding, making prompt specialist wound depth assessment essential.

options.label: Wash the blister gently, snip away loose dead skin with clean scissors, and tape a popsicle-stick splint across the knuckles until a checkup next week.
options.feedback: Never perform home debridement or makeshift splinting on a pediatric friction burn—only sterile specialist evaluation can protect joint capsules and prevent cooling scar contractures.

quiz.prompt: You feel completely normal—calm pulse, zero tremors—yet routine blood work prints a flatlined TSH of 0.02 and sky-high free T4 while you take daily hair-and-nails vitamins. What is the right call?

options.label: Stop all prescription medications and supplements for exactly one week on your own, then assume any remaining abnormal thyroid test is also a false alarm.
options.feedback: Never alter prescriptions or invent a solo washout calendar without physician oversight, and taking biotin never grants immunity against genuine coexisting thyroid disease.

options.label: Accept immediate antithyroid drugs or ablation because three calibrated lab values pointing in the exact same biological direction cannot all be wrong together.
options.feedback: Free biotin breaks both sandwich assays (falsely low TSH) and competitive assays (falsely high free T4/T3) simultaneously, forging an internally consistent fake Graves’ profile.

options.label: Show your doctor exact supplement labels disclosing biotin dose and timing so the care team and lab director can verify whether the assay is vulnerable.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Disclosing vitamin B7 lets clinicians and the lab check streptavidin-biotin interference and retest safely on an unaffected platform before treating a ghost.

quiz.prompt: Your three-year-old ferret suddenly goes limp in the hind legs, drools heavily, and starts seizing on the living-room floor, even though he played normally yesterday. What do you do right now?

options.label: Keep all fingers and liquids out of his mouth, move him off high surfaces clear of hard objects, and transport him immediately to emergency veterinary care.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Protecting his airway from aspiration while getting immediate emergency IV stabilization avoids turning a metabolic crash into fatal pneumonia.

options.label: Squirt a syringe of honey water into the side of his mouth immediately to raise blood sugar, then stay home if he perks up playfully by morning.
options.feedback: Seizing ferrets lose protective swallow reflexes so forced liquid pours into the lungs—and bouncing back on Tuesday never means the underlying insulinoma vanished.

options.label: Record a clear two-minute video of the seizure first, then fast him for several hours before his clinic visit so the veterinarian can witness a real crash.
options.feedback: Delaying transport for footage or purposefully provoking a hypoglycemic crash risks irreversible brain injury or death when your spoken history already guides testing.

quiz.prompt: At a crowded train station, a commuter tumbles down a moving escalator, bangs their head on steel steps, catches a jacket hem near the comb plate, and then insists they feel fine while sitting up dazed. What do you do?

options.label: Yank the trapped jacket straight out of the comb plate yourself and let them catch their train once they prove they can talk and stand.
options.feedback: Reaching into moving comb plates invites severe hand amputation, and an awake rider after a metal-step head strike can still harbor a lethal, slow-pooling cerebral bleed.

options.label: Keep hands out of the machinery, summon station staff and emergency care for head-strike assessment, and report only the exact sequence you actually witnessed.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Avoiding DIY machinery extraction, getting professional evaluation for blunt head trauma, and giving pure eyewitness facts protect both life and investigation.

options.label: Tell paramedics the escalator definitely jerked violently—even though you only looked up after hearing a shout—so engineers shut down the station immediately.
options.feedback: Inventing a mechanical failure you never witnessed misdirects engineers and can blind trauma clinicians to an internal pre-fall cardiac event that actually triggered the collapse.

quiz.prompt: You are a fit 43-year-old non-smoker with zero family heart history. While resting quietly, sudden heavy central chest pain starts radiating down your left arm, though you are not sweating or breathless. What happens next?

options.label: Call emergency medical services immediately instead of driving yourself, knowing that SCAD can strike healthy adults without sweating or ECG changes.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Calling EMS brings cardiac monitoring straight to your door and keeps you from losing consciousness behind the wheel during an occult NSTEMI.

options.label: Wait an hour on the couch and take a brisk walk test, since real heart attacks require cold sweats, nausea, shortness of breath, or high cholesterol.
options.feedback: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection routinely hits patients with zero conventional risk factors and zero secondary symptoms—waiting or straining risks lethal progression.

options.label: Drive yourself to an urgent-care clinic for a quick ECG and head straight home relieved if the first electrical tracing prints normal sinus rhythm.
options.feedback: Driving with acute ischemia risks fatal arrhythmia in traffic, and a spotless 12-lead ECG cannot rule out an NSTEMI that only serial troponin and imaging expose.

quiz.prompt: Your solitary female leopard gecko has stopped eating for a week, developed a swollen belly, and stalled mid-shed. Her enclosure mate list is zero. What is your safest next move?

options.label: Mist the tank heavily, boost basking heat, and wait two more weeks because solitary geckos cannot form eggs.
options.feedback: Female leopard geckos readily ovulate and shell infertile eggs without ever meeting a male, and a stuck shed during anorexia signals systemic dehydration rather than merely dry air.

options.label: Leave her abdomen completely untouched and schedule prompt exotic-veterinary imaging and blood work with her baseline log.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Avoiding home squeezing prevents catastrophic oviduct rupture, while imaging and blood work separate egg retention from follicular stasis, sand impaction, or organ disease.

options.label: Gently press along her lower belly to feel for eggs and administer oral liquid calcium to force smooth-muscle contractions.
options.feedback: Manual abdominal pressure risks tearing an inflamed oviduct into fatal coelomitis, and blind calcium dosing without diagnosing pre- versus post-ovulatory disease can worsen an acute crisis.

quiz.prompt: Your three-month-old is crying inconsolably with no fever. You pull off a footie sleeper and find the middle toe bright red and puffy past the base crease, with no hair visible anywhere. What should you do?

options.label: Spread over-the-counter hair-removal cream into the skin crease for five minutes to dissolve any invisible keratin strand.
options.feedback: Home depilatory creams are caustic on swollen, compromised infant skin and never guarantee complete release when deep inflammation or non-hair fabric fibers are involved.

options.label: Watch the toe at home for 24 hours and only go to the emergency room if the skin turns cold, pale, or purple.
options.feedback: Aftercare watchlists apply strictly after professional medical treatment—waiting on an untreated strangulated digit risks progressive ischemia and tissue loss.

options.label: Assume a buried tourniquet exists despite seeing no hair, drop all household tools, and seek prompt ER care.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Swollen skin folds over fine threads like rising dough, so magnified clinical exploration—and soft-tissue release if needed—protects the digit safely.

quiz.prompt: Two months after a gastric sleeve, your 22-year-old sister—who takes her oral vitamins daily and is not vomiting—develops worsening leg weakness, jerky eye movements, and mild confusion. What is the critical action?

options.label: Go immediately to emergency care, lead with her gastric sleeve date and family-observed confusion, and let doctors evaluate for urgent IV thiamine.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Compliant oral supplements and normal outward weight never guarantee thiamine absorption, and BOMSS guidelines call for prompt IV thiamine without waiting for lab or MRI confirmation.

options.label: Double her over-the-counter oral multivitamins at home and wait for her scheduled annual bariatric nutrition appointment to test blood levels.
options.feedback: When gut absorption or utilization is already failing behind a gastric sleeve, waiting on extra oral pills allows preventable central nervous system energy starvation to leave lasting memory deficits.

options.label: Assume a urinary tract infection or multiple sclerosis explains the confusion if her initial brain MRI looks atypical for classic vitamin deficiency.
options.feedback: A UTI cannot explain torsional or upbeat nystagmus, and classic acute Wernicke’s MRI sensitivity is only about 53%—meaning an atypical scan never rules out brain thiamine starvation.

quiz.prompt: Your three-year-old African pygmy hedgehog develops fast, labored breathing alongside a firm swelling under her neck and a visible lump near her upper jaw. What is the smartest immediate action?

options.label: Gently pry her mouth open with a cotton swab to check for stuck kibble, then wait a day since over half of oral lumps are just inflammation.
options.feedback: Forcing open a stressed prey mammal’s tiny jaw risks severe trauma and fractures, and waiting on rapid labored breathing is dangerous regardless of whether a mass is cancerous or inflammatory.

options.label: Assume the mouth mass is incurable cancer spreading to a neck lymph node and begin syringe force-feeding at home to stop weight loss.
options.feedback: Neither eyes nor fingers can tell cancer from suppurative inflammation or spot two separate primary tumors, and unguided syringe force-feeding risks fatal aspiration.

options.label: Call an exotic emergency veterinarian right away for transport guidance, leaving oral exams and lump diagnostics to the clinic.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Rapid breathing in a tiny airway demands urgent specialist assessment, and professional microscopy separates treatable inflammation from independent malignancies without DIY jaw trauma.

quiz.prompt: Eight months after a serious car crash where your Day-1 abdominal CT showed intact solid organs, you develop steadily worsening belly swelling, vomiting, and two days without passing gas or stool. What is your safest move?

options.label: Drink large volumes of electrolyte solution and an over-the-counter laxative to flush out a stubborn stool backup since your crash CT was clear.
options.feedback: Forcing fluid and laxatives against an unrecognized fibrotic bowel stricture raises intraluminal back-pressure and heightens the risk of catastrophic intestinal perforation.

options.label: Seek urgent emergency department assessment—calling an ambulance if pain is severe—and report both your symptoms and the prior car crash.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! A Day-1 CT captures only one moment in time and cannot rule out delayed ischemic scarring from mesenteric trauma, while inability to pass gas or stool with swelling is a classic obstruction emergency.

options.label: Wait another couple of months before seeing a surgeon because delayed seatbelt bowel obstructions typically take a full two years to become dangerous.
options.feedback: A single case report’s two-year timeline is historical documentation, never a safe waiting window—complete obstruction with vomiting requires immediate medical reassessment.

quiz.prompt: An elderly relative taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation suddenly develops huge dark bruises across her torso and arms without falling, along with profound fatigue. What is the safest immediate plan?

options.label: Seek urgent emergency care right away with her full medication list, without stopping or changing her prescribed doses yourself.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Extensive unexplained bruising can signal severe anemia or an occult autoimmune inhibitor hiding behind blood thinners, and holding or reversing anticoagulants safely requires inpatient monitoring and specialized assays.

options.label: Stop her warfarin for three days at home to run a washout test and see whether new bruises quit appearing before bothering the clinic.
options.feedback: Stopping prescribed blood thinners solo creates dangerous stroke risk while leaving potentially catastrophic hidden anemia or an acquired Factor VIII inhibitor completely untreated.

options.label: Wait for her next routine INR fingerstick next week because a therapeutic warfarin INR proves no separate clotting catastrophe can exist.
options.feedback: The patient in Chen’s case had a completely therapeutic INR of 2.7 while her PTT timed out past 180 seconds from a Factor VIII inhibitor—a normal INR never clears intrinsic-pathway hemorrhage.

quiz.prompt: Your young indoor cat suddenly starts crying in pain, dragging both back legs, and breathing fast with cold, bluish back paws. What is your safest move in the first 60 seconds?

options.label: Wrap his cold hind legs snugly in a warm heating pad and gently massage his thighs to encourage blood circulation back down to his toes.
options.feedback: Heating an ischemic limb boosts tissue oxygen demand while the aorta stays blocked—accelerating cellular death—and massaging starved nerves causes excruciating pain without dissolving a clot.

options.label: Check for a groin pulse yourself and wait an hour to see whether he bruised his spine jumping off furniture, since young kittens rarely get heart clots.
options.feedback: Aortic saddle clots can strike even a seven-month-old kitten with normal heart wall thickness, and wrestling a terrified cat for pulses triggers lethal catecholamine surges while burning critical time.

options.label: Keep handling minimal and calm, leave the legs unheated and unrubbed, and call an emergency veterinary hospital immediately for transport guidance.

quiz.prompt: While pouring a backyard patio, wet concrete sloshes over the top of your rubber boot and soaks your sock. Your leg barely stings yet. What is the single safest move right now?

options.label: Stop immediately, pull off the boot and soaked sock, flush the skin thoroughly with copious cool running water, and get hospital burn evaluation.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Wet cement spikes to pH 10–14 and silently saponifies tissue with delayed pain, so immediate removal, heavy water irrigation, and hospital evaluation stop deep liquefactive necrosis.

options.label: Splash household vinegar or diluted muriatic acid inside the boot first to neutralize the alkaline pH, then rinse briefly after finishing the pour.
options.feedback: Pouring acid onto alkaline calcium hydroxide triggers a violently exothermic neutralization reaction, inflicting a severe thermal burn straight on top of chemical tissue destruction.

options.label: Finish smoothing the patio since you have no sharp pain or fever, then rub thick barrier cream over the red patch once you shower at home.
options.feedback: Alkaline cement burns destroy deep tissue quietly with normal vitals, and smearing barrier cream onto exposed skin seals residual alkali right into the wound bed.

quiz.prompt: A relative with a forgotten adrenal scan from two years ago suddenly develops drenching sweats, chest pressure, and violent pounding palpitations, while a home pulse cuff reads 76 bpm. What is the right call?

options.label: Call emergency services immediately, have them rest without driving, and report the old adrenal mass plus all medications
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Palpitations with chest pain, sweats, or faintness demand emergency ambulance care even when heart rate sits in the 70s, and the prior adrenal mass gives ER teams a critical lead.

options.label: Reassure them that a resting pulse of 76 rules out an adrenaline crisis and drive them to an urgent clinic tomorrow
options.feedback: Objective tachycardia is not required for a pheochromocytoma crisis—forceful contractility and 220/135 mmHg vasoconstriction can strike at 75 bpm, and driving during a surge risks collapse.

options.label: Give a spare beta blocker tablet at home to blunt the pounding sensation before calling a primary-care office
options.feedback: Never give a beta blocker before specialist alpha blockade in suspected pheochromocytoma—blocking beta receptors first leaves vascular alpha clamps unopposed and can trigger catastrophic pressure failure.

options.label: Gently hold the head straight back into alignment and shine a penlight deep into the left ear canal to check for wax

options.label: Call an emergency vet immediately, avoid forcing the neck straight, and pad a small carrier with rolled towels as advised

options.label: Order an over-the-counter dewormer online and wait 24 hours to see if the rabbit starts passing droppings again first

options.label: Wait another two days with rest and fluids at home since the initial emergency ultrasound already cleared the abdomen
options.feedback: Bowel gas can obscure the pancreas on early ultrasound, and untested amylase/lipase are blank spaces—not normal clearance. Waiting days risks peritonitis and septic shock.

options.label: Give over-the-counter pain relievers and monitor quietly unless a dark bruise spreads across the upper stomach wall
options.feedback: Handlebar impacts act like blunt spears that can transect the deep pancreas against the spine with minimal external bruising; masking worsening pain delays surgical rescue.

options.label: Return promptly for urgent evaluation and explicitly report ‘bicycle handlebar struck the abdomen’ plus worsening vomiting
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Naming the handlebar mechanism prompts targeted pancreatic enzyme checks and cross-sectional CT/MRI before leaking enzymes trigger septic shock.

quiz.prompt: A non-diabetic coworker who recently started an over-the-counter supplement suddenly collapses at their desk, sweating profusely and unresponsive with suspected severe low blood sugar. What should you do first?

options.label: Carefully spoon orange juice or dissolved sugar water into their mouth while waiting to see if they wake up
options.feedback: Never give oral food or drink to an unconscious or seizing person—swallowing reflexes are impaired, turning sugar water into a severe choking and aspiration hazard.

options.label: Call emergency services immediately, give nothing by mouth while unresponsive, and hand responders any known supplement details
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Calling EMS protects the airway and gets controlled IV dextrose fast, while noting recent OTC supplements like alpha-lipoic acid helps clinicians look beyond routine diabetes.

options.label: Let them lie quietly for an hour before calling for help so emergency labs can capture their natural fasting glucose level
options.feedback: Only supervised hospital teams with IV dextrose in hand draw diagnostic blood during active hypoglycemia—delaying emergency rescue at work risks seizures, brain injury, or death.

quiz.prompt: You realize your small dog has been licking human zinc oxide diaper cream off her hind legs for several days and just passed dark-red urine while looking pale and weak. What is the safest move?

options.label: Give hydrogen peroxide to force vomiting at home so remaining zinc cream clears before your regular vet opens tomorrow
options.feedback: Never induce vomiting in a weak or symptomatic dog—impaired gag reflexes risk fatal aspiration pneumonia, and red urine signals active intravascular hemolysis needing ER care now.

options.label: Tell the poison hotline she likely licked only half a teaspoon so they can confirm whether quiet home observation is safe
options.feedback: Optimistic dose guesses corrupt toxicology calculations; prolonged licking over days is an unknown cumulative exposure, and collapse/red urine already demand immediate ER triage.

options.label: Go to an emergency vet immediately, grab a label photo only if it causes zero delay, and say the licked amount is unknown
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Immediate emergency care enables blood-smear review and transfusion if needed, while honest unknown-dose reporting keeps triage safely calibrated.

quiz.prompt: An older relative who wears partial dentures suddenly stops speaking mid-meal, clutches their throat with a silent ineffective cough, and you notice their lower plate is gone. What is the right immediate action?

options.label: Call emergency services immediately on speaker, follow choking first aid, avoid blind finger sweeps, and tell responders the lower denture is missing
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Immediate emergency activation and standard choking aid save seconds, avoiding blind sweeps prevents deeper impaction, and flagging the missing denture guides hospital detection.

options.label: Reach two fingers deep into the back of their throat right away to hook and pull out the smooth plastic plate before it slips farther
options.feedback: Blind finger sweeps inside the narrowing muscular laryngopharynx can push a partial obstruction deeper and wedge an irregular denture solidly shut.

options.label: Spend two minutes checking the floor and napkins for the denture first so you do not give paramedics false information about what they swallowed
options.feedback: Never delay calling emergency services or starting choking aid during a silent airway obstruction—every oxygen-starved minute counts, and 'unaccounted for' is all responders need.

quiz.prompt: A family member with a recently placed chemotherapy port flushed regularly at an outpatient clinic suddenly develops stabbing chest pain when inhaling, shortness of breath, and a newly swollen left calf. What is the right immediate step?

options.label: Elevate the swollen calf overnight with rest and wait for Monday’s routine oncology visit unless a high fever develops
options.feedback: Sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, and unilateral leg swelling are classic red flags for DVT and pulmonary embolism—waiting risks sudden fatal cardiopulmonary collapse.

options.label: Call an emergency ambulance right away, do not drive yourself, and report the port plus recent clinic flushes at triage
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Ambulance transport protects against sudden collapse, and flagging the port and routine maintenance flushes alerts clinicians to check for hidden heparin exposure and HIT.

options.label: Drive them to urgent care yourself and ask the nurse to flush the port with saline first to make sure it is not clogged
options.feedback: Never drive someone with suspected pulmonary embolism, and never ask for or attempt improvised port manipulation before emergency clinicians evaluate clots and flush records.

quiz.prompt: Your dog raids a box of ‘pet-friendly’ iron EDTA snail bait in the yard, vomits once ten minutes later, and then starts wagging her tail and asking for water. What is the safest action?

options.label: Call a vet or animal poison helpline immediately, bring the bait package or label photo, and avoid home vomiting or antacids
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! ‘Pet-friendly’ is not a safety guarantee, and tail-wagging after early vomiting can mask iron’s deceptive Stage-2 apparent recovery while systemic absorption climbs.

options.label: Give an over-the-counter antacid tablet to coat the stomach and watch her at home for six hours since she already threw up the pellets
options.feedback: Home antacids can alter gastric pH unpredictably, early vomiting does not confirm clearance, and iron toxicity stages are never a safe six-hour home countdown.

options.label: Skip the vet if the pellets were blue and labeled pet-friendly, and schedule a routine liver check next week only if she stops eating
options.feedback: Pellet dyes change across manufacturers, ‘pet-friendly’ marketing fails against scavenging dogs, and normal early appearance can hide severe rising iron levels.

quiz.prompt: A coworker in an industrial plant suspects a splash of hydrofluoric acid on their leg, notices the patch looks gray and feels oddly painless, and asks if you should drive them to urgent care with the leaking bottle. Next move?

options.label: Bag the leaking HF bottle and soaked pants so ER doctors can verify the exact concentration on arrival.
options.feedback: Hauling leaking containers or contaminated clothing into a vehicle or ER turns an enclosed ambulance or waiting room into an active off-gassing hazard.

options.label: Activate emergency response now without waiting for pain, stay clear without HF-rated PPE, and hand responders the SDS.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Hydrofluoric acid numbs surface nerves while fluoride ions silently chelate blood calcium toward cardiac arrest—so immediate activation with the SDS, never the leaking bottle, saves lives.

options.label: Wait an hour to see if redness or severe pain develops first, since painless skin means the acid only touched the surface.
options.feedback: Waiting for pain is hydrofluoric acid’s signature trap: hydrogen ions destroy nerve endings early while systemic hypocalcemia quietly builds toward ventricular fibrillation.

options.label: State clearly that the peritoneal cavity ultrasound showed no free fluid, give exact report times, and note ongoing flank agony.

options.label: Reassure triage that the abdomen is completely clear of bleeding because both the ultrasound and urine color looked normal.

options.feedback: Never self-drive or wait for low blood pressure—adrenaline vasoconstriction can hold pressure dangerously high while a retroperitoneal bleed silently empties the tank.

options.label: Call 911 immediately without home tests or waiting clocks, and hand responders exact symptom, stool, and vomiting timelines.

quiz.prompt: Two weeks after starting oral doxycycline for a serious illness, your cat’s diarrhea stops, yet she starts drooling heavily and passively bringing up undigested food without belly heaving. What is your next move?

options.label: Crush the next antibiotic tablet into water and syringe it down slowly to confirm whether her esophagus is still open.

options.label: Withhold food-or-water swallow tests, call the vet promptly with exact drug bottles and timelines, and rush to ER if breathing changes.

options.label: Photograph the street and bag the drifting string first so police have proof, then test whether the rider can swallow water cleanly.
options.feedback: Evidence gathering never outranks emergency medical care, and forcing water down an injured throat can turn a partial tear into a full breach.

options.label: Call 911 immediately, leave embedded string untouched without tight neck wraps, and report both the cut and the head-impact fall.

quiz.prompt: A previously healthy teenager with no family history of liver disease has yellowed eyes, dark cola-colored urine, five days of vomiting, and suddenly becomes confused and hard to wake—even though an urgent-care portal two days ago showed ALT below 5. What should you do?

options.label: Call 911 for an ambulance immediately, report the jaundice, dark urine, and sudden confusion, and bring the printed lab sheet with exact units.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Sudden confusion with jaundice is a medical emergency for acute liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy, and a paradoxically low ALT never clears severe synthetic liver collapse.

options.label: Plug the ALT and bilirubin numbers into an online Wilson calculator at home and drive her to the clinic tomorrow if the ratio looks abnormal.
options.feedback: Online ratio calculators are unit-dependent ICU triage tools rather than home clearance tests, and driving a confused patient risks airway collapse or seizures en route.

options.label: Encourage oral fluids and sleep off the exhaustion since the low ALT rules out acute liver inflammation and no one in the family has liver disease.
options.feedback: Autosomal-recessive disorders hide silently in carrier families, fulminant Wilson disease paradoxically depresses ALT, and sleeping off hepatic encephalopathy can be fatal.

options.label: Leave the fish unhandled, skip blind pond chemicals, document objective timelines and recent pond changes, and contact an aquatic veterinarian promptly.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Coelomic swelling is only a non-specific check-engine light, so avoiding DIY trauma or biofilter-killing drugs while giving an aquatic vet raw observations protects both fish and pond.

quiz.prompt: A worker catches his metal ring on a moving machine bracket. The ring finger looks pale and numb with an awkwardly angled knuckle, though the skin is still attached. What should happen in the next 60 seconds?

options.label: Leave the ring untouched, skip ice packs and home pulse-ox checks, keep him from driving, and summon emergency care reporting the snag mechanism and numbness.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Numbness and an odd knuckle angle signal potential neurovascular transection and joint dislocation—leaving the ring for specialist cutters and avoiding vasoconstricting ice protects remaining tissue.

options.label: Pack the finger tightly in ice to slow swelling, carefully work the ring off with soap, and drive him to urgent care if an X-ray shows a fracture.
options.feedback: Ice causes severe vasoconstriction that accelerates ischemic tissue death, pulling the ring can sever surviving vessels, and ring avulsions routinely destroy blood flow with zero bone fracture.

options.label: Clip a home pulse oximeter onto the fingertip to verify circulation and wait two hours to see whether warmth returns before calling emergency transport.
options.feedback: Consumer oximeters cannot rule out transected digital arteries in severe soft-tissue trauma, and waiting on an imagined ischemic clock wastes irreplaceable minutes.

quiz.prompt: Six days after urgent care diagnosed a rural ranch hand’s fever, vomiting, and belly pain as a stomach bug, he suddenly starts gasping so hard he cannot finish sentences and turns pale. What happens next?

options.label: Have him restrict water intake and take a leftover water pill at home so fluid stops accumulating in his lungs while waiting for clinic labs.
options.feedback: In capillary leak syndrome, lungs flood while intravascular blood concentrates into dry sludge; home fluid restriction or diuretics can trigger fatal shock.

options.label: Call 911 immediately, keep him out of the driver’s seat, and report both the sudden breathlessness and his rural ranch and travel history to emergency teams.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Gasping with broken sentences demands EMS immediately before any reference lab can return, and sharing rural or rodent-area history breaks the early stomach-bug anchor.

options.label: Drive him back to urgent care tomorrow only if a walk-in clinic confirms rodent exposure or a reference lab returns positive hantavirus antibodies.
options.feedback: Reference-lab hantavirus ELISA can take days—returning at Day 10 in the 2026 case—and waiting for lab labels or self-driving during respiratory failure can be lethal.

options.label: Hit the call button immediately to report the exact physical change and leave the IV pump completely untouched for staff.

options.label: Relax because the nurse confirmed your blood bag matched the request form and you are type O positive, the universal blood type.

options.label: Use a deep-tissue massage gun along the hardened vein to improve drainage and wait for your scheduled follow-up next week.

options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Persistent or worsening swelling on blood thinners is the exact trigger for imaging the underlying mechanical anatomy, while chest or breathing signs require immediate emergency care.

quiz.prompt: A four-year-old suddenly begins stumbling and losing leg strength, then develops drooping eyelids and rapid, shallow breathing—with no remembered woods trip or tick bite. What is your immediate priority?

options.label: Call 911 immediately for emergency airway evaluation and report the exact onset and upward progression of weakness to clinicians.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Rapid shallow breathing and drooping eyelids signal threatened airway and diaphragm failure—emergency stabilization always comes first, even with zero recalled outdoor exposure.

options.label: Put her in a hot shower right away and spend an hour combing through her hair at home to dislodge any hidden tick before calling a doctor.

options.label: Give a leftover oral antibiotic to neutralize tick neurotoxin and monitor overnight unless she starts complaining of skin numbness.

quiz.prompt: While hand-feeding a young macaw, the silicone tube tip detaches from the syringe and disappears down her throat. Ten minutes later she is perched brightly, acting normal, and showing zero choking or vomiting. What is the safest move?

options.label: Offer a small syringe of warm formula as a ‘feeding trial’ to check whether liquid moves smoothly past the tube and wait 24 hours to see if she vomits.
options.feedback: Wait-and-see logic fails avian patients—Case 1 harbored a tube and steel hub for 7 symptom-free days—and feeding trials risk crop distension and fatal aspiration across an epiglottis-free glottis.

options.label: Gently restrain the bird on her back and use rounded household tweezers to feel for the silicone edge inside the crop before calling a clinic.
options.feedback: Blind home retrieval lacerates or punctures delicate crop mucosa, and flat-on-the-back dorsal restraint compresses abdominal air sacs.

options.label: Call an avian-capable veterinarian immediately, report the exact detached part and ingestion time, and text a photo of an identical intact syringe en route without delaying care.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Immediate specialist contact prevents waiting until necrosis or obstruction hits, confirms avian micro-instrumentation is ready, and a photo of an identical syringe helps clinicians select the right endoscope and forceps before arrival.

quiz.prompt: Someone with months of clear watery drainage strictly from the left nostril and a headache that eases when lying flat suddenly develops fever, a stiff neck, and confusion—with no skin rash. What is the safest move?

options.label: Seek immediate emergency medical care for suspected meningitis without waiting for a rash or fluid testing, and disclose the months of unilateral watery drainage and positional headache.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Fever, neck stiffness, severe headache, and confusion are immediate meningitis red flags—bacterial meningitis frequently lacks a rash, and linking unilateral clear rhinorrhea alerts clinicians to an underlying skull-base breach.

options.label: Bear down firmly to collect a sample on a deep nasal swab and taste a drop for sweetness so the urgent-care clinic can confirm CSF before starting antibiotics.
options.feedback: Straining raises intracranial pressure, deep nasal probing shoves bacteria straight toward an open skull defect, and taste tests are useless internet mythology.

options.label: Take an extra dose of over-the-counter allergy medication and wait 24 hours to see whether a classic purple rash appears, since a prior sinus CT already read chronic sinusitis.
options.feedback: A prior routine sinus CT cannot exclude a subtle sphenoid skull-base defect or meningocele, and waiting for a rash during acute neurological deterioration can turn fatal.

quiz.prompt: A patient with newly confirmed Type 1 hereditary angioedema wakes up with a swollen upper lip and feels their throat beginning to tighten. They have no itchy hives. What is the safest immediate response?

options.label: Take a double dose of antihistamine and drink a tall glass of water to test whether the airway is truly narrowing before deciding whether to drive to urgent care.
options.feedback: Waiting on antihistamines wastes precious airway minutes on a non-histamine bradykinin cascade, and a forced swallow test risks aspiration or complete laryngeal spasm.

options.label: Call emergency services immediately rather than driving, follow their specialist-prescribed HAE emergency plan, and present their bradykinin-mediated diagnosis and records at triage.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Upper-airway swelling is an immediate ambulance emergency because laryngeal edema progresses non-linearly, and clear upfront HAE documentation overrides ER allergy anchoring.

options.label: Assume it is harmless because they have no family history of throat attacks and stop taking their prescribed blood-pressure pills immediately while waiting two days for it to self-resolve.
options.feedback: Laryngeal attacks can turn fatal rapidly regardless of family history, and while ACE inhibitors require medical review and switching in HAE, airway compromise requires emergency care first.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old mechanic who often smacks stubborn fittings with the heel of his palm notices a firm lump on the pinky side of his right hand, and two months later his right ring finger turns pale, ice-cold, and numb while his left hand stays warm. What is the safest course?

options.label: Plunge both hands into ice water to record a video proving Raynaud’s phenomenon and wait until a routine appointment next month if he can still feel his wrist pulse.
options.feedback: Home cold provocation is unsafe, symmetric wrist pulses did not rule out bilateral ulnar aneurysms in the 2022 case, and new unilateral ischemia with numbness cannot wait weeks.

options.label: Reassure himself that the warm left hand proves his systemic circulation is fine, switch to thicker padded work gloves, and keep working until the lump shrinks.
options.feedback: A perfectly warm opposite hand can still hide a 7-millimeter silent aneurysm via collateral flow, and generic glove swaps cannot rescue an acutely starved fingertip.

options.label: Seek immediate emergency vascular assessment for suspected acute perfusion loss, report the exact onset time, palm lump, and tool-impact history, and stop using the palm as a striking tool.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! New unilateral pallor, coldness, and numbness starting after age 30 break benign Raynaud’s rules and fit acute perfusion red flags—demanding urgent care first and ergonomic review afterward.

quiz.prompt: An adult with known hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and partially embolized pulmonary AVMs needs a routine dental scaling next month and develops sudden mouth tingling and right-sided facial droop today—though their home pulse oximeter reads 95% and they have no fever. What is the safest plan?

options.label: Seek immediate emergency care for the acute neurological signs while telling triage upfront about the PAVM right-to-left shunt—and once recovered, keep dental care on schedule with clinician-prescribed antibiotic prophylaxis rather than canceling dentistry.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Home oximetry and zero fever never exclude a shunted brain abscess, upfront PAVM disclosure connects neurology to chest anatomy, and continuing dentistry with specialist-tailored prophylaxis prevents worse daily gum bacteremia.

options.label: Skip the ER since 95% oxygen and a normal temperature rule out a shunt complication, cancel all future dental cleanings permanently, and stop taking prescribed oral iron supplements.
options.feedback: Finger oximeters cannot detect a cerebral abscess, abandoning dentistry increases uncontrolled gum bacteremia, and observational cohort associations never justify stopping prescribed iron.

options.label: Wait at home until their family gathers every printed CT binder from prior embolizations, assuming prior coil treatment dropped their shunt risk to zero.
options.feedback: Never delay emergency neurological care for printed paperwork—lead verbally with the shunt—and partial embolization never guarantees zero residual or reperfused shunt risk.

quiz.prompt: After surviving a severe hive-free intraoperative collapse with an acute tryptase spike, a patient receives specialist confirmation of chlorhexidine allergy and must return for another procedure. What is the safest approach?

options.label: Test a drop of pharmacy chlorhexidine on their forearm for 35 minutes at home the night before surgery to confirm whether the allergy is still active.
options.feedback: Self-re-exposure at home is strictly dangerous because anaphylaxis is unpredictable and a mild past skin reaction can escalate into lethal airway or circulatory collapse; 35 minutes is also not a home-testing rule.

options.label: Bring the specialist allergy documentation directly to the pre-op huddle so clinicians and pharmacy can remove not only chlorhexidine skin prep, but also hidden exposures like coated catheters, dressings, and lubricants.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Disclosing confirmed specialist evidence lets surgical and pharmacy teams audit hidden chlorhexidine-coated devices while safely keeping tested, non-triggering anesthetics available.

options.label: Ask to be charted simply as “allergic to anesthesia” and refuse all surgical antiseptics altogether to eliminate infection-control allergens.
options.feedback: Vague “anesthesia allergy” labels lock patients out of safe, effective drugs while missing hidden antiseptics, and rejecting antiseptics altogether creates severe surgical-infection hazards when safe alternatives like povidone-iodine exist.

quiz.prompt: Five days after a mild summer fever and an evening hike, your partner wakes up dragging one leg with new back pain, though they have zero memory of a mosquito bite, can feel light touch on the foot clearly, and notice mild shortness of breath. What is the safest move?

options.label: Test their knee-jerk reflex with a kitchen spoon at home and wait until morning, since preserved foot sensation and no remembered bite point to a pulled hiking muscle.
options.feedback: Anterior horn spinal injury destroys motor neurons while leaving adjacent sensory pathways intact, most bites go unremembered, and amateur home reflex testing generates dangerous false reassurance.

options.label: Call emergency services immediately—reporting the exact fever, weakness, breathing change, and outdoor timeline—because ascending neuroinvasive weakness can threaten respiratory muscles fast.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! New unexplained weakness paired with any breathing change is a drop-everything emergency (12 of 32 paralyzed patients in Colorado needed ventilation), and concrete functional timelines guide urgent clinical localization.

options.label: Drive to an urgent-care clinic and ask only for a blood sugar and basic chemistry panel, since normal routine blood work and normal CSF glucose rule out viral spinal cord infection.
options.feedback: Routine blood summaries and CSF glucose (52 mg/dL) were completely normal in the 2024 case—viruses lack bacterial sugar metabolism, and acute weakness with breathing trouble belongs in an emergency department via EMS.

quiz.prompt: Your 10-year-old dog had a pacemaker placed three years ago for heart block and has thrived ever since. After two weeks of a new daily cough, she wakes at 2 a.m. breathing rapidly with her mouth open and bluish gums. What is the right immediate action?

options.label: Spend twenty minutes locating her original implant serial card and surgical printout before driving to the ER, since emergency vets cannot examine a paced dog without full device paperwork.
options.feedback: Never delay oxygen for paperwork—grab whatever records are handy, tell the ER she has a pacemaker when you call ahead from the road, and let clinicians stabilize her breathing first.

options.label: Gently press over the pacemaker generator under her neck skin to verify it is intact and start a low-dose blood thinner until her scheduled cardiology check in two weeks.
options.feedback: Never manipulate an implanted device or self-prescribe anticoagulants—and a flawlessly firing pacemaker still cannot prevent a pulmonary clot or stop active cyanosis.

options.label: Transport her immediately to an emergency veterinary hospital, calling ahead so an oxygen cage is ready and immediately notifying the team that she has a permanent pacemaker.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Per Cornell emergency guidance, open-mouth resting dyspnea and cyanotic gums are immediate life threats demanding urgent oxygen—and early disclosure of the implant steers both emergency stabilization and cardiology coordination.

quiz.prompt: A child with short bowel syndrome who drinks from a private home well wakes up slurring words and stumbling, though by arrival in the ER his exam looks calmer and both routine lactate and brain MRI return normal. What is the safest next step?

options.label: Advocate for full evaluation of his short-bowel history—asking specifically whether a separate D-lactate assay is being run—while keeping hydration strictly under specialist ORS guidance and having the private well tested at a state-certified laboratory.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Metabolic encephalopathy waxes and wanes, routine L-lactate assays are blind to bacterial D-lactate, plain water worsens SBS electrolyte loss, and state-certified well testing catches hidden environmental coliforms.

options.label: Take him home once a stool PCR flags norovirus, encourage extra glasses of clear well water to flush out stomach bugs, and add an over-the-counter Lactobacillus probiotic.
options.feedback: Norovirus does not explain acute ataxia, extra plain water osmotically strips electrolytes in short bowel syndrome, and unvetted Lactobacillus probiotics can literally manufacture more neurotoxic D-lactate.

options.label: Wait at home unless E. coli shows up on a hardware-store water test strip, since a normal routine lactate and ‘not detected’ E. coli prove both the child and the well are safe.
options.feedback: Routine lactate ignores D-lactate, hardware test strips cannot replace state-certified labs, and ‘not detected’ E. coli only means below the 1.0 MPN limit—this family’s well had ND E. coli alongside >200.5 MPN/100 mL total coliforms.

quiz.prompt: Two weeks after a possible HIV exposure, someone develops a persistent fever, sore throat, swollen neck glands, and an itchy chest rash. A pharmacy rapid self-test reads negative, and at an urgent clinic a 4th-generation combo screen is reactive while a supplemental antibody differentiation test is negative. What is the safest course of action?

options.label: Accept the negative pharmacy rapid test and negative supplemental antibody test as final proof that the reactive combo screen was a false alarm, and retest only if the rash lasts a month.
options.feedback: Pharmacy rapid tests and supplemental differentiation tests hunt mature antibodies—in CDC STOP data, 55 of 99 discordant reactive-screen / negative-antibody panels (55.6%) were acutely infected on RNA PCR.

options.label: Pause any prescribed prevention medications for ten days to see if antibodies show up cleanly on a repeat pharmacy test at home.
options.feedback: Never stop prescribed prevention or treatment medications to experiment with test results, and never use a single case’s ten-day seroconversion gap as a universal home countdown clock.

options.label: Ensure a molecular HIV-1 RNA viral load test is completed to break the tie, confirm exactly which clinician owns the pending result and contact plan, and stay linked to clinical care.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Discordant combo-reactive and antibody-negative results require viral RNA PCR to resolve genuine biological uncertainty—catching acute surges (like 8.7 million copies/mL) before antibodies arrive while preventing false diagnoses in the 44.4% who are uninfected.

quiz.prompt: A five-year-old dairy cow that received a prophylactic stomach magnet last year suddenly stops eating her concentrate, drops sharply in milk yield, and stands with an arched back. Her temperature is 38.6°C and an initial blood draw shows a normal white blood cell count. What is the safest action?

options.label: Pinch her withers firmly to check for a pain grunt and wait several days, since a normal white count and an existing stomach magnet rule out perforating hardware.
options.feedback: Over half of 501 hospitalized hardware-disease cattle lacked elevated WBCs, magnets cannot capture non-magnetic copper or sediment-trapped/fibrin-walled steel, and caretaker withers pinching risks worsening perforation.

options.label: Contact a veterinarian for full clinical reassessment—sharing exact dates and her known magnet history without running home pain tests—and log feed/debris observations for systemic review.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Persistent appetite/milk drops and arched-back splinting demand veterinary reassessment even with a prior magnet and normal WBC (just like Cow 2 at 38.6°C), while avoiding harmful home manipulation.

options.label: Drop a second heavy magnet down her throat yourself immediately and blame the feed supplier for a contaminated batch before any imaging or veterinary exam is done.
options.feedback: Never perform DIY device administration or declare an unproven feed batch guilty—if the culprit is copper wire or fibrin-anchored metal, a second magnet fails just like the first.

quiz.prompt: Ten days after scraping your shin on garden edging, you are taking prescribed antibiotics for mild redness when your jaw grows steadily harder to open and your neck stiffens—with no fever, and you cannot find your childhood vaccine card. What is the safest move?

options.label: Seek immediate emergency medical care without waiting to hunt for shot records, tell clinicians about the scrape and your exact uncertainty on vaccination history, and never try to pry your jaw open.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Progressive trismus and rigidity require immediate clinical diagnosis regardless of fever or antibiotics, saying ‘I don’t know’ guides safer prophylaxis protocols, and forcing a locked jaw risks injury and generalized spasms.

options.label: Finish your prescribed antibiotic course first while spending the afternoon locating your pediatric vaccination paperwork so the clinic has exact dates before evaluating you.
options.feedback: Antibiotics are a raincoat against ordinary wound bacteria—they do not neutralize unbound tetanospasmin already attacking nerves—and searching for paperwork must never delay emergency care.

options.label: Order an urgent home wound swab and antibody test to confirm Clostridium tetani before heading to the ER, since a normal white blood cell count and lack of fever argue against tetanus.
options.feedback: Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis whose swab cultures are notoriously insensitive, and the 2026 adolescent case had zero fever alongside a normal WBC of 5.08 × 10³/µL.

quiz.prompt: After emergency IV potassium rapidly restores leg strength and normalizes the ECG in a young adult with newly discovered thyrotoxic periodic paralysis (TPP), which plan reflects safe clinical science?

options.label: Discharge the patient once leg strength and serum potassium normalize around hour 12, instructing them to avoid carbohydrates completely because carbs reliably trigger every TPP episode.
options.feedback: Hour-12 normalization hid a dangerous hour-36 rebound to 6.0 mEq/L as intracellular potassium flooded back out—and 65.9% of Chang’s 135 patients had no identified trigger at all.

options.label: Confirm the trigger safely at home with a high-sugar meal challenge after discharge, keeping over-the-counter potassium pills nearby in case weakness starts.
options.feedback: Deliberately inducing hypokalemia is life-threatening—even the hospital-monitored research glucose load carried strict clinical oversight and yielded paralysis in only 18.2%—and unmonitored potassium dosing risks fatal rebound hyperkalemia.

options.label: Continue supervised electrolyte, cardiac rhythm, and clinical monitoring past initial strength recovery to catch silent rebound hyperkalemia, then transition to ongoing clinician-directed thyroid management.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Feeling strong never proves compartments have finished shifting—silent K⁺ of 6.0 mEq/L still threatens cardiac rhythm—and durable control requires supervised endocrine care.

quiz.prompt: An administrative worker at a precision-metal shop who regularly walks the production floor is diagnosed with lung ‘sarcoidosis’ from non-necrotizing granulomas, then relapses with blurred vision and slurred speech as steroids taper. What is the strongest evidence-based next step?

options.label: Bag up shop-floor dust yourself for home testing and install a stronger personal dust mask before changing anything medically, since a biopsy already proved sarcoidosis.
options.feedback: A non-necrotizing granuloma is a shared tissue pattern—not a material ID—and DIY dust baggies or guessed respirators never replace specialist testing or qualified engineering source control.

options.label: Give clinicians the full physical history of production-floor proximity and alloys used, discuss specialist immune testing (such as BeLPT) alongside individualized organ evaluation, and involve qualified occupational safety teams for source control.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Real physical proximity overrides misleading job titles, BeLPT separates beryllium-driven granulomas from idiopathic sarcoidosis, and qualified source control protects both the patient and coworkers.

options.label: Reassure yourself that administrative staff cannot inhale toxic doses and assume blood beryllium-level testing will rule out chronic beryllium disease.
options.feedback: Airborne dust ignores job titles, and CBD is an immune hypersensitivity reaction diagnosed via cellular proliferation memory (BeLPT)—not by measuring blood metal concentration.

quiz.prompt: Over several months, a patient’s trouble swallowing progresses from dry solid foods to water alongside mild weight loss, undigested regurgitation, and a wet-sounding voice after meals—despite normal blood panels and an endoscopy showing healthy pink esophageal lining. What is the right clinical takeaway?

options.label: Seek prompt specialist follow-up for functional motility evaluation (such as high-resolution manometry), because clean blood work and normal-looking lining cannot rule out failed peristalsis or a non-relaxing sphincter.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Structural scopes rule out tumors or inflammation, not failing myenteric pressure waves—and progressive solid-to-liquid dysphagia plus a wet post-meal voice demand timely functional workup.

options.label: Treat it as stubborn acid reflux using over-the-counter antacids and store-bought liquid thickeners at home, since a normal endoscopy excludes serious swallowing disorders.
options.feedback: Familiar ‘heartburn’ must never disguise progressive dysphagia, a normal mucosal lining does not test esophageal motility, and thickeners or diet changes should never be self-prescribed without formal diagnosis.

options.label: Rely on a single barium swallow alone; if liquid barium clears on time with no bird-beak sign, achalasia is ruled out.
options.feedback: In the 2026 Mirabadi case, timed barium clearing looked normal with no bird-beak sign—yet high-resolution manometry revealed Type II achalasia with 10 of 10 failed protocol swallows.

quiz.prompt: Four days into hospital treatment for equine sand colic, a horse’s follow-up abdominal radiograph drops into the ‘clearance’ bracket—yet the horse remains sweaty, stops eating, and keeps looking back at its flank. What is the right evidence-based interpretation?

options.label: Discharge the horse home with a barn-aisle exercise routine and a daily scoop of supplement powder, since radiographic clearance proves the colic cause is resolved.
options.feedback: Radiographic clearance neither guarantees zero residual sand nor cures non-sand mechanical problems—and DIY exercise or supplement regimens never replace veterinary reassessment of active pain.

options.label: Assume the pain is harmless soreness from passing sand and wait another four days before repeating radiographs, since the German clinic protocol ran on a four-day timetable.
options.feedback: Never treat a study’s four-day recheck window as a universal waiting rule—delaying reassessment of active pain risks missing surgical emergencies.

options.label: Prioritize immediate veterinary reassessment of the living horse—including ultrasound and surgical triage if needed—because an improved X-ray never excuses persistent abdominal pain.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! In the 2026 Lousberg study, a horse that achieved radiographic sand clearance still suffered severe colic requiring surgery for a right dorsal colon displacement—trust the terrain over the map.

quiz.prompt: A researcher working with live vaccinia accidentally pricks her finger through a glove during an evening bench session. Her puncture looks microscopic, and she worries an ER physician won’t recognize the strain. What is the safest immediate action?

options.label: Wash immediately, initiate the institution’s occupational exposure pathway (or go straight to emergency care for severe acute injury), explicitly report the exact agent and biosafety officer’s contact without bringing any vial or swab, and lock down contact precautions plus a 48-hour follow-up plan.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Bringing exact agent intelligence and biosafety contacts—never contaminated vials—steers clinicians past routine Staph algorithms while locking in contact precautions before viral replication escalates.

options.label: Seal the contaminated syringe in a Ziploc bag to hand straight to the ER triage nurse so clinicians can run PCR immediately, then wait six days—the historical CDC median—if the skin stays calm.
options.feedback: Never transport live pathogens into a public waiting room, and the CDC 2008 series’ 6-day median delay documented a dangerous access failure—never a safe waiting period.

options.label: Run a single surface swab on day two; if the lab returns ‘inconclusive,’ assume the wash removed all virus and return to normal duties without covering the finger.
options.feedback: Inconclusive swabs in the 2019 case lacked a human DNA adequacy signal—meaning the swab failed to capture enough cells to test—never ruling out replicating deep-tissue vaccinia.

options.label: Load him immediately into your horse trailer and haul him rapidly over rural roads to the clinic while checking up his nostrils with a flashlight before departure.
options.feedback: Never probe a bleeding horse’s nose or trailer blindly without veterinary direction—loading stress, blood-pressure spikes, or disturbing a fragile pouch clot can trigger instant fatal carotid hemorrhage.

options.label: Keep the horse quiet, avoid probing or trailering blindly, and call an emergency equine veterinarian immediately to report the bleed, timing, and any subtle breathing or swallowing signs so the vet directs exam and transport decisions.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Even a self-stopping small bleed can be a sentinel event held back only by a fragile arterial clot—immediate veterinary escalation and letting professionals direct movement protect the dam.

options.label: Wait until morning since the bleeding stopped, and test his swallowing with watery soaked grain tonight to make sure his cranial nerves are unaffected.
options.feedback: Never wait out a stopped nosebleed, and never run DIY swallow or watery-feed experiments—if cranial nerves are impaired, forced feeding drives food straight into the lungs as fatal aspiration pneumonia.

quiz.prompt: On a remote trail, your small dog darts into brush and yelps; you see two tiny punctures above her eye with zero bleeding, though she received a rattlesnake vaccine months ago. What is the safest protocol?

options.label: Snap a close-up photo of the snake so the ER knows which antivenom to pick, wrap a snug tourniquet above the neck or limb, and monitor for external bleeding before calling a vet.
options.feedback: Approaching a live snake risks biting you too, tourniquets worsen local hemotoxin damage, and the Florida dachshund’s blood completely lost clotting ability (>999 s ACT) without shedding a single drop of external blood.

options.label: Monitor her quietly at home for a few hours since her prior rattlesnake vaccine record covers mild-looking, non-bleeding punctures, and drive to a clinic only if her hind legs start rippling.
options.feedback: A prior vaccine record never clears a new bite—Leonard’s 2014 data had wide statistical uncertainty (CI 0.66–11.37, p = 0.1673)—and waiting for late systemic signs like myokymia wastes critical shock-and-clotting time.

options.label: Separate cleanly from the hazard without approaching the snake, skip all DIY field interventions, call ahead to an emergency veterinary hospital to confirm ICU and F(ab')₂ antivenom availability while reporting objective timing and vaccine history, and transport promptly.

options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! In Mulpuri’s 2023 case, switching from charge-based CE-HPLC to an enzymatic assay dropped HbA1c from 9.9%–10.1% to 5.4% and unmasked silent Hemoglobin Wayne I—whereas repeating the same column or trusting ADAG’s eAG formula only recycles the illusion.

quiz.prompt: Minutes after eating an amusement-park liquid nitrogen snack—having waited until the smoking vapor cloud disappeared—a teenager develops sudden severe abdominal pain, visible belly swelling, and shortness of breath, yet reports zero mouth burns or sore throat. What is the safest response?

options.label: Call emergency medical services immediately, give zero water, milk, food, or antacids, avoid touching or tasting the leftover snack, and report the suspected liquid nitrogen exposure with exact timing and any existing photo or receipt.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! In Kim’s 2018 case, a 13-year-old suffered a 4 cm stomach perforation with zero mouth or throat injury; immediate EMS without oral fluids protects the sterile peritoneal cavity while giving surgeons vital exposure history.

options.label: Offer a glass of milk to coat the stomach and wait to see if the gas passes, since the vapor cloud had already vanished and an unburned throat rules out deep cryogenic stomach injury.
options.feedback: Fading fog never proves safe internal temperature, a spotless throat never rules out a ruptured stomach, and pouring milk or water into a perforated organ floods the sterile abdominal cavity.

options.label: Delay calling EMS long enough to smell and taste the bottom of the snack cup for doctors, then call Poison Control first while massaging the swollen abdomen to help vent trapped nitrogen.
options.feedback: Never risk cryogenic self-injury playing detective, never massage an acute surgical abdomen, and never let Poison Control calls delay physical emergency care when severe pain, distension, or breathlessness hits.

clinicalFigures.caption: Coronal abdominal CT scan showing extensive pneumoperitoneum (yellow arrows)—free gas escaped beyond the stomach wall after rapid liquid-to-gas expansion following liquid nitrogen cocktail ingestion.

quiz.prompt: A woman with a history of recurrent hydronephrosis and regular 28-day periods has her right ureteral double-J stent removed after a completely normal cystoscopy. Less than a day later, she produces zero urine and develops worsening right flank pain. What is the safest response?

options.label: Drink large glasses of water and cranberry juice to flush the blockage and wait a full 24 hours, since normal cystoscopy cleared the urinary lining and normal periods rule out endometriosis.
options.feedback: Forcing fluids into a clamped ureter spikes destructive hydrostatic pressure inside the kidney, cystoscopy cannot see extrinsic scar tissue outside the pipe, and normal 28-day cycles never rule out ureteral endometriosis.

options.label: Seek immediate emergency evaluation without forcing fluids, and tell triage the exact flank pain side, sudden anuria, prior hydronephrosis, and recent stent removal so clinicians can urgently scan and relieve any upstream blockage.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! In Al Ayoubi et al.’s 2025 case, complete anuria struck within 24 hours of stent removal with an empty bladder beneath a swollen right kidney—urgent assessment and decompression protect remaining renal function immediately.

options.label: Skip the emergency room and schedule a routine gynecology visit next month, because painless or regular periods mean the kidney back pressure is mild and reversible.
options.feedback: Pain and renal function do not move together—in Yang et al.’s 2021 surgical cohort, 19 of 40 patients (48%) with hydronephrosis were completely asymptomatic, and acute anuria requires immediate emergency decompression.

quiz.prompt: A patient with long-standing cardiomyopathy and active lupus on hydroxychloroquine has recently lost substantial weight and developed worsening kidney labs. Tonight she becomes severely breathless while lying flat, feels suddenly dizzy with a racing irregular heartbeat, and remembers her annual retinal eye exam was spotless two months ago. What is the safest action?

options.label: Trust the spotless annual eye exam as proof against hydroxychloroquine heart toxicity and skip her pills for four days at home to see if her breathing clears up.
options.feedback: A retinal exam inspects the back of the eye—not the myocardium—and abruptly self-stopping an immunomodulator as a home experiment risks triggering a dangerous lupus flare or lupus myocarditis without diagnosing the acute cardiac threat.

options.label: Assume the breathlessness is simply her familiar 11-year-old heart failure flaring up, sleep propped on extra pillows, and drive herself to an outpatient clinic next week.
options.feedback: A familiar diagnosis must never excuse sudden deterioration: NHS guidance flags lying-down breathlessness and Plaquenil warnings flag racing heartbeat and dizziness as immediate emergencies—and driving yourself while oxygen-starved or near-syncopal is dangerous.

options.label: Call emergency services immediately without driving herself, do not self-stop her immunomodulator as a home test, and give ER clinicians her complete medication, cardiac, weight-loss, and kidney history.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Lying-down breathlessness, dizziness, and racing irregular heartbeats demand urgent emergency evaluation for both mechanical pump failure and electrical QTc arrhythmia, while medication changes remain strictly clinician-directed across cardiology, nephrology, and rheumatology.

clinicalFigures.caption: Endomyocardial biopsy electron microscopy showing hallmark hydroxychloroquine lysosomal cardiotoxicity: (a, 12,000×) elongated enlarged mitochondria (orange arrows), myelin figure (green arrow), and curvilinear body (red arrow); (b, 20,000×) myelin figure (yellow arrow).
clinicalFigures.spoilerNote: Transmission electron microscopy of cardiac biopsy tissue from the primary peer-reviewed case report.

quiz.prompt: An 11-year-old reportedly spayed cat has lost weight and sprayed pungent urine vertically on walls for months, and over the last three weeks she has begun acting like she is in heat and aggressively attacking anyone who reaches near her. Two routine urinalyses, a urine culture, and baseline CBC and chemistry panels have all come back normal. What is the safest next step?

options.label: Warn the veterinary clinic beforehand about her aggression so they can plan pre-visit anxiolytics or safe sedation, bring her full timeline and prior negative urinary workups, and pursue stepwise medical reassessment without ever punishing her.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Normal routine labs and a past spay record never rule out hidden endocrine drivers like a 6-mm ovarian remnant (or mimics like external estrogen exposure), and advance notice lets veterinary teams evaluate aggressive cats safely.

options.label: Accept that normal routine blood and urine tests prove a purely behavioral dominance issue, scold her firmly whenever she sprays, and hold her down at home to palpate her belly for lumps.
options.feedback: Cornell Feline Health Center guidance strictly warns against physical or verbal punishment—it escalates fear and stress without touching hidden biology—and forceful home restraint risks serious bites and injury to both owner and cat.

options.label: Assume an ovarian remnant is impossible because her adoption file says she was spayed ten years ago, and skip further imaging since hormone bloodwork alone can map the exact tissue and prove past surgical error.
options.feedback: A reported spay history is a map rather than a guarantee, hormone panels catch circulating signals without locating anatomy or proving past incompetence, and persistent signs demand linked imaging, endocrine, and tissue evaluation.

clinicalFigures.caption: Reference contrast-enhanced abdominal CT of an ovarian remnant tumor (granulosa cell tumor) in a spayed cat across transverse (A, B), coronal (C), and sagittal (D) views—illustrating how residual ovarian tissue can drive hormonal syndromes long after spay (not the 6 mm remnant in Jones et al. 2019).

quiz.prompt: After a minor household stair stumble and months of thigh ache and his leg giving out, a 59-year-old man is found to have two distinct femoral stress fractures. His serum calcium (9.4 mg/dL), intact PTH (50 pg/mL), alkaline phosphatase (135 U/L), creatinine (1.0 mg/dL), and 24-hour urine phosphate (0.821 g/24 hr; printed normal 0.3–1 g/day) all sit inside printed normal ranges, while his serum phosphate is 1.5 mg/dL (normal 2.5–4.8) and vitamin D is 22 ng/mL. What is the most accurate clinical takeaway?

options.label: Prioritize orthopedic stabilization first, recognize that excreting 0.821 g/24 hr of urinary phosphate during severe hypophosphatemia signals inappropriate renal phosphate wasting requiring metabolic workup, and track any specialized hormone labs with exact original units intact.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Printed urine reference ranges never establish physiological appropriateness when blood phosphate is critically low (1.5 mg/dL)—fixing the acute fracture comes first, followed by systematic metabolic investigation and strict unit tracking (RU/mL vs. pg/mL).

options.label: Reassure him that normal calcium, normal PTH, normal creatinine, and a mid-range 24-hour urine phosphate rule out metabolic bone disease, and treat his mild vitamin D of 22 ng/mL with over-the-counter supplements alone.
options.feedback: Normal calcium, PTH, and creatinine do not exclude severe osteomalacia, mild vitamin D deficiency alone does not account for bilateral femoral stress fractures without secondary PTH elevation, and normal-looking urine phosphate during hypophosphatemia is active renal wasting.

options.label: Delay urgent orthopedic fracture stabilization to demand an immediate whole-body 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT, because receptor scans achieve 100% localization across every patient and eliminate any need for biopsy.
options.feedback: Acute fracture stabilization always comes first; El-Maouche et al.’s 2016 NIH cohort localized tumors in only 6/11 (54.5%) total referrals (100% applied only to the 6 localized cases), false positives occur across modalities, and imaging is a compass requiring histologic proof.

clinicalFigures.spoilerNote: Femur radiographs from the primary peer-reviewed case report.
