quiz.prompt: A 76-year-old man wakes with numbness in both legs, low back pain, and difficulty passing urine, rapidly losing the ability to walk over four days. His initial thoracic MRI shows cord swelling and enhancement, and his lumbar puncture shows normal opening pressure (100 mm H2O) with mild lymphocytes—yet five days of IVIG and dexamethasone produce zero improvement. What is the safest clinical understanding and next step?

options.label: Assume a spinal dural arteriovenous fistula is impossible because the collapse took four days instead of months and his lumbar puncture opening pressure was normal, so wait 48 hours and test his strength by walking down the hallway.
options.feedback: Rapid progression never excludes diseases typically described as slow, CSF opening pressure measures fluid outside the cord rather than pressurized spinal veins, and DIY walking tests or 48-hour waiting deals risk serious falls and lost neurologic reserve.

options.label: Treat zero response to immunotherapy and ongoing neurologic loss as an urgent reassessment trigger, transfer actual prior scan images alongside written reports to an experienced vascular spinal team, and remember that sealing a fistula stops damage without guaranteeing full walking recovery.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Lack of improvement after steroids/IVIG is critical pivot data, raw scan pixels let specialists catch vascular flow shadows and incomplete prior vessel coverage (including pelvic iliac branches), and realistic follow-up separates vascular closure from nerve regeneration.

options.label: Conclude that the lumbar puncture and steroids caused his paralysis, demand an immediate invasive spinal angiogram on arrival at triage, and avoid sleeping on his stomach afterward to guarantee the fistula cannot recur.
options.feedback: Untreated venous congestion—not the diagnostic tap or steroids—drove the cord injury; specialist vascular teams decide when invasive angiography is warranted, and prone sleeping in Su et al. (2025) was strictly an unproven single-case hypothesis.

clinicalFigures.caption: Contrast-enhanced thoracic spine MRI (A–D: T2, STIR, contrast-enhanced, and axial views) demonstrating spinal cord edema and abnormal perimedullary vascular flow shadows (red arrows) mimicking transverse myelitis.
clinicalFigures.spoilerNote: Spinal MRI from the primary peer-reviewed case report.
clinicalFigures.citation: Fig. 1 from Su et al. (2025), Journal of Medical Case Reports · PMC12330131

clinicalFigures.caption: Contrast-enhanced spinal MR angiography exposing the true culprit: engorged, varicose spinal veins (red arrows) pressurized by an occult dural arteriovenous fistula.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome has suffered four weeks of dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. A head CT and leg-vein ultrasound two weeks earlier were clear, and vertigo was suspected—but today she has thumb-indenting ankle swelling, unintended weight loss, and a serum albumin of 18.1 g/L (normal >36.0 g/L). A different lab later reports an albumin of 1.81 g/dL. What is the safest clinical interpretation and next step?

options.label: Treat 1.81 g/dL as a catastrophic tenfold drop from 18.1 g/L, start daily high-protein whey shakes at home, and schedule a separate podiatry visit for her ankles so her vertigo clinic can stay focused on her ears.
options.feedback: 18.1 g/L and 1.81 g/dL are the exact same physical concentration (10 deciliters per liter), whey shakes cannot fix a systemic protein leak, and splitting ankle edema from vomiting hides the connected biology.

options.label: Accept that her earlier negative clot scans rule out urgent illness, demand immediate off-label cetuximab as a guaranteed permanent cure that prevents gastric cancer, and reject any repeat endoscopy as proof the first test was botched.
options.feedback: Off-label cetuximab is a severe-case individualized choice with major toxicities (rash, skin fissures, hypomagnesemia) and unproved cancer prevention, repeat deeper biopsies reflect diagnostic sampling science rather than error, and sudden worsening swelling with breathlessness or chest symptoms demands emergency triage.

options.label: Recognize that 18.1 g/L and 1.81 g/dL represent identical severe hypoalbuminemia requiring one unified whole-body workup—not protein shakes—while escalating urgently for sudden red/hot painful swelling or immediately for breathlessness, chest symptoms, faintness, or vomiting blood.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Always verify g/L vs. g/dL units first, link persistent vomiting, weight loss, and pitting edema into one clinical investigation to find the true source of protein loss, and act immediately on NHS cardiopulmonary or GI-bleeding red flags.

clinicalFigures.caption: Coronal CT revealing massive, hyperemic hypertrophic gastric rugal folds in the body of the stomach (A, star)—the hallmark Ménétrier gastropathy leaking blood protein into the gut—alongside edematous bowel wall thickening (B, arrow).
clinicalFigures.spoilerNote: Abdominal CT from the primary peer-reviewed case report.
clinicalFigures.citation: Fig. 2 from Carlsen et al. (2019), Clinical Journal of Gastroenterology · PMC6885025

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old patient with a revised metal-on-polyethylene hip replacement has developed worsening breathlessness, numbness in both feet, and fading hearing alongside new right groin pain and a limp. One mitochondrial DNA screen came back negative. What is the safest next step?

options.label: Climb stairs carrying heavy boxes to test whether the hip grinds reliably, order a private online heavy-metal blood test first so you arrive with proof, and pause coronary follow-up until cobalt results return.
options.feedback: Home load or grinding provocation risks fresh mechanical damage and debris release, no private direct-to-consumer assay is required before calling a doctor, and suspected metal toxicity never cancels competing cardiac or endocrine disease.

options.label: Contact your medical and orthopedic teams promptly without provoking the hip or waiting on private labs, bring your exact operative implant report across specialties, and keep competing heart and thyroid evaluations running in parallel.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Even non-MoM revised metal-on-polyethylene hips can shed cobalt and chromium from metal junctions, prompt clinical contact beats home provocation, and bridging orthopedic records never replaces parallel care for concurrent conditions like coronary stenosis.

options.label: Rule out hip involvement because the bearing is metal-on-polyethylene rather than a recalled metal-on-metal resurfacing—and if an older plasma cobalt value is lower than a newer whole-blood number, demand immediate removal surgery.
options.feedback: Stepien et al.’s catastrophic metallosis occurred with a revised metal-on-polyethylene hip, plasma and whole blood are non-interchangeable matrices that cannot be compared raw, and neither a recall nor an isolated number automatically mandates revision surgery.

quiz.prompt: A two-year-old yellow Labrador known from a prior cheek swab to carry two copies of the DNM1 c.767G>T mutation suddenly develops wobbly hind legs and cannot walk twenty minutes into intense retrieving—yet he stays fully conscious, bright, and wagging his tail. What is the safest immediate response?

options.label: Let him rest five minutes until his wagging tail convinces you the crisis passed, then toss a few short retrieves to test his limit and record clear video for the vet.
options.feedback: An eager, tail-wagging demeanor never proves physiological safety in high-drive retrievers—some dogs die during collapse episodes—and you must never provoke a repeat collapse or delay care to film.

options.label: Skip the emergency clinic because his existing EE genetic printout already explains the wobble, douse him in ice water to cool him fast, and squirt sugar paste into his mouth.
options.feedback: Carrying two DNM1 copies never immunizes a dog against lethal lookalikes like cardiac arrhythmias, heatstroke, or acute metabolic crises; ice water risks shock, and forcing oral pastes into a weak dog risks aspiration.

options.label: Stop all activity at the first sign of incoordination and go straight for professional veterinary evaluation, reporting exact activity observations alongside his genetic record.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Sudden weakness or inability to walk is an immediate veterinary emergency regardless of alertness or prior DNA printouts—treat the living crisis first, then build an individualized vet activity plan.

clinicalFigures.caption: An alert, athletic Labrador Retriever—the breed most frequently affected by autosomal recessive DNM1 exercise-induced collapse (EIC), in which hind-limb motor control fails during intense excitement while the dog stays fully awake and eager to play (not the index dog in Basso et al. 2014).

quiz.prompt: In a region where feline sporotrichosis is emerging, an indoor-outdoor cat develops weeks of expanding, oozing ulcers on the face and paws along with a visibly swollen nose and high-pitched noisy breathing. Two days later, the owner notices a persistent sore on their own wrist despite not recalling a deep bite. What is the safest course of action?

options.label: Call the veterinary clinic ahead so they can prepare isolation for the cat, follow their handling and pet-separation plan instead of improvising wound care, and have a physician evaluate the wrist lesion with explicit disclosure of sick-cat contact.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Expanding ulcers with nasal deformity and stridor warrant prompt, pre-notified veterinary assessment, while a human caregiver’s new skin lesion requires medical review with explicit animal-contact disclosure—even without a remembered scratch—because fungal sporotrichosis will not respond to routine bacterial antibiotics.

options.label: Clean the cat’s necrotic scabs at home with dish gloves and leftover dog antibiotics, and skip seeing a human doctor for the wrist sore since you do not remember being bitten or scratched.
options.feedback: Improvised home debridement and leftover antibacterial prescriptions endanger both the cat and the caregiver—antibiotics target bacteria, not fungi—and Schubach et al.’s Rio cohort showed 137 of 421 cat-exposed human cases recalled no bite or scratch at all.

options.label: Release the cat outdoors immediately to keep the household safe, because the Rio de Janeiro data proved petting an infected cat carries an 84.7% transmission rate and a 10% infection prevalence across all domestic cats.
options.feedback: Abandoning a sick cat worsens community spread and welfare without solving exposure, 84.7% (421/497) was the proportion of already-confirmed clinic patients reporting cat contact rather than a petting-risk probability, and 10/101 came from selected close-contact cats—not general population prevalence.

clinicalFigures.caption: Cytological smear and skin histopathology from the cat with Sporothrix brasiliensis sepsis (A–D), revealing severe mixed inflammatory infiltrate packed with abundant intracellular and extracellular oval fungal yeasts invading deep dermal tissue.
clinicalFigures.spoilerNote: Cytology and histopathology microscopy from the primary peer-reviewed veterinary case report.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old patient previously treated for a growth hormone-secreting pituitary macroadenoma logs into a patient portal and sees that their latest IGF-1 blood level has finally entered the normal reference range. They also feel well enough to ignore persistent loud snoring and elevated blood pressure. What is the safest interpretation and next step?

options.label: Cut their monthly endocrine injection dose in half immediately so hormones do not drop too low, and cancel blood-pressure, sleep, heart, and colon follow-ups now that the hormone ratio is normal.
options.feedback: Self-adjusting endocrine therapy off a patient portal is dangerous, and Arosio et al.’s nationwide cohort showed excess mortality persisted (SMR 1.3; 88 vs. 66 deaths) even in patients controlled at their last IGF-1 visit because prior hormone exposure leaves cardiovascular, metabolic, airway, and colonic legacy risks.

options.label: Keep all prescribed doses unchanged pending specialist review, and ask the coordinating endocrinology team how blood pressure, glucose, sleep quality, cardiac structure, bowel-polyp screening, and remaining pituitary axes will be monitored long-term.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Normalizing IGF-1 stops active hormonal flooding—like fixing a burst pipe—but NIDDK and NHS guidance stress that holistic whole-body follow-up and monitoring of remaining pituitary hormones remain essential under clinician direction.

options.label: Conclude that because the Italian cohort reported an overall SMR of 1.7, modern treatment has a 70% fatality rate regardless of control, so additional surgical or medical follow-up is pointless.
options.feedback: An SMR of 1.7 (153 observed vs. 90 expected deaths across 811 patients diagnosed in 1980–2002) is a historical aggregate ratio—not a 70% fatality rate or a forecast for modern care—and treating it with fatalism sacrifices effective, life-preserving comorbidity management.

clinicalFigures.caption: Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI of the sella turcica pinpointing a 17 × 23 × 17 mm growth-hormone-secreting pituitary macroadenoma (white arrow) silently driving years of acromegaly and snoring.

quiz.prompt: A healthy 48-year-old accidentally inhales a daily ferrous sulfate iron tablet while swallowing. After a hard coughing spell she spits out what looks like the intact pill, but two hours later she develops relentless blood-flecked coughing fits, pain behind her breastbone, and shortness of breath while sitting still. What is the safest action?

options.label: Drink a large glass of water and eat dense bread to flush any leftover iron residue down, and stay home since spitting out the intact tablet proves the danger passed.
options.feedback: Water and bread travel down the esophagus rather than the trachea—and aspirating water risks washing caustic iron deeper into smaller airways—while Caterino et al.’s Case 1 proved coughing up an intact iron pill can still leave a progressive chemical burn ending in surgical bilobectomy.

options.label: Drive herself to an urgent care clinic once the coughing eases, and plan to crush all future iron tablets into water at home so they cannot get stuck again.
options.feedback: Driving yourself with resting breathlessness and potential severe hypoxia risks sudden confusion or collapse behind the wheel, and self-crushing or dissolving engineered tablets at home can destroy release profiles or burn the mouth and esophagus.

options.label: Call local emergency services immediately without driving herself, tell responders it was a ferrous sulfate tablet with the exact timeline and formulation, skip swallow challenges, and arrange specialist follow-up for delayed airway scarring plus a formal swallow and formulation review.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Iron pill aspiration is a chemical mucosal emergency whose burn persists even if a tablet is coughed out, requiring urgent professional airway care, longitudinal post-discharge monitoring, and clinician-guided swallow/formulation planning rather than DIY fixes.

quiz.prompt: A nine-year-old cat develops new appetite loss and excessive drooling, is diagnosed with a congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunt, and undergoes surgical attenuation. After hospital discharge, her post-operative bile acids come back completely normal—then one evening she suddenly becomes unsteady and has a brief seizure. What is the safest interpretation and action?

options.label: Seek urgent veterinary neurological reassessment immediately and keep her exact vascular map and surgical history with her chart—normalized post-op bile acids do not rule out late post-operative seizures or residual shunt flow.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! In Valiente et al.’s 34-cat cohort, roughly 23.5% developed post-op seizures—including three seizing cats with completely normal bile acids and one with normal ammonia. Biochemical labs and neurological status are two separate dashboard dials.

options.label: Trust the normalized post-operative bile acids as proof that the shunt is 100% cured, run an at-home fasting-and-meal test tomorrow, and try to capture a second seizure on video before calling the clinic.
options.feedback: Normalized bile acids never guarantee a seizure-free brain or zero residual flow, home fasting or meal challenges are unsafe for a sick animal, and waiting to provoke or film a repeat neurological episode delays urgent care.

options.label: Assume a nine-year-old cat cannot have a true congenital shunt—meaning it must be an acquired shunt—and ask a new clinic to tie off any remaining small vessels immediately without reviewing her prior vascular map.
options.feedback: Congenital shunts can remain compensated for nine years before diagnosis, and confusing congenital with acquired physiology is perilous—closing an acquired pressure-relief shunt around a diseased liver can be rapidly fatal, so the exact prior vascular map is mandatory.

quiz.prompt: After completing antimicrobial treatment for confirmed Babesia microti infection, an older adult with an intact spleen feels well and receives one negative follow-up PCR test—though his antibody serology remains positive. He plans to donate blood soon and assumes his intact spleen guarantees he could never suffer severe hemolytic relapse. What is the safest, scientifically accurate course?

options.label: Go ahead and donate blood since a single negative PCR proves the parasite is permanently gone, and treat the lingering positive antibody test as proof that antibiotics failed and must be restarted immediately.
options.feedback: Leiby et al.’s donor study showed Babesia parasitemia is intermittent and can dip below PCR detection limits while antibodies persist for months or years as immune memory—so one negative PCR never self-clears blood donation, and a persistent antibody alone does not prove treatment failure.

options.label: Proactively disclose his prior babesiosis diagnosis, testing, and treatment to the blood service so modern eligibility rules govern—never self-clearing off one negative PCR—and seek prompt re-evaluation if fatigue, pallor, or jaundice ever return.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! Because Babesia survives refrigeration and surfaces intermittently while IgG immune memory and DAT autoantibodies can outlast active infection—even with an intact spleen—blood-bank disclosure is mandatory and clinical symptom changes always warrant reassessment.

options.label: Rely on his intact spleen as biological protection against severe hemolysis, skip telling the blood bank since 97.7% inter-lab PCR agreement means negative tests never miss hiding parasites, and watch only for a visible tick bite next summer.
options.feedback: An intact spleen did not prevent transfusion-requiring wAIHA in Bleik and Matubia’s 75-year-old patient, 97.7% agreement measures lab reproducibility rather than omniscient detection below threshold, and poppy-seed tick nymphs routinely transmit infection without being seen.

clinicalFigures.caption: Peripheral blood smear capturing both halves of the double hit: intracellular Babesia microti merozoites inside red cells (black arrows) alongside dense, round autoimmune spherocytes (green arrows) produced by secondary warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

quiz.prompt: After decades of daily abdominal insulin injections, a patient’s HbA1c stays stubbornly elevated despite repeated dose increases. Her lower abdomen feels softly swollen and rubbery with no distinct hard lump, so she suspects trapped absorption—and plans to move tomorrow morning’s full high dose over to a fresh, untouched side of her belly on her own. What is the safest course?

options.label: Move her full usual dose to the untouched abdominal site tomorrow morning since there is no hard palpable lump to worry about, and keep juice on hand to pour into her mouth if she passes out.
options.feedback: Nagase et al. proved insulin-derived amyloidosis can exist with zero palpable mass, abruptly switching a barrier-calibrated dose to healthy skin risks severe hypoglycemic coma, and pouring juice into an unconscious person’s mouth risks fatal airway aspiration.

options.label: Keep injecting into the swollen patch but multiply her dose by 2.5× to overcome the ~40% absorption ratio reported in Nagase et al.’s Case 1 until her next routine visit.
options.feedback: Case 1’s ~40% AUC ratio is a single-patient experimental snapshot—never a universal bioavailability rule or home dosing multiplier—and self-multiplying insulin doses creates a life-threatening overdose hazard.

options.label: Contact her diabetes clinician before changing her injection site, bring her glucose logs and insulin devices for hands-on site palpation, and transition only under a clinician-guided dose reduction and monitoring plan.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! UK MHRA guidance explicitly warns patients to contact a doctor before moving injections away from altered tissue—even without a hard mass—so doses can be lowered proactively to prevent a sudden absorption floodgate.

quiz.prompt: Three weeks after nursing your unvaccinated dog bare-handed through acute fever, vomiting, and diarrhea—which cleared up after your vet prescribed antibiotics—you develop a high fever, severe muscle aches, and diarrhea. Your dog looks completely healthy today. What is the safest immediate move?

options.label: Have your vet run a urine PCR on your recovered dog first; if the dog’s urine PCR comes back negative today, you can safely rule out leptospirosis and treat your fever at home.
options.feedback: In Nakashiro et al. (2024), the recovered dog’s post-antibiotic urine PCR was completely negative even though canine MAT titers stood at 800—a negative test weeks after antimicrobials never rules out earlier urinary shedding.

options.label: Seek human medical care promptly, tell the clinician up front about your dog’s prior illness and bare-handed urine/vomit contact, and authorize your doctor and veterinarian to share clinical summaries.
options.feedback: Survived Tuesday! CDC guidance stresses immediate medical evaluation without waiting for shock vitals or pet test results, and bridging the human and veterinary records unlocked the life-saving diagnosis in Nakashiro et al.’s case.

options.label: Skip the zoonotic history if you live in a dry suburban desert neighborhood and your dog only visits an indoor doggy daycare, since Leptospira requires tropical floodwaters to spread.
options.feedback: Iverson et al.’s 2021 Maricopa County investigation documented 71 confirmed or probable canine leptospirosis cases across arid Phoenix suburbs, with strong epidemiological clustering around congregate dog daycare and boarding settings.

exam.q: Your buddy touches a homemade fractal wood-burning table and locks up around the probe. Your VERY FIRST move?

options.label: Pull them backward by their dry hoodie
options.why: High voltage punches straight through dry cloth—now paramedics have two cardiac arrests.

options.label: Cut the main breaker or wall power before touching them or the bench
options.why: Correct. Dead circuit first, then 911, CPR, and AED.

options.label: Knock the probe loose with a wooden broom handle
options.why: At 2,000–15,000 V, ordinary wood stops being a reliable insulator.

exam.q: You graze your fingertip with a 3,000-PSI paint sprayer. It leaves a 2-mm pinprick that barely bleeds. What do you do?

options.label: Wash it, bandage it, and see if it swells tomorrow
options.why: Waiting overnight is how tiny pinholes become finger amputations.

options.label: Squeeze hard to push the paint back out
options.why: Squeezing forces solvent deeper along tendon sheaths.

options.label: Go immediately to an ER with hand surgery and bring the paint/solvent label
options.why: Correct. High-pressure injection is an immediate surgical emergency even with minimal pain.

exam.q: A healthy adult uses OTC benzocaine toothache gel, turns gray, and stays stuck at SpO₂ 86% on 100% oxygen. What is lying?

options.label: The standard 2-wavelength finger pulse oximeter—demand co-oximetry and IV methylene blue
options.why: Correct. Methemoglobinemia freezes pulse oximeters near ~85% regardless of real hypoxia.

options.label: The oxygen tank is probably empty
options.why: Arterial dissolved oxygen (PaO₂) is actually sky-high; the iron in hemoglobin is chemically rusted to Fe³⁺.

options.label: The patient is just hyperventilating from anxiety
options.why: Chocolate-brown arterial blood is biochemistry, not anxiety.

exam.q: A patient with a ruptured varicose vein in the ankle is spraying bright blood across the bathroom floor. Fastest life-saving move?

options.label: Wrap a bulky loose towel around the whole calf and sit upright in a chair
options.why: Gravity keeps venous pressure high and bulky towels spread pressure away from the pinpoint leak.

options.label: Lie flat, elevate the leg high above the heart, and press ONE firm finger directly on the pinpoint bleeding hole
options.why: Correct. Elevation drops venous pressure instantly; pinpoint direct pressure seals the leak.

options.label: Soak the foot in cold water to constrict the vein
options.why: Warm or cold soaking hides blood volume loss while exsanguination continues.

exam.q: You drop a single drop of minoxidil hair-growth foam on your pillowcase. Who in the house is in mortal danger?

options.label: Your indoor cat—even trace pillow/hand transfer can trigger fatal feline heart/lung fluid collapse
options.why: Correct. Cats lack the enzymes to clear minoxidil safely; wash hands thoroughly and ban pets from treated pillows.

options.label: Nobody—minoxidil is only risky if someone drinks the bottle
options.why: Documented feline fatalities have occurred from grooming trace residue off owners’ hands and bedding.

options.label: Only houseplants near the bed
options.why: The plants are fine; your cat’s myocardium is not.

exam.q: A toddler swallows a lithium coin (button) battery and is still smiling and breathing normally. Which move is right?

options.label: Wait 24 hours to see if it passes in the diaper
options.why: Button batteries can burn through an esophagus in 2 hours—and keep eroding into the aorta even days later.

options.label: Head straight to the ER for immediate X-ray localization (and if >12 mo old & <12 h since swallow, give honey en route per NBIH guidance)
options.why: Correct. Never wait for symptoms and never induce vomiting.

options.label: Induce vomiting immediately at home
options.why: Vomiting can re-lodge the battery directly against the esophagus or airway.

exam.q: A coworker collapses inside a manure/sludge tank—and the air doesn’t even smell like rotten eggs anymore. Why is that terrifying?

options.label: The gas dissipated, so it’s safe to climb down and pull them out
options.why: That’s how 1 victim becomes 4. High-concentration H₂S paralyzes your sense of smell instantly.

options.label: High-concentration hydrogen sulfide (>100 ppm) knocks out olfactory nerves—NEVER enter without SCBA; call hazmat/911
options.why: Correct. “No smell” in a confined tank can mean lethal knockdown concentration.

options.label: Hold your breath and tie a rope around your waist
options.why: One involuntary gasp at >700 ppm causes instant knockdown collapse.

exam.q: A patient taking prescription nitroglycerin grabs a gas-station “Royal Honey” packet and suddenly feels dizzy with blue-tinted vision. What happened?

options.label: Hidden 60–150 mg sildenafil/tadalafil inside the honey collided with nitroglycerin, triggering distributive blood-pressure shock + retinal PDE6 blue vision
options.why: Correct. Tell paramedics about the supplement immediately so they NEVER give more nitrates.

options.label: Simple raw-honey allergy
options.why: Honey doesn’t inhibit retinal PDE6 or crash blood pressure with nitrates—unlabeled Viagra does.

options.label: Too much natural caffeine
options.why: Caffeine raises blood pressure; PDE5 + nitrate synergy bottoms it out.

exam.q: Your Labrador recovers from backyard wild-mushroom poisoning—her liver ALT dropped 87% by Day 8! On Day 24 she stops eating again, but ALT is nearly normal. What does that mean?

options.label: Her liver is healed, so she’s just being picky
options.why: A falling ALT only means fewer hepatocytes are actively bursting—it never rules out Act Two.

options.label: Treat returning lethargy/anorexia as a fresh ER emergency (this dog crashed into life-threatening Addison’s adrenal crisis with near-normal ALT)
options.why: Correct. The changing patient ALWAYS outranks a pretty lab graph.

options.label: Give extra water and wait a week for the next recheck
options.why: Her blood sugar was 43 mg/dL and potassium was climbing toward cardiac arrest.

exam.q: A healthy homeowner gets struck in the eye by a snapped rusted bungee hook. Eye pressure checks out normal at 16 mmHg. Safe to skip ophthalmology?

options.label: Yes—normal pressure means the eyeball is structurally intact
options.why: This exact patient had 20/800 vision, a torn iris root (iridodialysis), and internal bleeding (hyphema) at 15–17 mmHg.

options.label: No—shield the eye without pressure and get urgent ophthalmology evaluation for any recoil vision drop, irregular pupil, or hyphema
options.why: Correct. Normal pressure never cancels visible internal injury.

options.label: Flush with tap water for 20 minutes and press a cold compress directly onto the eye
options.why: Never press on a blunt-trauma globe—that is for chemical splashes, not mechanical recoil.

exam.q: A heavy-duty commercial truck tire ran flat for a mile and needs air back up to 105 PSI. Where should you stand?

options.label: Crouched directly facing the sidewall so you can watch the bulge
options.why: You just parked your sternum 50 cm from a potential 265 PSI zipper-failure blast cone.

options.label: Inside a steel restraining cage? No—put the TIRE in a steel cage, use a clip-on chuck, and stand ≥2.5 m away along the tread line
options.why: Survived Tuesday! And if a commercial tire was driven flat, scrap/inspect it internally before ever re-inflating.

options.label: Lean over the top of the tire holding a short manual gauge
options.why: If steel sidewall cords unzip under pressure, the air wave throws nearby bodies across the bay.

exam.q: You need to transport dry ice, but your SUV has no cargo compartment separate from the passenger cabin. What is the safer choice?

options.label: Tape the cooler lid shut airtight so the CO₂ stays inside
options.why: Never seal a dry ice container airtight. Gas buildup can rupture the container.

options.label: Do not carry it in that SUV. Use a vehicle with a separate, ventilated cargo compartment.
options.why: Open windows and fresh-air mode do not make a shared cabin safe. Keep dry ice out of passenger airspace and use packaging that allows gas to escape.

options.label: Turn on cabin A/C recirculation so it stays cool and sublimates slower
options.why: Recirculation does not bring in outside air. Do not transport dry ice in the occupied cabin.

exam.q: You find someone unresponsive in a filled bathtub with a plugged-in smartphone charger in the water—just a ‘five-volt’ cable with a CE mark printed on the brick. What is your first move?

options.label: Reach straight in to yank the low-voltage phone out—a five-volt USB cable can’t deliver lethal household current
options.why: When a penny-sized substandard capacitor fails closed inside a defective brick, galvanic isolation disappears—dumping 230-volt mains AC straight into wet metal and bathwater.

options.label: Touch nothing, call 911 from a dry room reporting electricity and water, and wait for power shutoff
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Reaching into energized bathwater turns one victim into two—wait for verified power isolation before CPR, and keep phone chargers out of bathrooms permanently.

options.label: Stand on the bathmat and fish the charging cord out of the tub using a wooden broom handle
options.why: Improvised household items like wooden brooms offer false confidence around wet rooms and mains current—let trained crews confirm power is isolated first.

exam.q: Three days after a backyard cookout, you develop sharp, localized abdominal pain—but zero fever, normal bowel movements, and a clear plain abdominal X-ray. What crucial sentence must you tell the ER doctor?

options.label: “It’s probably just mild food poisoning, I’ll take Pepto and go home.”
options.why: Grill-brush wire perforations are frequently walled off by omentum—normal stool and zero free air do not rule out an abscess.

options.label: “We ate off a grill cleaned with a wire bristle brush—could we check thin-slice CT for a stray bristle?”
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Plain X-rays routinely miss thin stainless grill bristles; thin-slice CT catches them.

options.label: “I would have tasted metal if I swallowed a wire.”
options.why: Almost no documented wire-bristle ingestion victims ever felt or tasted the wire going down.

exam.q: You layered bleach over a hydrochloric-acid toilet cleaner in a small bathroom, and suddenly a sharp sting hits your throat and chest—even though the room looks completely clear. What do you do in the next 60 seconds?

options.label: Drop the sponge, hold your breath out the door, get outside to fresh air, and call 911 or Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Evacuating immediately cuts off chlorine gas exposure before it reacts with airway moisture to cause mucosal HCl/HOCl burns and pulmonary edema.

options.label: Hold your breath just long enough to finish rinsing the tile, or pour vinegar or ammonia onto the puddle to neutralize the fumes.
options.why: Home chemistry does not accept apologies: staying to finish rinsing keeps your lungs absorbing chlorine gas, and pouring another chemical onto the spill risks creating fresh clouds of toxic fumes.

options.label: Step straight into that bathroom's shower to flush your eyes and skin, then wait to see if the chest irritation clears.
options.why: Re-entering a fume-filled bathroom to use its shower locks you inside the gas chamber; rinse at a kitchen sink or outdoor hose instead, and treat chest pain, wheezing, or shortness of breath as an immediate 911 call.

exam.q: You spot last night's pot of cooked pasta still sitting at room temperature on the stove—and next to it, a home-canned low-acid vegetable jar whose lid has started to bulge. How do you handle dinner?

options.label: Trash the overnight pasta, never open or taste the bulging jar, and chill cooked starches in shallow containers within 2 hours next time.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Both Bacillus cereus cereulide and botulinum neurotoxin punish kitchen thrift, so the 2-hour fridge rule and strict zero-tasting of bulging jars are your real firewalls.

options.label: Bring the leftover pasta to a furious rolling boil to sterilize it, and crack the jar just enough for a tiny sniff-and-taste check.
options.why: Boiling kills bacteria while leaving heat-stable cereulide toxin smugly intact to collapse your mitochondria—and one tiny taste of a bulging jar is how Clostridium botulinum cleaves SNARE vesicles and steals your airway.

options.label: Reheat the pasta anyway, and if relentless vomiting with drowsiness or double vision shows up later, wait it out as ordinary food poisoning.
options.why: Severe starch vomiting with confusion or drowsiness requires urgent ER liver and metabolic labs, while double vision or drooping eyelids signal a botulism airway crisis where early antitoxin decides the outcome.

exam.q: Hours after sharing freshly caught, piping-hot barracuda that tasted spotless, your lips tingle, dizziness hits, and grabbing a glass of ice water burns like fire. What is your move?

options.label: Go straight to an ER, name the reef fish and meal time, warn dining companions, and plan a six-month trigger ban.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Cold-burns-like-fire allodynia is ciguatera's calling card, and prompt ER care handles sudden bradycardia and low pressure while warning everyone who shared the heat-proof platter.

options.label: Treat it as traveler's diarrhea and wash it down with a cold beer—fresh, seared fish cannot cause poisoning.
options.why: P-CTX-1 is odorless, tasteless, and completely heat-proof, so ice chests and searing pans touch nothing—and alcohol only dislodges fat-stored toxin to flare nerve symptoms harder.

options.label: Stay home unless companions fall ill too, and drink iced coffee to shake off the lightheadedness.
options.why: Lightheadedness after reef predators can signal vagal bradycardia slowing the heart toward 41 bpm, and caffeine is a classic trigger that kicks ciguatoxin nerve firing back into overdrive.

exam.q: Shortly after stirring a single teaspoon of unblended Turkish Black Sea rhododendron honey into boiling herbal tea, cold sweats, nausea, and severe dizziness hit as your pulse crashes toward 38 beats a minute. What do you do?

options.label: Lie flat immediately, call 911, and tell paramedics and ER clinicians out loud about the artisanal rhododendron honey jar.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Lying flat protects brain perfusion through 70/40 hypotension and AV block, and naming the honey guides the ER straight to 0.5–1.0 mg IV atropine instead of a misdirected heart-attack chase.

options.label: Walk it off and brew another hot mug—boiling tea neutralized any plant toxins, and honey from those same mountains was fine last spring.
options.why: Boiling water doesn't touch grayanotoxins, unblended batches vary wildly from season to season, and standing up with complete AV block and 70/40 blood pressure puts you on the floor.

options.label: Drive yourself to a clinic and leave out the honey so doctors focus straight on the ST-segment elevation.
options.why: Driving during vagal-reflex bradycardia risks sudden syncope behind the wheel, and hiding the honey leaves a 15-nanomolar Bezold-Jarisch fakeout disguised as a blocked coronary artery.

exam.q: A relative wearing a prescribed fentanyl pain patch becomes unresponsive in a 106°F hot bath. Paramedics peel the patch off and revive them with Narcan. Why is refusing ER transport still lethal?

options.label: The bathwater soaked through the skin and diluted their sodium
options.why: The culprit isn’t water—it’s the huge reservoir of fentanyl that heat already drove deep into the dermis.

options.label: Narcan wears off in 30–90 minutes while the saturated skin depot keeps pumping fentanyl into the bloodstream for up to 17 hours
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Peeling the patch stops NEW transfer, not the drug already parked inside the skin.

options.label: Because fentanyl patches explode when removed wet
options.why: No explosion—just silent re-narcotization once short-acting naloxone fades.

exam.q: Four hours after an excess extended-release bupropion (XL) ingestion, the patient is chatting calmly with a tight 94-millisecond QRS—while a rapid urine screen blames amphetamines. What is the safe call?

options.label: Clear them for discharge since four hours have passed with calm conversation and a normal 94-ms QRS.
options.why: Osmotic XL polymer shells run on a slow zero-order fuse: nearly half of delayed bupropion seizures hit out of nowhere between Hours 8 and 24 alongside sudden cardiogenic shock.

options.label: Flag 'XL / extended-release' to override the false amphetamine screen and keep continuous monitoring for 24 hours.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Calling out the XL formulation cuts straight past misleading amphetamine screens and locks in the mandatory 24-hour hospital telemetry watch before delayed seizures or connexin-43 shock arrive.

options.label: Pivot strictly to illicit amphetamine toxicity and sign out once the early screening panels look calm.
options.why: Rapid urine immunoassays routinely misread bupropion as amphetamines, and chasing that decoy while leaving early drops telemetry right before active hydroxybupropion surges.

exam.q: Someone who chewed concentrated gas-station 7-OH kratom tablets collapses with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing—yet the quick ER opiate screen comes back completely negative. What saves them?

options.label: Skip naloxone because the opiate screen is negative and a legal herbal chew sold at the register can’t cause true opioid apnea
options.why: Concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine tablets flood brainstem µ-opioid receptors while dodging morphine-ring immunoassay antibodies—the same tests that still falsely flag poppy-seed bagels.

options.label: Discharge them once naloxone restores breathing—the antidote clears every cardiac and drug-interaction hazard from kratom
options.why: Naloxone reverses brainstem apnea but does nothing to unblock cardiac hERG channels—leaving QTc prolongation, Type-1 Brugada arrhythmias, and CYP2D6 buildup active.

options.label: Call 911, give naloxone despite the negative screen, share all meds, and demand 12-lead ECG monitoring
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Naloxone rescues breathing while 12-lead telemetry guards against hERG arrhythmias and full med disclosure catches 2-to-5-fold CYP2D6/CYP3A4 pileups.

exam.q: A healthy-looking baby has been chewing a 'natural' artisan teething bracelet from a local fair, and a routine capillary finger-prick lead screen comes back at or above 3.5 µg/dL. What is your next step?

options.label: Remove the bracelet, seal it with vendor info for public health, and get a confirmatory venous blood draw.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Unmarked metal spacer beads can hide 17,000 ppm lead alongside choking hazards, and a venous confirmation draw launches certified source tracing and proper pediatric follow-up.

options.label: Clear the bracelet with a home lead-swab kit and order online chelation drops while keeping it on.
options.why: Home swab tests cannot reliably clear infant jewelry, unregulated internet chelation drops are dangerous, and keeping beaded jewelry on a baby preserves both lead ingestion and strangulation hazards.

options.label: Blame vintage house paint alone and dry-scrape any chipped trim around the nursery yourself.
options.why: Dry-scraping or sanding old paint blasts localized lead into breathable dust, while assuming the house is the sole culprit leaves a 17,000-ppm chewable source wrapped right on the infant's wrist.

exam.q: After going all-out in your very first indoor spin class, your thighs swell rock-hard and your urine turns the color of cola—though an earlier clinic check showed completely normal kidney labs. What is your next move?

options.label: Respect the 'earned' soreness, trust those normal kidney labs, and hop back on the bike for a light recovery spin.
options.why: That isn't weakness leaving your body—it's sheared sarcolemmas dumping myoglobin and CK past 100,000 U/L toward your renal tubules well before basic kidney labs sound the alarm.

options.label: Skip driving yourself and get straight to the ER for IV fluids, serial CK and electrolyte labs, and cardiac monitoring.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Rock-hard swollen thighs plus cola-colored urine mean exertional rhabdomyolysis needs monitored hospital IV resuscitation, not grit behind the steering wheel.

options.label: Stay home and chug gallons of water mixed with a DIY baking-soda electrolyte cocktail until your urine runs clear.
options.why: Chugging gallons while urine output falters or playing home chemist with Reddit baking-soda mixes can turn a renal-tubule emergency into a dangerous electrolyte crisis.

exam.q: You wear reusable monthly contacts—sometimes in the shower—and now one eye is intensely painful, blurry, and light-sensitive despite steroid drops calming the redness. What should you do?

options.label: Keep using the steroid drops since the redness faded, and give your lenses a fresh tap-water rinse.
options.why: Corticosteroid drops act like a polite curtain over Acanthamoeba keratitis—muting surface redness while double-walled amoebic cysts dig deeper—and tap water is the delivery truck that brought the parasite.

options.label: Pry out the lens even if it feels stuck, scrub the case in the sink, and drive yourself to clinic.
options.why: Forcing a stuck lens tears an inflamed cornea, scrubbing the case erases the exact lab specimen ophthalmologists need, and driving yourself with impaired vision compounds an eye crisis.

options.label: Remove the lens gently only if unstuck, seal lenses and case for lab testing, and get a ride to eye care.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Delivering the sealed lenses, case, and a complete list of every prior drop—especially steroids—lets an ophthalmologist catch Acanthamoeba before it wrecks the cornea.

exam.q: It’s a mild 72°F afternoon when you spot a young child alone inside a parked van with cracked windows and no driver in sight. What is your first move?

options.label: Wait ten minutes beside the van for the driver—72°F sweater weather with cracked windows stays comfortable inside
options.why: Shortwave sunlight pours through glass and traps longwave heat rapidly—72°F outside easily climbs to 112°F behind the glass even with cracked windows.

options.label: If you get the child into shade and their skin cools down, give them a sports drink and skip the ER
options.why: Pouring drinks into a drowsy or confused child risks pulmonary aspiration, and cooler skin never proves organs escaped endothelial vascular collapse.

options.label: Call 911 right now, follow dispatch to cool externally with wet cloths, and get ER care
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Any child alone in a parked vehicle is an instant 911 call—and no app arrival ping ever replaces physically walking every row.

exam.q: Sudden sharp one-sided pelvic pain and shoulder-tip pain hit someone who could be pregnant. Yesterday’s serum beta-hCG fell to 10 mIU/mL, there is zero external bleeding, and a fresh home urine strip shows one negative line. What now?

options.label: Lie down, call 911 instead of driving, and flag the pregnancy possibility and falling hCG
options.why: Survived Tuesday! A ruptured ectopic tube can hemorrhage into the abdomen below a urine test’s detection floor—and falling hCG never cancels a rupture.

options.label: Take a second urine strip, press deep on the belly, and sleep it off with heat
options.why: A second urine stick only repeats the same detection-floor blind spot, while poking the abdomen and sleeping on an internal bleed lets blood pressure crater silently.

options.label: Drive yourself to urgent care since there’s no vaginal bleeding to worry about
options.why: Intraperitoneal hemoperitoneum hides cleanly inside the abdomen—and dropping blood pressure behind the wheel turns one surgical emergency into a highway wreck.

exam.q: A wide-awake CLL patient gets an impossible 9.5 mmol/L plasma potassium sent via hospital pneumatic tube—while in the next bay, a dialysis patient has high potassium and a spotless ECG. Which rule avoids both traps?

options.label: Hand-walk a bedside blood gas for the CLL mismatch, and never clear a dialysis patient by ECG alone.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Pneumatic wall chutes shred fragile leukemic cells ex vivo into fake 9.5 readings, while 1 in 4 truly hyperkalemic ER patients still present with a deceptively spotless ECG.

options.label: Rush the CLL patient to emergency dialysis since three machines agreed on 9.5, and discharge the dialysis patient's clean ECG.
options.why: Three lab machines reading the same sheared tube will happily agree on an artifact—risking catastrophic hypokalemia—while letting a clean ECG clear a high-risk kidney patient misses real hyperkalemia.

options.label: Send a chilled redraw back through the pneumatic tube for both patients and wait an hour for central-lab confirmation.
options.why: Another high-speed ride through the wall chute shears fragile CLL white cells all over again, chilling blood invites cold red-cell leak, and true kidney hyperkalemia cannot spare an hour's wait.

exam.q: You're filling out pre-op forms before routine surgery: a blood relative once survived an operating-room crisis with a rigid jaw and dark post-op urine, though their later blood DNA panel came back negative. What do you tell the anesthesiologist?

options.label: Leave it off the form—a negative blood DNA panel clears malignant hyperthermia, and surgical teams can always catch a crisis early on the thermometer.
options.why: Fever arrives late—unlatched RyR1 calcium pores can already be burning ATP at 10–20× resting speed and doubling ETCO₂ while the thermometer looks normal, and a negative gene panel never clears an index survivor.

options.label: Disclose the family scare pre-op, request non-triggering TIVA or regional blocks, and assume susceptibility without CHCT/IVCT clearance.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Obeying the asymmetric genetic testing rule lets your team replace volatile gases and succinylcholine with safe IV anesthetics like propofol and rocuronium—preventing the furnace from igniting.

options.label: Cancel surgery altogether since no anesthetic is safe for carriers, or ask them just to watch body temperature closely during standard sevoflurane anesthesia.
options.why: Suspected carriers undergo surgery safely with total intravenous anesthesia or regional blocks—whereas rolling the dice on sevoflurane and waiting on a thermometer lets rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia erupt first.

exam.q: Your dog just chewed into a brodifacoum rat-bait block, yet at Hour 4 an urgent-care clotting test reads a tidy 8.2 seconds—and the local feed store sells cheap Vitamin K₃ over the counter. What is your move?

options.label: Head home relieved by the normal 8.2-second Hour-4 clotting test, since a dangerous anticoagulant would have spiked the lab by now.
options.why: At Hour 4, pre-existing clotting factors are still coasting on borrowed time while brodifacoum locks hepatic VKORC1 shut for weeks—clearing the dog early invites spontaneous hemothorax days later.

options.label: Save the wrapper, refuse Hour-4 clearance, give 28–30+ days of Vitamin K₁ with fatty food, and recheck PT 48 hours post-stop.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Matching brodifacoum's multi-week liver lock with a full month of fatty-food-paired prescription Vitamin K₁—and checking PT 48 hours post-stop—keeps spontaneous hemorrhage off the calendar.

options.label: Save on clinic refills by giving feed-store Vitamin K₃ (menadione) for a few days, then stop once the dog looks energetic.
options.why: Livestock Vitamin K₃ (menadione) fails to stop superwarfarin bleeding and actively poisons red blood cells and kidneys—and quitting K₁ early before brodifacoum clears invites lethal rebound hemorrhage.

exam.q: Your two-month-old, 14-pound mixed-breed puppy suddenly develops a tight, swollen belly, paces restlessly, and looks distressed—yet her gums are pink, her temperature is normal, and she isn’t retching at all. What do you do?

options.label: Wait for unproductive retching before going in—bloat is a Great Dane emergency, not a 14-pound puppy problem
options.why: Gastric dilatation-volvulus ignores breed stereotypes: this exact two-month-old 6.4-kg crossbreed puppy had full clockwise torsion and a ‘Popeye arm’ twist with pink gums and zero retching.

options.label: Call the 24-hour ER vet on speaker while loading her now—no waiting, peroxide, or belly pressing
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Sudden abdominal distension plus distress means leave now—sealed gas expansion rapidly compresses the caudal vena cava and threatens gastric-wall ischemia.

options.label: Massage her swollen belly gently, give a splash of hydrogen peroxide, or try relieving the gas yourself at home
options.why: Never squeeze, massage, tube, needle, or give peroxide to a distended dog—clockwise rotation seals off the outflow and turns home fixes lethal.

exam.q: Midway through mowing your yard, a sudden sharp sting hits your upper belly. You shut the mower off, lift your shirt, and see spotless skin with zero blood, yet the deep pain stays severe. What is your move?

options.label: Ice the sore spot on the couch and watch overnight for a bruise, since a real metal puncture would leave an obvious bleeding wound.
options.why: Elastic skin and fat can snap shut behind a 200-mph wire like self-healing rubber, hiding peritoneal penetration while bowel contamination brews silently.

options.label: Seek immediate emergency medical evaluation and tell triage plainly that you felt a sudden strike or sting while mowing the lawn.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Spotless skin and calm early vitals never outrank sudden severe abdominal pain, and naming the mower triggers targeted imaging before complications start.

options.label: Press a clean magnifying glass and tweezers over the tender patch first to check for a splinter before deciding whether to visit urgent care.
options.why: Bathroom tweezers cannot detect a 7-centimeter wire buried beneath muscle and peritoneum, and probing tiny punctures introduces bacteria or dislodges vessel tamponade.

exam.q: Right after a hard sneezing fit, a dark ink-like cloud drops across your right eye. There is zero pain, your eye looks completely normal in the mirror, and it is late evening. What should you do?

options.label: Wait until morning to see if the cloud clears on its own, because true retinal emergencies always cause sharp pain and visible eye redness.
options.why: The retina has zero somatic pain receptors, so severe hemorrhage or retinal detachment can unfold completely painlessly behind a spotless cornea.

options.label: Gently massage the closed eyelid and try bearing down once to test whether the shadow moves before driving yourself to an optometrist.
options.why: Pressing on the globe or repeating a Valsalva strain risks worsening intraocular bleeding, and driving with acute monocular vision loss endangers everyone on the road.

options.label: Have someone else drive you immediately to an emergency room or urgent eye clinic for dilated specialist assessment, despite the lack of pain.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! A painless dark cloud after a sneeze demands urgent specialist evaluation because neither a normal mirror check nor zero pain rules out retinal injury.

exam.q: One of your two lean nine-month-old guinea pigs develops a cloudy eye and ravenous appetite without extra thirst, while her sister looks spotless. What is the safest first step?

options.label: Schedule prompt exotic veterinary evaluation for the cloudy eye, keep normal high-fiber hay flowing, and avoid DIY fasting or home dosing.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Diabetes in guinea pigs can strike without excess thirst, a clear-eyed sibling can hide worse glucose, and sudden fasting risks lethal GI stasis.

options.label: Cut out hay and pellets for 24 hours to reset blood sugar while watching whether her water bottle starts draining faster than usual.
options.why: Withholding food from a hindgut-fermenting guinea pig can trigger fatal gastrointestinal stasis and hepatic lipidosis within 48 hours—far faster than high glucose.

options.label: Relax for a few weeks because young lean guinea pigs rarely get diabetes, and a negative home urine strip rules out dangerous crashes.
options.why: Suspected type 1 diabetes strikes young lean guinea pigs without obvious thirst, and negative urine strips cannot detect insulin-driven hypoglycemia or hidden hyperglycemia in a cage-mate.

exam.q: You feel completely normal—calm pulse, zero tremors—yet routine blood work prints a flatlined TSH of 0.02 and sky-high free T4 while you take daily hair-and-nails vitamins. What is the right call?

options.label: Stop all prescription medications and supplements for exactly one week on your own, then assume any remaining abnormal thyroid test is also a false alarm.
options.why: Never alter prescriptions or invent a solo washout calendar without physician oversight, and taking biotin never grants immunity against genuine coexisting thyroid disease.

options.label: Accept immediate antithyroid drugs or ablation because three calibrated lab values pointing in the exact same biological direction cannot all be wrong together.
options.why: Free biotin breaks both sandwich assays (falsely low TSH) and competitive assays (falsely high free T4/T3) simultaneously, forging an internally consistent fake Graves’ profile.

options.label: Show your doctor exact supplement labels disclosing biotin dose and timing so the care team and lab director can verify whether the assay is vulnerable.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Disclosing vitamin B7 lets clinicians and the lab check streptavidin-biotin interference and retest safely on an unaffected platform before treating a ghost.

exam.q: At a crowded train station, a commuter tumbles down a moving escalator, bangs their head on steel steps, catches a jacket hem near the comb plate, and then insists they feel fine while sitting up dazed. What do you do?

options.label: Yank the trapped jacket straight out of the comb plate yourself and let them catch their train once they prove they can talk and stand.
options.why: Reaching into moving comb plates invites severe hand amputation, and an awake rider after a metal-step head strike can still harbor a lethal, slow-pooling cerebral bleed.

options.label: Keep hands out of the machinery, summon station staff and emergency care for head-strike assessment, and report only the exact sequence you actually witnessed.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Avoiding DIY machinery extraction, getting professional evaluation for blunt head trauma, and giving pure eyewitness facts protect both life and investigation.

options.label: Tell paramedics the escalator definitely jerked violently—even though you only looked up after hearing a shout—so engineers shut down the station immediately.
options.why: Inventing a mechanical failure you never witnessed misdirects engineers and can blind trauma clinicians to an internal pre-fall cardiac event that actually triggered the collapse.

exam.q: A toddler reaches behind a running home treadmill and pulls back with a postage-stamp-sized red friction burn over two knuckles that is barely bleeding at all. What is your next step?

options.label: Press an ice cube onto the knuckles, dab on soothing home ointment, and bandage it since the tiny, dry scrape spared deeper blood vessels.
options.why: Frictional heat cauterizes tiny capillaries to hide deep full-thickness joint damage, while ice chokes off surviving blood supply and ointments trap heat and bacteria.

options.label: Skip ice and home creams, keep any stuck fabric untouched, and take the child promptly for professional medical burn assessment of joint depth.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Postage-stamp 0.3% treadmill burns can expose finger tendons and joint capsules with almost no bleeding, making prompt specialist wound depth assessment essential.

options.label: Wash the blister gently, snip away loose dead skin with clean scissors, and tape a popsicle-stick splint across the knuckles until a checkup next week.
options.why: Never perform home debridement or makeshift splinting on a pediatric friction burn—only sterile specialist evaluation can protect joint capsules and prevent cooling scar contractures.

exam.q: You are a fit 43-year-old non-smoker with zero family heart history. While resting quietly, sudden heavy central chest pain starts radiating down your left arm, though you are not sweating or breathless. What happens next?

options.label: Call emergency medical services immediately instead of driving yourself, knowing that SCAD can strike healthy adults without sweating or ECG changes.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Calling EMS brings cardiac monitoring straight to your door and keeps you from losing consciousness behind the wheel during an occult NSTEMI.

options.label: Wait an hour on the couch and take a brisk walk test, since real heart attacks require cold sweats, nausea, shortness of breath, or high cholesterol.
options.why: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection routinely hits patients with zero conventional risk factors and zero secondary symptoms—waiting or straining risks lethal progression.

options.label: Drive yourself to an urgent-care clinic for a quick ECG and head straight home relieved if the first electrical tracing prints normal sinus rhythm.
options.why: Driving with acute ischemia risks fatal arrhythmia in traffic, and a spotless 12-lead ECG cannot rule out an NSTEMI that only serial troponin and imaging expose.

exam.q: Your three-year-old ferret suddenly goes limp in the hind legs, drools heavily, and starts seizing on the living-room floor, even though he played normally yesterday. What do you do right now?

options.label: Keep all fingers and liquids out of his mouth, move him off high surfaces clear of hard objects, and transport him immediately to emergency veterinary care.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Protecting his airway from aspiration while getting immediate emergency IV stabilization avoids turning a metabolic crash into fatal pneumonia.

options.label: Squirt a syringe of honey water into the side of his mouth immediately to raise blood sugar, then stay home if he perks up playfully by morning.
options.why: Seizing ferrets lose protective swallow reflexes so forced liquid pours into the lungs—and bouncing back on Tuesday never means the underlying insulinoma vanished.

options.label: Record a clear two-minute video of the seizure first, then fast him for several hours before his clinic visit so the veterinarian can witness a real crash.
options.why: Delaying transport for footage or purposefully provoking a hypoglycemic crash risks irreversible brain injury or death when your spoken history already guides testing.

exam.q: Two months after a gastric sleeve, your 22-year-old sister—who takes her oral vitamins daily and is not vomiting—develops worsening leg weakness, jerky eye movements, and mild confusion. What is the critical action?

options.label: Go immediately to emergency care, lead with her gastric sleeve date and family-observed confusion, and let doctors evaluate for urgent IV thiamine.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Compliant oral supplements and normal outward weight never guarantee thiamine absorption, and BOMSS guidelines call for prompt IV thiamine without waiting for lab or MRI confirmation.

options.label: Double her over-the-counter oral multivitamins at home and wait for her scheduled annual bariatric nutrition appointment to test blood levels.
options.why: When gut absorption or utilization is already failing behind a gastric sleeve, waiting on extra oral pills allows preventable central nervous system energy starvation to leave lasting memory deficits.

options.label: Assume a urinary tract infection or multiple sclerosis explains the confusion if her initial brain MRI looks atypical for classic vitamin deficiency.
options.why: A UTI cannot explain torsional or upbeat nystagmus, and classic acute Wernicke’s MRI sensitivity is only about 53%—meaning an atypical scan never rules out brain thiamine starvation.

exam.q: A teenager falls onto a bicycle handlebar while wearing a helmet, has mild initial belly soreness, and an early ER ultrasound is called ‘unremarkable’ without checking pancreatic enzymes. Two days later belly pain worsens with vomiting. What is the safest move?

options.label: Wait another two days with rest and fluids at home since the initial emergency ultrasound already cleared the abdomen
options.why: Bowel gas can obscure the pancreas on early ultrasound, and untested amylase/lipase are blank spaces—not normal clearance. Waiting days risks peritonitis and septic shock.

options.label: Give over-the-counter pain relievers and monitor quietly unless a dark bruise spreads across the upper stomach wall
options.why: Handlebar impacts act like blunt spears that can transect the deep pancreas against the spine with minimal external bruising; masking worsening pain delays surgical rescue.

options.label: Return promptly for urgent evaluation and explicitly report ‘bicycle handlebar struck the abdomen’ plus worsening vomiting
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Naming the handlebar mechanism prompts targeted pancreatic enzyme checks and cross-sectional CT/MRI before leaking enzymes trigger septic shock.

exam.q: A shop air nozzle slips and blasts near a coworker’s left eye. Within minutes the eyelids and cheek puff up dramatically, the eye cannot look upward, and vision turns blurry—yet they insist it doesn’t hurt at all. What happens next?

options.label: Press gently on the cheek to check for crackling air pockets, then measure the compressor PSI so the ER knows the exact force.
options.why: Palpating swollen facial tissue at home can push trapped gas deeper toward the orbit or cranial cavity, and delaying care to test compressor pressure wastes critical time.

options.label: Keep hands off the eye, stop them from driving, and get immediate emergency specialist care reporting compressed-air exposure and vision changes.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Zero pain never clears a compressed-air blast—vision blur and restricted eye movement demand urgent specialist imaging to hunt for orbital gas or skull-vault pneumocephalus.

options.label: Have them rest at home with a cool compress and leftover eye drops unless pain starts or an urgent-care X-ray reveals a broken bone.
options.why: Compressed air can dissect soft tissue into the skull without cracking a single bone or triggering pain, and home drops or wait-and-see plans miss hidden globe or intracranial trauma.

exam.q: Ten days after surgical pinning of your chinchilla’s broken forearm, you notice him eating pellets eagerly and putting weight on the paw—though he still cannot curl his toes around hay. What should you do?

options.label: Put the climbing shelves back into his cage since weight-bearing and a strong appetite mean the bone callus has restored full strength.
options.why: Weight-bearing returns weeks before radiographic bone union, and premature jumping can break a soft callus or rotate an internal pin inside a 0.7-mm bone canal.

options.label: Gently press along his forearm and press a small stick against his toes to check whether the nerve reflex and hardware are aligned properly.
options.why: Never palpate or provoke a healing limb at home; amateur flexing can worsen soft-tissue injury and cannot detect microscopic implant rotation visible only on X-ray.

options.label: Keep the prescribed recovery confinement intact, avoid home limb tests, and report the exact spontaneous difference between standing and grasping to the vet.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Gross weight-bearing, fine-motor grasping, and radiographic union run on separate clocks, so preserving confinement and reporting spontaneous function lets the vet safely guide follow-up imaging.

exam.q: Months after cutting his hand on an unhardened epoxy tool and recovering from forearm lumps, a flooring technician returns to mixing resin and develops violent sneezing every shift that clears on weekends—yet a standard DGEBA patch test comes back negative. What makes sense?

options.label: Assume the sneezing is an unrelated seasonal cold and re-enter the mixing room with standard hardware-store gloves to test whether fumes trigger it again.
options.why: Deliberate self-rechallenge risks worsening sensitization, standard gloves can degrade against specific amine hardeners, and negative DGEBA patch kits never exclude other resin-system chemicals.

options.label: Bring exact site product and SDS inventories plus raw work-versus-weekend timelines to an occupational specialist, while reviewing ventilation and exposure controls.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Nearly one in five confirmed epoxy-allergic workers react to non-DGEBA hardeners or additives, so full chemical inventories and upstream controls matter far more than one negative patch kit.

options.label: Request a repeat CRP blood test and clear him for epoxy work as long as CRP stays under 5 mg/L and no new skin nodules appear on his arm.
options.why: CRP below 5 mg/L stayed silent even while his hand was visibly inflamed, and absent skin bumps never rule out active occupational rhinitis from workplace resin systems.

exam.q: Four days after starting apixaban for a right-arm DVT following heavy swimming, your arm is visibly more swollen and painful, though your home pulse oximeter reads 96% and your wrist pulse feels strong. What is your safest move?

options.label: Use a deep-tissue massage gun along the hardened vein to improve drainage and wait for your scheduled follow-up next week.
options.why: Aggressively massaging or percussing a thrombosed vein risks snapping off clot fragments straight into the pulmonary arteries, and worsening swelling demands early reassessment.

options.label: Double your apixaban dose overnight since a 96% oxygen reading and strong radial pulse prove neither your lungs nor circulation are compromised.
options.why: Never self-adjust anticoagulants—and a strong arterial wrist pulse plus 96% room-air SpO₂ can persist right alongside both total venous outflow obstruction and a segmental lung clot.

options.label: Seek prompt clinical reassessment with an honest timeline of progression and missed doses, and call 911 if chest pain or breathlessness starts.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Persistent or worsening swelling on blood thinners is the exact trigger for imaging the underlying mechanical anatomy, while chest or breathing signs require immediate emergency care.

exam.q: You cooked rice three days ago, stored it in a slightly warm 8–9°C fridge, and now plan to fry it piping hot for dinner—after a tiny test spoonful made you briefly nauseated this morning. What is the right call?

options.label: Stir-fry the rice extra hot until steaming throughout so the high pan temperature destroys both Bacillus cereus and any toxin inside.
options.why: Pan-frying or microwaving kills live Bacillus cereus bacteria, but standard cooking heat cannot break the molecular ring of preformed cereulide toxin.

options.label: Take one more small taste and sniff closely—if the rice smells completely fresh and normal, it is safe to serve to guests.
options.why: Cereulide is completely odorless and tasteless, and taking a ‘check bite’ simply adds another dose of a heat-stable mitochondrial poison.

options.label: Discard the rice immediately, never serve it, and seek medical care if severe vomiting, dehydration, lethargy, or confusion develops.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Three days at 8–9°C lets surviving spores manufacture heat-proof cereulide—and brief early vomiting after a taste is a warning to dump the batch, not fry it hotter.

exam.q: A nonverbal seven-year-old who accepts only dry crackers and cereal develops a worsening limp, refuses to stand, and wakes crying at night—yet has no bleeding gums. What is the right clinical move?

options.label: Withhold her preferred crackers for several days until hunger pushes her to eat citrus fruit, and schedule a routine checkup next month.
options.why: Withholding safe foods from a child with severe sensory food aversion accelerates malnutrition and dehydration—and refusal to bear weight with night pain demands urgent medical care.

options.label: Seek immediate medical evaluation for sudden non-weight-bearing and give clinicians an honest, exact list of every food and drink she actually consumes.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Refusing to bear weight and waking in pain require urgent assessment to distinguish malignancy, infection, and scurvy—and an unvarnished diet inventory supplies the fastest diagnostic clue.

options.label: Rule out vitamin C deficiency at home since scurvy causes bleeding gums first and modern children eating daily calories rarely lack micronutrients.
options.why: Calories supply energy, not the ascorbic acid cofactor needed to cross-link collagen—and modern pediatric scurvy frequently presents with bone pain and limping without textbook bleeding gums.

exam.q: A family member who finished rituximab for lymphoma a month ago and recently started oral steroids develops worsening shortness of breath at rest, cannot finish sentences, and has a new itchy rash—even though a parasite blood antibody test last month was negative. What is your move?

options.label: Call an ambulance immediately, report the lymphoma, recent rituximab and steroids, and hand ER staff the exact wording and date of the negative antibody test.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Gasping at rest and broken sentences require EMS immediately, and naming B-cell-depleting therapy plus exact prior lab wording helps clinicians reopen a silent antibody screen.

options.label: Stop the prescribed oral steroids immediately at home, order an antiparasitic online, and drive them to their routine oncology visit next week.
options.why: Abruptly stopping steroids or self-dosing unprescribed antiparasitics is dangerous, and driving a hypoxic patient who cannot finish sentences delays emergency oxygen and critical care.

options.label: Wait at home until their clinic repeats a white blood cell differential, since a parasitic flare would show elevated eosinophils and a snake-like rash.
options.why: CDC guidance warns that eosinophilia frequently vanishes in severe Strongyloides hyperinfection on steroids, and disseminated rashes can appear as purple spots rather than classic trails.

exam.q: Over three weeks, one koi in your backyard pond develops a steadily swelling belly and stops taking surface pellets while the other fish appear normal. What is the safest course of action?

options.label: Dose the entire pond immediately with broad-spectrum antibiotics and extra salt to cover bacterial dropsy before scheduling a checkup.
options.why: Blind antibiotics cannot treat an internal mass or organ enlargement and can wipe out nitrifying biofilter bacteria, causing an ammonia spike that endangers every healthy fish.

options.label: Net the koi carefully, check whether the belly feels soft or firm, and use a sterile syringe from an online guide to see if fluid drains.
options.why: Handling stress alone can kill a compromised fish, and unguided home needle punctures without anesthesia or ultrasound risk lethal internal hemorrhage or infection.

options.label: Leave the fish unhandled, skip blind pond chemicals, document objective timelines and recent pond changes, and contact an aquatic veterinarian promptly.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Coelomic swelling is only a non-specific check-engine light, so avoiding DIY trauma or biofilter-killing drugs while giving an aquatic vet raw observations protects both fish and pond.

exam.q: A worker catches his metal ring on a moving machine bracket. The ring finger looks pale and numb with an awkwardly angled knuckle, though the skin is still attached. What should happen in the next 60 seconds?

options.label: Leave the ring untouched, skip ice packs and home pulse-ox checks, keep him from driving, and summon emergency care reporting the snag mechanism and numbness.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Numbness and an odd knuckle angle signal potential neurovascular transection and joint dislocation—leaving the ring for specialist cutters and avoiding vasoconstricting ice protects remaining tissue.

options.label: Pack the finger tightly in ice to slow swelling, carefully work the ring off with soap, and drive him to urgent care if an X-ray shows a fracture.
options.why: Ice causes severe vasoconstriction that accelerates ischemic tissue death, pulling the ring can sever surviving vessels, and ring avulsions routinely destroy blood flow with zero bone fracture.

options.label: Clip a home pulse oximeter onto the fingertip to verify circulation and wait two hours to see whether warmth returns before calling emergency transport.
options.why: Consumer oximeters cannot rule out transected digital arteries in severe soft-tissue trauma, and waiting on an imagined ischemic clock wastes irreplaceable minutes.

exam.q: A four-year-old suddenly begins stumbling and losing leg strength, then develops drooping eyelids and rapid, shallow breathing—with no remembered woods trip or tick bite. What is your immediate priority?

options.label: Call 911 immediately for emergency airway evaluation and report the exact onset and upward progression of weakness to clinicians.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Rapid shallow breathing and drooping eyelids signal threatened airway and diaphragm failure—emergency stabilization always comes first, even with zero recalled outdoor exposure.

options.label: Put her in a hot shower right away and spend an hour combing through her hair at home to dislodge any hidden tick before calling a doctor.
options.why: Never delay emergency care to conduct a home tick search, and a hot shower will not reliably detach an engorged tick cemented into skin by barbed mouthparts.

options.label: Give a leftover oral antibiotic to neutralize tick neurotoxin and monitor overnight unless she starts complaining of skin numbness.
options.why: Antibiotics never neutralize tick salivary neurotoxin, and sensory pathways can stay completely intact even while motor paralysis shuts down breathing muscles.

exam.q: Two days after returning to sea level from a trip above 10,000 feet, a healthy young adult with no known medical conditions develops worsening upper-left abdominal pain radiating to the left shoulder and mild yellowing of the eyes. What is the safest move?

options.label: Seek immediate medical evaluation and report the exact mountain elevation and descent timeline—without waiting for trait testing or assuming sea-level air will reverse the pain.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Most patients in Colorado’s splenic-infarct referral series did not know they carried sickle cell trait beforehand, left-shoulder pain signals diaphragmatic irritation from an injured spleen, and sea-level air cannot reverse infarcted tissue.

options.label: Rest overnight with extra fluids since returning to sea level restores normal oxygen saturation and stops high-altitude illness.
options.why: Descending restores ambient oxygen, not necrotic splenic tissue; waiting out worsening upper-left abdominal and referred shoulder pain risks missed splenic infarction or rupture.

options.label: Order an outpatient hemoglobin electrophoresis test first and go to the emergency room only if the HbS percentage exceeds 50%.
options.why: Never delay emergency care for lab confirmation—and sickle cell trait typically sits below 50% HbS (40% in the Ecuador case), where protein fraction never serves as a safe-vs-unsafe threshold.

exam.q: An older relative with mild chronic kidney disease suddenly stops passing much urine, develops leg swelling, and passes black tarry stools over three days—yet feels no chest pain, has clear breathing, and sees no red blood in the toilet. What is the right move?

options.label: Have them drink extra water over the weekend to flush the kidneys, and wait for routine clinic blood work unless they start coughing up blood.
options.why: Pushing water onto failing kidneys can trigger dangerous fluid overload, and severe renal-limited anti-GBM disease plus GI bleeding can escalate to lethal potassium levels with completely clear lungs.
