options.label: Seek urgent emergency care right away, bringing any old baseline kidney lab numbers plus their full prescription and supplement list.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Sudden oliguria and black stools demand immediate stabilization for dangerous potassium, acid, and GI bleeding, while old baseline creatinine values immediately prove an acute drop.

options.label: Stop their blood-pressure pills at home and wait to consent to emergency treatments until autoimmune antibody results come back from the lab.
options.why: Never stop prescribed medications solo or delay urgent stabilization like dialysis or transfusions for specialized serology—metabolic crises kill long before antibody panels finish.

exam.q: After playing along a crystal-clear lake shoreline in February, your dog suddenly begins shaking, loses coordination, and vomits while you are rinsing him off. What should you do right now?

options.label: Induce vomiting immediately at home so he clears any swallowed shoreline plants before driving to the clinic.
options.why: Never induce vomiting in a neurologically impaired dog—impaired airway reflexes can send vomit straight into the lungs, causing fatal aspiration.

options.label: Walk back down to the beach first to scoop a jar of shoreline debris for lab confirmation, since clear winter water rarely carries algae.
options.why: Benthic cyanobacterial mats thrive beneath crystal-clear water even in winter, and delaying emergency supportive veterinary care to collect environmental samples costs irreplaceable minutes.

options.label: Stop him from licking his coat, transport him immediately to an emergency vet, and report the exact lake access point, timing, and any shoreline mat contact.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! There is no specific antidote for dihydroanatoxin-a, so blocking further ingestion and rushing straight to emergency supportive veterinary care is the only lifeline.

exam.q: A friend accidentally sweeps a red laser pointer labeled '5 mW' across your right eye for two seconds. Your eye feels zero pain and looks completely white, yet a small blurry dark spot sits in the middle of words when you read. What is your move?

options.label: Skip driving, arrange immediate specialist eye assessment, and report the affected eye, exact central reading blind spot, and laser exposure—without waiting to verify device power.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Retinal photoreceptors have no pain nerves, printed 5-mW labels cannot be verified at home, and immediate specialist imaging (OCT/autofluorescence) is needed regardless of pain.

options.label: Print an eye chart and Amsler grid at home; if you can still read the 20/20 line tomorrow morning, skip the clinic since the label caps power at 5 milliwatts.
options.why: Patients with permanent foveal laser burns can score 20/20 on a distance wall chart while retaining a persistent central scotoma, and cheap online pointers are frequently mislabeled.

options.label: Put on dark UV sunglasses and shine the laser onto a dark notebook cover to see whether it smokes so you can tell the doctor if it is truly overpowered.
options.why: Ordinary sunglasses do not block coherent laser beams, and specular reflections off household surfaces can inflict a second permanent retinal burn.

exam.q: A denture wearer whose plates have grown loose over the past few years notices persistent dizziness, pale skin, a pounding heartbeat, and new tingling in both feet—though a home pulse oximeter reads 98%. What is the safest action?

options.label: Stop using the denture adhesive, seek prompt medical evaluation (or emergency transport if palpitations persist or pair with chest pain, breathlessness, or faintness), bring the adhesive tube and all product lists, and never self-prescribe copper pills.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! A 98% pulse oximeter cannot detect catastrophic anemia, tingling extremities are an explicit FDA warning sign to halt adhesive use and see a physician, and full product disclosure plus monitored clinical care solve the crisis safely.

options.label: Reassure yourself with the 98% oxygen reading, switch to a slightly thinner layer of the same paste, and add over-the-counter copper tablets to rebalance your minerals at home.
options.why: Pulse oximetry measures hemoglobin saturation percentage—not total hemoglobin volume—and playing bathroom chemist with unmonitored copper pills risks swinging into a separate trace-metal toxicity.

options.label: Drive straight to a blood-draw lab to request an isolated serum ferritin test before calling a doctor, since normal ferritin rules out severe blood-production problems.
options.why: Never drive yourself when dizzy with severe palpitations—and ferritin is an acute-phase reactant that sat at a deceptively normal 47.7 ng/mL even while the primary patient’s hemoglobin was 4.5 g/dL.

exam.q: A 42-year-old adult develops unexplained amenorrhea, intense thirst, weight loss, and a mildly elevated ALT of 51 U/L (reference 5–40), followed later by confirmed HJV-related iron overload. Which clinical move reflects sound evidence?

options.label: Dismiss HJV hemochromatosis because ‘juvenile’ onset stops before age 30 and an ALT of 51 rules out heavy liver iron deposition.
options.why: ‘Juvenile’ is historical shorthand rather than an age exclusion—both HJV sisters presented at ages 37 and 52 with identical ALTs of 51 despite massive biopsy-proven liver iron loading.

options.label: Connect the multi-system symptoms for coordinated specialist workup, pursue physician-directed phlebotomy with ongoing organ surveillance even after ferritin normalizes, and arrange formal genetics-led family evaluation.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Bridging endocrine and liver silos catches systemic iron overload, monitored phlebotomy halts ongoing oxidation without guaranteeing automatic organ reversal, and formal genetics cleanly distinguishes carriers from affected relatives.

options.label: Once phlebotomy drops serum ferritin below 50 ng/mL, discontinue endocrinology and cardiology follow-up and maintain iron control with regular community blood drives and green tea.
options.why: Dropping ferritin stops ongoing metal accumulation but does not automatically repair damaged pancreatic beta cells, liver scarring, or heart muscle—and DIY blood drives or green-tea protocols are never substitutes for medical management.

exam.q: You buy a native-species newt at an amphibian expo; the breeder shows a plump, active animal and a negative Bsal qPCR lab report from three weeks ago. Two weeks after bringing it home, another salamander in your room develops skin erosions and stops moving normally. What is the right protocol?

options.label: Release the healthy-looking native newt into a nearby natural stream so it escapes the tank outbreak, then treat the sick salamander with an aquarium-forum chemical bath.
options.why: Never release any captive amphibian—even a native species carries global captive-trade exposure history and can ignite a wildlife catastrophe—and DIY forum baths risk harm while delaying diagnosis.

options.label: Walk straight into the nearest small-animal veterinary waiting room with the sick salamander while assuming the new acquisition is cleared by its three-week-old negative PCR.
options.why: Unannounced clinic entry risks contaminating waiting rooms with resilient spores, and a three-week-old negative PCR is only a past snapshot—not permanent clearance.

options.label: Call an amphibian-experienced veterinarian before transporting the animal, halt all transfers and tank shuffles, share exact species and movement records, follow local wildlife reporting rules, and secure professional disposal plans for tank water and materials.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Calling ahead enables clinic isolation, freezing movement contains network uncertainty, movement ledgers guide tracing, and keeping captive animals and untreated tank water away from wild ecosystems prevents ecological spillover.

exam.q: While vaccinating a calf, a coworker is knocked beneath a metal gate and stomped by the mother cow. He pulls himself outside the fence fully alert, speaking clearly, and complains only of shortness of breath and soreness. What is the safest immediate response?

options.label: Call 911 immediately, clearly report the gate-and-cow crush mechanism alongside pasture access and animal location, keep bystanders out of the unsafe pen, and wait for EMS transport rather than driving him in a pickup.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Alertness (GCS 15) and an isolated breathing complaint can mask 13 broken rib levels, pneumothorax, and solid-organ lacerations; reporting the crush mechanism triggers proper trauma triage, and EMS can decompress a tension pneumothorax en route.

options.label: Load him into the passenger seat of a farm truck and drive rapidly to the nearest clinic because he is fully awake and waiting for an ambulance wastes precious minutes.
options.why: Driving a crush-trauma patient down bumpy rural roads risks turning a simple lung air leak into a fatal tension pneumothorax miles from emergency chest decompression.

options.label: Monitor him at the farmhouse for a few hours and call emergency services only if he starts coughing up blood or loses consciousness.
options.why: NHS rib-injury guidance stresses that serious accidents and worsening breathlessness warrant immediate emergency evaluation without waiting for multiple severe symptoms to stack up.

exam.q: Someone with months of clear watery drainage strictly from the left nostril and a headache that eases when lying flat suddenly develops fever, a stiff neck, and confusion—with no skin rash. What is the safest move?

options.label: Seek immediate emergency medical care for suspected meningitis without waiting for a rash or fluid testing, and disclose the months of unilateral watery drainage and positional headache.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Fever, neck stiffness, severe headache, and confusion are immediate meningitis red flags—bacterial meningitis frequently lacks a rash, and linking unilateral clear rhinorrhea alerts clinicians to an underlying skull-base breach.

options.label: Bear down firmly to collect a sample on a deep nasal swab and taste a drop for sweetness so the urgent-care clinic can confirm CSF before starting antibiotics.
options.why: Straining raises intracranial pressure, deep nasal probing shoves bacteria straight toward an open skull defect, and taste tests are useless internet mythology.

options.label: Take an extra dose of over-the-counter allergy medication and wait 24 hours to see whether a classic purple rash appears, since a prior sinus CT already read chronic sinusitis.
options.why: A prior routine sinus CT cannot exclude a subtle sphenoid skull-base defect or meningocele, and waiting for a rash during acute neurological deterioration can turn fatal.

exam.q: A 48-year-old mechanic who often smacks stubborn fittings with the heel of his palm notices a firm lump on the pinky side of his right hand, and two months later his right ring finger turns pale, ice-cold, and numb while his left hand stays warm. What is the safest course?

options.label: Plunge both hands into ice water to record a video proving Raynaud’s phenomenon and wait until a routine appointment next month if he can still feel his wrist pulse.
options.why: Home cold provocation is unsafe, symmetric wrist pulses did not rule out bilateral ulnar aneurysms in the 2022 case, and new unilateral ischemia with numbness cannot wait weeks.

options.label: Reassure himself that the warm left hand proves his systemic circulation is fine, switch to thicker padded work gloves, and keep working until the lump shrinks.
options.why: A perfectly warm opposite hand can still hide a 7-millimeter silent aneurysm via collateral flow, and generic glove swaps cannot rescue an acutely starved fingertip.

options.label: Seek immediate emergency vascular assessment for suspected acute perfusion loss, report the exact onset time, palm lump, and tool-impact history, and stop using the palm as a striking tool.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! New unilateral pallor, coldness, and numbness starting after age 30 break benign Raynaud’s rules and fit acute perfusion red flags—demanding urgent care first and ergonomic review afterward.

exam.q: Five days after a mild summer fever and an evening hike, your partner wakes up dragging one leg with new back pain, though they have zero memory of a mosquito bite, can feel light touch on the foot clearly, and notice mild shortness of breath. What is the safest move?

options.label: Test their knee-jerk reflex with a kitchen spoon at home and wait until morning, since preserved foot sensation and no remembered bite point to a pulled hiking muscle.
options.why: Anterior horn spinal injury destroys motor neurons while leaving adjacent sensory pathways intact, most bites go unremembered, and amateur home reflex testing generates dangerous false reassurance.

options.label: Call emergency services immediately—reporting the exact fever, weakness, breathing change, and outdoor timeline—because ascending neuroinvasive weakness can threaten respiratory muscles fast.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! New unexplained weakness paired with any breathing change is a drop-everything emergency (12 of 32 paralyzed patients in Colorado needed ventilation), and concrete functional timelines guide urgent clinical localization.

options.label: Drive to an urgent-care clinic and ask only for a blood sugar and basic chemistry panel, since normal routine blood work and normal CSF glucose rule out viral spinal cord infection.
options.why: Routine blood summaries and CSF glucose (52 mg/dL) were completely normal in the 2024 case—viruses lack bacterial sugar metabolism, and acute weakness with breathing trouble belongs in an emergency department via EMS.

exam.q: Your 10-year-old dog had a pacemaker placed three years ago for heart block and has thrived ever since. After two weeks of a new daily cough, she wakes at 2 a.m. breathing rapidly with her mouth open and bluish gums. What is the right immediate action?

options.label: Spend twenty minutes locating her original implant serial card and surgical printout before driving to the ER, since emergency vets cannot examine a paced dog without full device paperwork.
options.why: Never delay oxygen for paperwork—grab whatever records are handy, tell the ER she has a pacemaker when you call ahead from the road, and let clinicians stabilize her breathing first.

options.label: Gently press over the pacemaker generator under her neck skin to verify it is intact and start a low-dose blood thinner until her scheduled cardiology check in two weeks.
options.why: Never manipulate an implanted device or self-prescribe anticoagulants—and a flawlessly firing pacemaker still cannot prevent a pulmonary clot or stop active cyanosis.

options.label: Transport her immediately to an emergency veterinary hospital, calling ahead so an oxygen cage is ready and immediately notifying the team that she has a permanent pacemaker.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Per Cornell emergency guidance, open-mouth resting dyspnea and cyanotic gums are immediate life threats demanding urgent oxygen—and early disclosure of the implant steers both emergency stabilization and cardiology coordination.

exam.q: A child with short bowel syndrome who drinks from a private home well wakes up slurring words and stumbling, though by arrival in the ER his exam looks calmer and both routine lactate and brain MRI return normal. What is the safest next step?

options.label: Advocate for full evaluation of his short-bowel history—asking specifically whether a separate D-lactate assay is being run—while keeping hydration strictly under specialist ORS guidance and having the private well tested at a state-certified laboratory.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Metabolic encephalopathy waxes and wanes, routine L-lactate assays are blind to bacterial D-lactate, plain water worsens SBS electrolyte loss, and state-certified well testing catches hidden environmental coliforms.

options.label: Take him home once a stool PCR flags norovirus, encourage extra glasses of clear well water to flush out stomach bugs, and add an over-the-counter Lactobacillus probiotic.
options.why: Norovirus does not explain acute ataxia, extra plain water osmotically strips electrolytes in short bowel syndrome, and unvetted Lactobacillus probiotics can literally manufacture more neurotoxic D-lactate.

options.label: Wait at home unless E. coli shows up on a hardware-store water test strip, since a normal routine lactate and ‘not detected’ E. coli prove both the child and the well are safe.
options.why: Routine lactate ignores D-lactate, hardware test strips cannot replace state-certified labs, and ‘not detected’ E. coli only means below the 1.0 MPN limit—this family’s well had ND E. coli alongside >200.5 MPN/100 mL total coliforms.

exam.q: A patient with newly confirmed Type 1 hereditary angioedema wakes up with a swollen upper lip and feels their throat beginning to tighten. They have no itchy hives. What is the safest immediate response?

options.label: Take a double dose of antihistamine and drink a tall glass of water to test whether the airway is truly narrowing before deciding whether to drive to urgent care.
options.why: Waiting on antihistamines wastes precious airway minutes on a non-histamine bradykinin cascade, and a forced swallow test risks aspiration or complete laryngeal spasm.

options.label: Call emergency services immediately rather than driving, follow their specialist-prescribed HAE emergency plan, and present their bradykinin-mediated diagnosis and records at triage.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Upper-airway swelling is an immediate ambulance emergency because laryngeal edema progresses non-linearly, and clear upfront HAE documentation overrides ER allergy anchoring.

options.label: Assume it is harmless because they have no family history of throat attacks and stop taking their prescribed blood-pressure pills immediately while waiting two days for it to self-resolve.
options.why: Laryngeal attacks can turn fatal rapidly regardless of family history, and while ACE inhibitors require medical review and switching in HAE, airway compromise requires emergency care first.

exam.q: A researcher working with live vaccinia accidentally pricks her finger through a glove during an evening bench session. Her puncture looks microscopic, and she worries an ER physician won’t recognize the strain. What is the safest immediate action?

options.label: Wash immediately, initiate the institution’s occupational exposure pathway (or go straight to emergency care for severe acute injury), explicitly report the exact agent and biosafety officer’s contact without bringing any vial or swab, and lock down contact precautions plus a 48-hour follow-up plan.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Bringing exact agent intelligence and biosafety contacts—never contaminated vials—steers clinicians past routine Staph algorithms while locking in contact precautions before viral replication escalates.

options.label: Seal the contaminated syringe in a Ziploc bag to hand straight to the ER triage nurse so clinicians can run PCR immediately, then wait six days—the historical CDC median—if the skin stays calm.
options.why: Never transport live pathogens into a public waiting room, and the CDC 2008 series’ 6-day median delay documented a dangerous access failure—never a safe waiting period.

options.label: Run a single surface swab on day two; if the lab returns ‘inconclusive,’ assume the wash removed all virus and return to normal duties without covering the finger.
options.why: Inconclusive swabs in the 2019 case lacked a human DNA adequacy signal—meaning the swab failed to capture enough cells to test—never ruling out replicating deep-tissue vaccinia.

exam.q: You walk into the barn at dusk and see a small trickle of blood from both nostrils of your gelding; within ten minutes the bleeding stops completely and he stands quietly. What is the safest action?

options.label: Load him immediately into your horse trailer and haul him rapidly over rural roads to the clinic while checking up his nostrils with a flashlight before departure.
options.why: Never probe a bleeding horse’s nose or trailer blindly without veterinary direction—loading stress, blood-pressure spikes, or disturbing a fragile pouch clot can trigger instant fatal carotid hemorrhage.

options.label: Keep the horse quiet, avoid probing or trailering blindly, and call an emergency equine veterinarian immediately to report the bleed, timing, and any subtle breathing or swallowing signs so the vet directs exam and transport decisions.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Even a self-stopping small bleed can be a sentinel event held back only by a fragile arterial clot—immediate veterinary escalation and letting professionals direct movement protect the dam.

options.label: Wait until morning since the bleeding stopped, and test his swallowing with watery soaked grain tonight to make sure his cranial nerves are unaffected.
options.why: Never wait out a stopped nosebleed, and never run DIY swallow or watery-feed experiments—if cranial nerves are impaired, forced feeding drives food straight into the lungs as fatal aspiration pneumonia.

exam.q: A lean patient with no diabetes symptoms gets a routine CE-HPLC HbA1c of 10.0%—and an automated portal alert displays an estimated average glucose of 240 mg/dL—yet recent fasting glucoses sit in the 80s and a post-breakfast glucose measured 89 mg/dL. What is the safest clinical next step?

options.label: Bring complete lab reports with explicit fasting versus post-meal context to the clinician, ask the laboratory to investigate hemoglobin-variant interference using a chemically distinct assay (such as an enzymatic method) plus alternative markers, and make no unilateral medication changes.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! In Mulpuri’s 2023 case, switching from charge-based CE-HPLC to an enzymatic assay dropped HbA1c from 9.9%–10.1% to 5.4% and unmasked silent Hemoglobin Wayne I—whereas repeating the same column or trusting ADAG’s eAG formula only recycles the illusion.

options.label: Order a second CE-HPLC HbA1c at the same hospital lab to see if the first draw was a clerical typo, and treat the automated 240 mg/dL estimated average glucose as independent mathematical confirmation.
options.why: Repeating the same vulnerable CE-HPLC column faithfully reproduces co-elution every time, and the 2008 ADAG eAG equation explicitly excluded hemoglobinopathies—it merely translates a false input into a 132-point phantom average.

options.label: Assume a confirmed silent hemoglobin variant permanently rules out diabetes for life, erase the erroneous 10.0% reading from the chart, and skip future glycemic monitoring unless overt symptoms appear.
options.why: A hemoglobin variant never immunizes anyone against developing true diabetes later in life, and erasing chart history invites future clinics—especially after analyzer upgrades—to repeat the exact same diagnostic trap.

exam.q: Your aging pet sugar glider starts skipping favorite foods and dragging his hind legs. An online husbandry group insists it is either calcium deficiency or iron overload and urges dosing calcium tonight while stripping all iron from his diet. What is the safest action?

options.label: Give over-the-counter calcium immediately and switch to an iron-free homemade diet derived from Taiwan’s 2022 ALT reference table before calling a clinic.
options.why: Unprescribed supplements risk toxicity and alter diagnostic clues, stripping essential iron risks fatal anemia, and Lin’s 2022 ALT range (24.9–189.4 U/L in adults ≤7 years) can never be converted into a safe dietary iron formula.

options.label: Demand an immediate liver biopsy and routine serum iron screening panel at the nearest general dog-and-cat clinic so you can confirm hemochromatosis tonight.
options.why: Living liver biopsies in a sick ~82-gram glider carry immense hemorrhage and anesthetic risk requiring specialist judgment, and routine serum iron panels lack validated living diagnostic cutoffs for sugar gliders.

options.label: Contact a qualified exotic veterinarian promptly (or immediately for collapse, seizures, or open-mouth breathing), withhold DIY supplements or panicked iron elimination, and bring complete logs of every food brand, treat, and powder for professional assessment.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Hind-limb weakness is a check-engine light with multiple possible causes—from metabolic bone disease and trauma to the swollen kidneys and multi-organ failure seen alongside liver hemochromatosis in Nojiri’s 14-year-old glider.

exam.q: A frail hospitalized relative taking ordinary daily doses of paracetamol (acetaminophen) has eaten almost nothing for two weeks and suddenly develops deep, rapid breathing and marked drowsiness. What is the safest immediate step?

options.label: Alert the bedside medical team or emergency services immediately, provide the complete list of all prescription and OTC paracetamol/acetaminophen products plus the exact two-week nutritional decline, and avoid DIY acid-neutralizing fixes or unilateral medication experiments.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! In Eid’s 2024 case and 2024 EMA guidance, severe breathing changes or reduced responsiveness during therapeutic paracetamol plus malnutrition require immediate clinical evaluation—where doctors can check albumin-corrected anion gaps even if arterial pH still reads 7.40.

options.label: Reassure yourself because their total daily paracetamol stayed at 1–2 grams—far below acute overdose thresholds—and check whether their arterial pH is near 7.40 before escalating.
options.why: Pyroglutamic acidosis occurs at ordinary 1–2 g/day therapeutic doses when cysteine-depleted malnutrition breaks glutathione feedback, and Eid’s patient maintained a deceptive 7.40 pH while bicarbonate crashed to 13 mmol/L.

options.label: Wait to see if a specialized urine organic acid test comes back positive first, and once a repeat urine test later normalizes, automatically restart daily paracetamol at the rehabilitation facility.
options.why: Never delay emergency evaluation waiting on mass-spectrometry urine tests, and a normalized repeat urine profile only shows the loop paused—it never grants automatic clearance to restart paracetamol before whole-body nutritional recovery.

exam.q: A boater spots a loggerhead turtle floating sluggishly near shore with no visible shell damage or cuts, snapping abruptly whenever the boat drifts closer. Based on Parga’s 2020 study and NOAA public guidance, what is the safest response?

options.label: Keep a safe distance, never chase or prod the turtle, and immediately report exact coordinates and visual observations to authorized wildlife responders.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Scratch-free shells and snapping reflexes never rule out vascular gas embolism or aspiration—distance, exact observations, and trained authorized responders protect both animal and boater.

options.label: Assume the snapping proves vigorous health and herd the turtle toward deeper water so it can self-recompress any nitrogen bubbles.
options.why: Hyper-reactive snapping can be an agonizing pain response to expanding internal bubbles, NOAA strictly forbids chasing or corralling, and telemetry never proved self-recompression as a field rescue tactic.

options.label: Haul the turtle aboard to test its reflexes for two hours and improvise a pressurized recovery tank if it stays weak.
options.why: Holding a turtle at surface pressure can worsen expanding vascular bubbles, prodding reflexes causes harm, and hyperbaric therapy in Spain was specialized n = 2 clinical care—never a DIY procedure.

exam.q: A 68-year-old relative who has taken an olmesartan blood pressure pill smoothly for four years develops weeks of severe diarrhea, vomiting, and weight loss; emergency IV fluids bring creatinine back to normal and blood albumin reads normal, yet bowel symptoms keep raging. What is the safest next step?

options.label: Ensure continued prompt clinical investigation with a full list of all long-term prescriptions and combination pills, recognize that normal albumin and improved kidney labs do not prove intestinal healing, and never stop or swap blood pressure medication without clinician oversight.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! In Kulai et al.’s 2016 case, normal albumin (40 g/L) and 5-day kidney recovery masked near-complete duodenal villous atrophy—resolving the root cause requires coordinated medical evaluation and supervised antihypertensive substitution, never unilateral pill stoppage.

options.label: Stop taking the olmesartan pill immediately on your own tonight and launch a self-directed heavy wheat-bread challenge at home to rule out celiac disease before calling the clinic.
options.why: Never abruptly quit blood pressure medication on your own—uncontrolled hypertension risks stroke, heart attack, and kidney failure—and DIY gluten experiments can derail legitimate clinical celiac workups.

options.label: Close the case and wait it out at home with ginger ale, since four trouble-free years clear a daily medication and five days of normalized kidney blood work prove the intestine has recovered.
options.why: Olmesartan enteropathy can emerge after years of uneventful use, and IV fluid resuscitation resets kidney filtration on a far faster clock than intestinal villi can regrow (14 weeks in Kulai’s patient).

exam.q: While hiking public land, you spot a dead eagle with visibly singed feathers lying directly beneath a wooden power pole. Based on Thomason et al. (2023) and the 2024 USGS avian electrocution case definition, what is the safest and most accurate action?

options.label: Walk underneath the pole to flip the bird over for entrance wounds, collect a singed feather as evidence, and tell the utility company that electrocution is confirmed.
options.why: Approaching power infrastructure risks lethal arc or step-potential shock, handling remains or taking feathers violates the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, and external visuals cannot confirm electrocution or rule out gunshot.

options.label: Stay far clear of the electrical infrastructure and remains, contact the appropriate local or regional wildlife authority from a safe distance, and report exact location plus visual observations without declaring electrocution as a proven cause.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Keeping distance prevents electrical injury, hands-off reporting preserves legal custody, and under the 2024 USGS definition and Jordan Valley case, only laboratory radiography and pathology can distinguish electrocution from concealed gunshot.

options.label: Assume shooting is the guaranteed cause since 66.3% of all wild birds in the western United States are shot, and call an out-of-state federal reporting hotline.
options.why: The 66.3% figure (116/175) applies strictly to assigned causes along selected power-line corridors—not all wild U.S. birds (and 116/410 is 28.3% of total remains)—and reports must go to the correct local/regional authority without assuming a verdict.

exam.q: Three years after an emergency abdominal surgery where the hospital discharge note recorded a correct sponge count, a patient develops worsening abdominal pain, cannot pass gas or stool, and feels a firm lump despite an earlier routine ultrasound calling it a benign cyst. What is the safest response?

options.label: Stay home and press firmly on the lump to check whether it feels fluid-filled, since three years is well past the two-year window and a recorded “correct” surgical count rules out retained material.
options.why: Never probe an abdominal mass at home, two years is one individual timeline rather than a safe expiration window (retained items can surface decades later), and 199 of 247 performed counts in retained-sponge sentinel events were recorded as “correct.”

options.label: Drive yourself to a routine outpatient clinic next week to demand a specific blood panel that checks for woven cotton fibers.
options.why: Inability to pass gas or stool with worsening abdominal pain is an NHS emergency red flag for bowel obstruction requiring immediate emergency services (not self-driving or waiting), and standard blood panels cannot detect cotton textiles.

options.label: Call local emergency services immediately without driving yourself, share your full prior surgical history and approximate dates alongside the earlier ultrasound result, and let emergency clinicians reassess the evolving symptoms.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Inability to pass stool or gas with pain signals urgent bowel-obstruction risk requiring ambulance care, provisional ultrasound labels can evolve when adhesions shift, and clear surgical history equips clinicians to look past old paperwork.

exam.q: A homeowner spots a strangely quiet, apathetic juvenile raccoon sitting motionless beside their backyard porch in broad daylight while their dog barks from the patio door. What is the safest response?

options.label: Put on gardening gloves, place the quiet raccoon in a cardboard box in the car, and drive it home or to a clinic yourself since there is no visible diarrhea or bleeding.
options.why: Prey-wired wildlife mask severe systemic illness until collapse—in Pütsch et al.’s 2025 report, both fatally co-infected sanctuary raccoons showed only brief apathy with zero observed diarrhea before sudden death, and CDC guidance strictly advises against handling or transporting sick wildlife.

options.label: Assume it is harmless because wildlife surveys find parvovirus DNA in healthy-looking hunted raccoons, leave food outside to help it recover, and let your vaccinated dog sniff it through the fence.
options.why: Feeding wildlife congregates animals and spreads disease, juvenile or imperfect immunity is never an excuse to allow wildlife contact, and while PCR detection in wild raccoons does not equal tissue disease, physical distance remains the primary One Health barrier.

options.label: Bring the dog indoors immediately, maintain strict physical distance without feeding or touching the raccoon, contact local animal control or authorized wildlife services, and keep pets current on veterinarian-managed core vaccines.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Physical distance protects both people and pets from potential zoonotic or cross-species pathogens while letting authorized wildlife professionals evaluate sick animals safely.

exam.q: Three weeks after starting allopurinol—having skipped genetic testing—a patient develops a spreading measles-like body rash, fever, and diarrhea, but has zero mouth sores or skin blisters. An HLA-B*58:01 blood test was just ordered and will take days to return. What is the safest action?

options.label: Wait safely at home until the HLA-B*58:01 genetic report comes back, since the absence of mouth blisters rules out severe internal organ drug reactions like DRESS.
options.why: In Lucas & Droney’s 2022 case, the patient had zero mucosal lesions yet suffered acute kidney injury (creatinine 214 µmol/L) and liver injury (ALT/AST 224 U/L)—DRESS is a clinical diagnosis that never waits on DNA paperwork.

options.label: Seek immediate clinical evaluation right now based on the rash and systemic symptoms—with bloodwork to assess kidneys, liver, and blood cells—rather than waiting on pending HLA results or mouth sores.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Real-time symptoms and organ labs write the DRESS diagnosis while the house is on fire; HLA-B*58:01 explains genetic susceptibility but never substitutes for urgent clinical assessment.

options.label: Assume a consumer DNA ancestry kit taken two years ago clears them of severe allopurinol reactions, and restart a smaller test dose once the skin redness begins fading.
options.why: Consumer ancestry kits never replace validated clinical genotyping, skin often clears while internal liver injury still worsens, and culprit drugs must never be restarted or micro-dosed after suspected DRESS.

exam.q: Minutes after eating an amusement-park liquid nitrogen snack—having waited until the smoking vapor cloud disappeared—a teenager develops sudden severe abdominal pain, visible belly swelling, and shortness of breath, yet reports zero mouth burns or sore throat. What is the safest response?

options.label: Call emergency medical services immediately, give zero water, milk, food, or antacids, avoid touching or tasting the leftover snack, and report the suspected liquid nitrogen exposure with exact timing and any existing photo or receipt.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! In Kim’s 2018 case, a 13-year-old suffered a 4 cm stomach perforation with zero mouth or throat injury; immediate EMS without oral fluids protects the sterile peritoneal cavity while giving surgeons vital exposure history.

options.label: Offer a glass of milk to coat the stomach and wait to see if the gas passes, since the vapor cloud had already vanished and an unburned throat rules out deep cryogenic stomach injury.
options.why: Fading fog never proves safe internal temperature, a spotless throat never rules out a ruptured stomach, and pouring milk or water into a perforated organ floods the sterile abdominal cavity.

options.label: Delay calling EMS long enough to smell and taste the bottom of the snack cup for doctors, then call Poison Control first while massaging the swollen abdomen to help vent trapped nitrogen.
options.why: Never risk cryogenic self-injury playing detective, never massage an acute surgical abdomen, and never let Poison Control calls delay physical emergency care when severe pain, distension, or breathlessness hits.

exam.q: A woman with a history of recurrent hydronephrosis and regular 28-day periods has her right ureteral double-J stent removed after a completely normal cystoscopy. Less than a day later, she produces zero urine and develops worsening right flank pain. What is the safest response?

options.label: Drink large glasses of water and cranberry juice to flush the blockage and wait a full 24 hours, since normal cystoscopy cleared the urinary lining and normal periods rule out endometriosis.
options.why: Forcing fluids into a clamped ureter spikes destructive hydrostatic pressure inside the kidney, cystoscopy cannot see extrinsic scar tissue outside the pipe, and normal 28-day cycles never rule out ureteral endometriosis.

options.label: Seek immediate emergency evaluation without forcing fluids, and tell triage the exact flank pain side, sudden anuria, prior hydronephrosis, and recent stent removal so clinicians can urgently scan and relieve any upstream blockage.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! In Al Ayoubi et al.’s 2025 case, complete anuria struck within 24 hours of stent removal with an empty bladder beneath a swollen right kidney—urgent assessment and decompression protect remaining renal function immediately.

options.label: Skip the emergency room and schedule a routine gynecology visit next month, because painless or regular periods mean the kidney back pressure is mild and reversible.
options.why: Pain and renal function do not move together—in Yang et al.’s 2021 surgical cohort, 19 of 40 patients (48%) with hydronephrosis were completely asymptomatic, and acute anuria requires immediate emergency decompression.

exam.q: A patient with long-standing cardiomyopathy and active lupus on hydroxychloroquine has recently lost substantial weight and developed worsening kidney labs. Tonight she becomes severely breathless while lying flat, feels suddenly dizzy with a racing irregular heartbeat, and remembers her annual retinal eye exam was spotless two months ago. What is the safest action?

options.label: Trust the spotless annual eye exam as proof against hydroxychloroquine heart toxicity and skip her pills for four days at home to see if her breathing clears up.
options.why: A retinal exam inspects the back of the eye—not the myocardium—and abruptly self-stopping an immunomodulator as a home experiment risks triggering a dangerous lupus flare or lupus myocarditis without diagnosing the acute cardiac threat.

options.label: Assume the breathlessness is simply her familiar 11-year-old heart failure flaring up, sleep propped on extra pillows, and drive herself to an outpatient clinic next week.
options.why: A familiar diagnosis must never excuse sudden deterioration: NHS guidance flags lying-down breathlessness and Plaquenil warnings flag racing heartbeat and dizziness as immediate emergencies—and driving yourself while oxygen-starved or near-syncopal is dangerous.

options.label: Call emergency services immediately without driving herself, do not self-stop her immunomodulator as a home test, and give ER clinicians her complete medication, cardiac, weight-loss, and kidney history.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Lying-down breathlessness, dizziness, and racing irregular heartbeats demand urgent emergency evaluation for both mechanical pump failure and electrical QTc arrhythmia, while medication changes remain strictly clinician-directed across cardiology, nephrology, and rheumatology.

exam.q: An 11-year-old reportedly spayed cat has lost weight and sprayed pungent urine vertically on walls for months, and over the last three weeks she has begun acting like she is in heat and aggressively attacking anyone who reaches near her. Two routine urinalyses, a urine culture, and baseline CBC and chemistry panels have all come back normal. What is the safest next step?

options.label: Warn the veterinary clinic beforehand about her aggression so they can plan pre-visit anxiolytics or safe sedation, bring her full timeline and prior negative urinary workups, and pursue stepwise medical reassessment without ever punishing her.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Normal routine labs and a past spay record never rule out hidden endocrine drivers like a 6-mm ovarian remnant (or mimics like external estrogen exposure), and advance notice lets veterinary teams evaluate aggressive cats safely.

options.label: Accept that normal routine blood and urine tests prove a purely behavioral dominance issue, scold her firmly whenever she sprays, and hold her down at home to palpate her belly for lumps.
options.why: Cornell Feline Health Center guidance strictly warns against physical or verbal punishment—it escalates fear and stress without touching hidden biology—and forceful home restraint risks serious bites and injury to both owner and cat.

options.label: Assume an ovarian remnant is impossible because her adoption file says she was spayed ten years ago, and skip further imaging since hormone bloodwork alone can map the exact tissue and prove past surgical error.
options.why: A reported spay history is a map rather than a guarantee, hormone panels catch circulating signals without locating anatomy or proving past incompetence, and persistent signs demand linked imaging, endocrine, and tissue evaluation.

exam.q: After a minor household stair stumble and months of thigh ache and his leg giving out, a 59-year-old man is found to have two distinct femoral stress fractures. His serum calcium (9.4 mg/dL), intact PTH (50 pg/mL), alkaline phosphatase (135 U/L), creatinine (1.0 mg/dL), and 24-hour urine phosphate (0.821 g/24 hr; printed normal 0.3–1 g/day) all sit inside printed normal ranges, while his serum phosphate is 1.5 mg/dL (normal 2.5–4.8) and vitamin D is 22 ng/mL. What is the most accurate clinical takeaway?

options.label: Prioritize orthopedic stabilization first, recognize that excreting 0.821 g/24 hr of urinary phosphate during severe hypophosphatemia signals inappropriate renal phosphate wasting requiring metabolic workup, and track any specialized hormone labs with exact original units intact.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Printed urine reference ranges never establish physiological appropriateness when blood phosphate is critically low (1.5 mg/dL)—fixing the acute fracture comes first, followed by systematic metabolic investigation and strict unit tracking (RU/mL vs. pg/mL).

options.label: Reassure him that normal calcium, normal PTH, normal creatinine, and a mid-range 24-hour urine phosphate rule out metabolic bone disease, and treat his mild vitamin D of 22 ng/mL with over-the-counter supplements alone.
options.why: Normal calcium, PTH, and creatinine do not exclude severe osteomalacia, mild vitamin D deficiency alone does not account for bilateral femoral stress fractures without secondary PTH elevation, and normal-looking urine phosphate during hypophosphatemia is active renal wasting.

options.label: Delay urgent orthopedic fracture stabilization to demand an immediate whole-body 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT, because receptor scans achieve 100% localization across every patient and eliminate any need for biopsy.
options.why: Acute fracture stabilization always comes first; El-Maouche et al.’s 2016 NIH cohort localized tumors in only 6/11 (54.5%) total referrals (100% applied only to the 6 localized cases), false positives occur across modalities, and imaging is a compass requiring histologic proof.

exam.q: A two-year-old yellow Labrador known from a prior cheek swab to carry two copies of the DNM1 c.767G>T mutation suddenly develops wobbly hind legs and cannot walk twenty minutes into intense retrieving—yet he stays fully conscious, bright, and wagging his tail. What is the safest immediate response?

options.label: Let him rest five minutes until his wagging tail convinces you the crisis passed, then toss a few short retrieves to test his limit and record clear video for the vet.
options.why: An eager, tail-wagging demeanor never proves physiological safety in high-drive retrievers—some dogs die during collapse episodes—and you must never provoke a repeat collapse or delay care to film.

options.label: Skip the emergency clinic because his existing EE genetic printout already explains the wobble, douse him in ice water to cool him fast, and squirt sugar paste into his mouth.
options.why: Carrying two DNM1 copies never immunizes a dog against lethal lookalikes like cardiac arrhythmias, heatstroke, or acute metabolic crises; ice water risks shock, and forcing oral pastes into a weak dog risks aspiration.

options.label: Stop all activity at the first sign of incoordination and go straight for professional veterinary evaluation, reporting exact activity observations alongside his genetic record.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Sudden weakness or inability to walk is an immediate veterinary emergency regardless of alertness or prior DNA printouts—treat the living crisis first, then build an individualized vet activity plan.

exam.q: A healthy 48-year-old accidentally inhales a daily ferrous sulfate iron tablet while swallowing. After a hard coughing spell she spits out what looks like the intact pill, but two hours later she develops relentless blood-flecked coughing fits, pain behind her breastbone, and shortness of breath while sitting still. What is the safest action?

options.label: Drink a large glass of water and eat dense bread to flush any leftover iron residue down, and stay home since spitting out the intact tablet proves the danger passed.
options.why: Water and bread travel down the esophagus rather than the trachea—and aspirating water risks washing caustic iron deeper into smaller airways—while Caterino et al.’s Case 1 proved coughing up an intact iron pill can still leave a progressive chemical burn ending in surgical bilobectomy.

options.label: Drive herself to an urgent care clinic once the coughing eases, and plan to crush all future iron tablets into water at home so they cannot get stuck again.
options.why: Driving yourself with resting breathlessness and potential severe hypoxia risks sudden confusion or collapse behind the wheel, and self-crushing or dissolving engineered tablets at home can destroy release profiles or burn the mouth and esophagus.

options.label: Call local emergency services immediately without driving herself, tell responders it was a ferrous sulfate tablet with the exact timeline and formulation, skip swallow challenges, and arrange specialist follow-up for delayed airway scarring plus a formal swallow and formulation review.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Iron pill aspiration is a chemical mucosal emergency whose burn persists even if a tablet is coughed out, requiring urgent professional airway care, longitudinal post-discharge monitoring, and clinician-guided swallow/formulation planning rather than DIY fixes.

exam.q: After completing antimicrobial treatment for confirmed Babesia microti infection, an older adult with an intact spleen feels well and receives one negative follow-up PCR test—though his antibody serology remains positive. He plans to donate blood soon and assumes his intact spleen guarantees he could never suffer severe hemolytic relapse. What is the safest, scientifically accurate course?

options.label: Go ahead and donate blood since a single negative PCR proves the parasite is permanently gone, and treat the lingering positive antibody test as proof that antibiotics failed and must be restarted immediately.
options.why: Leiby et al.’s donor study showed Babesia parasitemia is intermittent and can dip below PCR detection limits while antibodies persist for months or years as immune memory—so one negative PCR never self-clears blood donation, and a persistent antibody alone does not prove treatment failure.

options.label: Proactively disclose his prior babesiosis diagnosis, testing, and treatment to the blood service so modern eligibility rules govern—never self-clearing off one negative PCR—and seek prompt re-evaluation if fatigue, pallor, or jaundice ever return.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Because Babesia survives refrigeration and surfaces intermittently while IgG immune memory and DAT autoantibodies can outlast active infection—even with an intact spleen—blood-bank disclosure is mandatory and clinical symptom changes always warrant reassessment.

options.label: Rely on his intact spleen as biological protection against severe hemolysis, skip telling the blood bank since 97.7% inter-lab PCR agreement means negative tests never miss hiding parasites, and watch only for a visible tick bite next summer.
options.why: An intact spleen did not prevent transfusion-requiring wAIHA in Bleik and Matubia’s 75-year-old patient, 97.7% agreement measures lab reproducibility rather than omniscient detection below threshold, and poppy-seed tick nymphs routinely transmit infection without being seen.

exam.q: A 76-year-old man wakes with numbness in both legs, low back pain, and difficulty passing urine, rapidly losing the ability to walk over four days. His initial thoracic MRI shows cord swelling and enhancement, and his lumbar puncture shows normal opening pressure (100 mm H2O) with mild lymphocytes—yet five days of IVIG and dexamethasone produce zero improvement. What is the safest clinical understanding and next step?

options.label: Assume a spinal dural arteriovenous fistula is impossible because the collapse took four days instead of months and his lumbar puncture opening pressure was normal, so wait 48 hours and test his strength by walking down the hallway.
options.why: Rapid progression never excludes diseases typically described as slow, CSF opening pressure measures fluid outside the cord rather than pressurized spinal veins, and DIY walking tests or 48-hour waiting deals risk serious falls and lost neurologic reserve.

options.label: Treat zero response to immunotherapy and ongoing neurologic loss as an urgent reassessment trigger, transfer actual prior scan images alongside written reports to an experienced vascular spinal team, and remember that sealing a fistula stops damage without guaranteeing full walking recovery.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Lack of improvement after steroids/IVIG is critical pivot data, raw scan pixels let specialists catch vascular flow shadows and incomplete prior vessel coverage (including pelvic iliac branches), and realistic follow-up separates vascular closure from nerve regeneration.

options.label: Conclude that the lumbar puncture and steroids caused his paralysis, demand an immediate invasive spinal angiogram on arrival at triage, and avoid sleeping on his stomach afterward to guarantee the fistula cannot recur.
options.why: Untreated venous congestion—not the diagnostic tap or steroids—drove the cord injury; specialist vascular teams decide when invasive angiography is warranted, and prone sleeping in Su et al. (2025) was strictly an unproven single-case hypothesis.

exam.q: In a region where feline sporotrichosis is emerging, an indoor-outdoor cat develops weeks of expanding, oozing ulcers on the face and paws along with a visibly swollen nose and high-pitched noisy breathing. Two days later, the owner notices a persistent sore on their own wrist despite not recalling a deep bite. What is the safest course of action?

options.label: Call the veterinary clinic ahead so they can prepare isolation for the cat, follow their handling and pet-separation plan instead of improvising wound care, and have a physician evaluate the wrist lesion with explicit disclosure of sick-cat contact.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Expanding ulcers with nasal deformity and stridor warrant prompt, pre-notified veterinary assessment, while a human caregiver’s new skin lesion requires medical review with explicit animal-contact disclosure—even without a remembered scratch—because fungal sporotrichosis will not respond to routine bacterial antibiotics.

options.label: Clean the cat’s necrotic scabs at home with dish gloves and leftover dog antibiotics, and skip seeing a human doctor for the wrist sore since you do not remember being bitten or scratched.
options.why: Improvised home debridement and leftover antibacterial prescriptions endanger both the cat and the caregiver—antibiotics target bacteria, not fungi—and Schubach et al.’s Rio cohort showed 137 of 421 cat-exposed human cases recalled no bite or scratch at all.

options.label: Release the cat outdoors immediately to keep the household safe, because the Rio de Janeiro data proved petting an infected cat carries an 84.7% transmission rate and a 10% infection prevalence across all domestic cats.
options.why: Abandoning a sick cat worsens community spread and welfare without solving exposure, 84.7% (421/497) was the proportion of already-confirmed clinic patients reporting cat contact rather than a petting-risk probability, and 10/101 came from selected close-contact cats—not general population prevalence.

exam.q: After decades of daily abdominal insulin injections, a patient’s HbA1c stays stubbornly elevated despite repeated dose increases. Her lower abdomen feels softly swollen and rubbery with no distinct hard lump, so she suspects trapped absorption—and plans to move tomorrow morning’s full high dose over to a fresh, untouched side of her belly on her own. What is the safest course?

options.label: Move her full usual dose to the untouched abdominal site tomorrow morning since there is no hard palpable lump to worry about, and keep juice on hand to pour into her mouth if she passes out.
options.why: Nagase et al. proved insulin-derived amyloidosis can exist with zero palpable mass, abruptly switching a barrier-calibrated dose to healthy skin risks severe hypoglycemic coma, and pouring juice into an unconscious person’s mouth risks fatal airway aspiration.

options.label: Keep injecting into the swollen patch but multiply her dose by 2.5× to overcome the ~40% absorption ratio reported in Nagase et al.’s Case 1 until her next routine visit.
options.why: Case 1’s ~40% AUC ratio is a single-patient experimental snapshot—never a universal bioavailability rule or home dosing multiplier—and self-multiplying insulin doses creates a life-threatening overdose hazard.

options.label: Contact her diabetes clinician before changing her injection site, bring her glucose logs and insulin devices for hands-on site palpation, and transition only under a clinician-guided dose reduction and monitoring plan.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! UK MHRA guidance explicitly warns patients to contact a doctor before moving injections away from altered tissue—even without a hard mass—so doses can be lowered proactively to prevent a sudden absorption floodgate.

exam.q: A 41-year-old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome has suffered four weeks of dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. A head CT and leg-vein ultrasound two weeks earlier were clear, and vertigo was suspected—but today she has thumb-indenting ankle swelling, unintended weight loss, and a serum albumin of 18.1 g/L (normal >36.0 g/L). A different lab later reports an albumin of 1.81 g/dL. What is the safest clinical interpretation and next step?

options.label: Treat 1.81 g/dL as a catastrophic tenfold drop from 18.1 g/L, start daily high-protein whey shakes at home, and schedule a separate podiatry visit for her ankles so her vertigo clinic can stay focused on her ears.
options.why: 18.1 g/L and 1.81 g/dL are the exact same physical concentration (10 deciliters per liter), whey shakes cannot fix a systemic protein leak, and splitting ankle edema from vomiting hides the connected biology.

options.label: Accept that her earlier negative clot scans rule out urgent illness, demand immediate off-label cetuximab as a guaranteed permanent cure that prevents gastric cancer, and reject any repeat endoscopy as proof the first test was botched.
options.why: Off-label cetuximab is a severe-case individualized choice with major toxicities (rash, skin fissures, hypomagnesemia) and unproved cancer prevention, repeat deeper biopsies reflect diagnostic sampling science rather than error, and sudden worsening swelling with breathlessness or chest symptoms demands emergency triage.

options.label: Recognize that 18.1 g/L and 1.81 g/dL represent identical severe hypoalbuminemia requiring one unified whole-body workup—not protein shakes—while escalating urgently for sudden red/hot painful swelling or immediately for breathlessness, chest symptoms, faintness, or vomiting blood.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Always verify g/L vs. g/dL units first, link persistent vomiting, weight loss, and pitting edema into one clinical investigation to find the true source of protein loss, and act immediately on NHS cardiopulmonary or GI-bleeding red flags.

exam.q: A nine-year-old cat develops new appetite loss and excessive drooling, is diagnosed with a congenital extrahepatic portosystemic shunt, and undergoes surgical attenuation. After hospital discharge, her post-operative bile acids come back completely normal—then one evening she suddenly becomes unsteady and has a brief seizure. What is the safest interpretation and action?

options.label: Seek urgent veterinary neurological reassessment immediately and keep her exact vascular map and surgical history with her chart—normalized post-op bile acids do not rule out late post-operative seizures or residual shunt flow.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! In Valiente et al.’s 34-cat cohort, roughly 23.5% developed post-op seizures—including three seizing cats with completely normal bile acids and one with normal ammonia. Biochemical labs and neurological status are two separate dashboard dials.

options.label: Trust the normalized post-operative bile acids as proof that the shunt is 100% cured, run an at-home fasting-and-meal test tomorrow, and try to capture a second seizure on video before calling the clinic.
options.why: Normalized bile acids never guarantee a seizure-free brain or zero residual flow, home fasting or meal challenges are unsafe for a sick animal, and waiting to provoke or film a repeat neurological episode delays urgent care.

options.label: Assume a nine-year-old cat cannot have a true congenital shunt—meaning it must be an acquired shunt—and ask a new clinic to tie off any remaining small vessels immediately without reviewing her prior vascular map.
options.why: Congenital shunts can remain compensated for nine years before diagnosis, and confusing congenital with acquired physiology is perilous—closing an acquired pressure-relief shunt around a diseased liver can be rapidly fatal, so the exact prior vascular map is mandatory.

exam.q: A 58-year-old patient with a revised metal-on-polyethylene hip replacement has developed worsening breathlessness, numbness in both feet, and fading hearing alongside new right groin pain and a limp. One mitochondrial DNA screen came back negative. What is the safest next step?

options.label: Climb stairs carrying heavy boxes to test whether the hip grinds reliably, order a private online heavy-metal blood test first so you arrive with proof, and pause coronary follow-up until cobalt results return.
options.why: Home load or grinding provocation risks fresh mechanical damage and debris release, no private direct-to-consumer assay is required before calling a doctor, and suspected metal toxicity never cancels competing cardiac or endocrine disease.

options.label: Contact your medical and orthopedic teams promptly without provoking the hip or waiting on private labs, bring your exact operative implant report across specialties, and keep competing heart and thyroid evaluations running in parallel.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Even non-MoM revised metal-on-polyethylene hips can shed cobalt and chromium from metal junctions, prompt clinical contact beats home provocation, and bridging orthopedic records never replaces parallel care for concurrent conditions like coronary stenosis.

options.label: Rule out hip involvement because the bearing is metal-on-polyethylene rather than a recalled metal-on-metal resurfacing—and if an older plasma cobalt value is lower than a newer whole-blood number, demand immediate removal surgery.
options.why: Stepien et al.’s catastrophic metallosis occurred with a revised metal-on-polyethylene hip, plasma and whole blood are non-interchangeable matrices that cannot be compared raw, and neither a recall nor an isolated number automatically mandates revision surgery.

exam.q: A 40-year-old patient previously treated for a growth hormone-secreting pituitary macroadenoma logs into a patient portal and sees that their latest IGF-1 blood level has finally entered the normal reference range. They also feel well enough to ignore persistent loud snoring and elevated blood pressure. What is the safest interpretation and next step?

options.label: Cut their monthly endocrine injection dose in half immediately so hormones do not drop too low, and cancel blood-pressure, sleep, heart, and colon follow-ups now that the hormone ratio is normal.
options.why: Self-adjusting endocrine therapy off a patient portal is dangerous, and Arosio et al.’s nationwide cohort showed excess mortality persisted (SMR 1.3; 88 vs. 66 deaths) even in patients controlled at their last IGF-1 visit because prior hormone exposure leaves cardiovascular, metabolic, airway, and colonic legacy risks.

options.label: Keep all prescribed doses unchanged pending specialist review, and ask the coordinating endocrinology team how blood pressure, glucose, sleep quality, cardiac structure, bowel-polyp screening, and remaining pituitary axes will be monitored long-term.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! Normalizing IGF-1 stops active hormonal flooding—like fixing a burst pipe—but NIDDK and NHS guidance stress that holistic whole-body follow-up and monitoring of remaining pituitary hormones remain essential under clinician direction.

options.label: Conclude that because the Italian cohort reported an overall SMR of 1.7, modern treatment has a 70% fatality rate regardless of control, so additional surgical or medical follow-up is pointless.
options.why: An SMR of 1.7 (153 observed vs. 90 expected deaths across 811 patients diagnosed in 1980–2002) is a historical aggregate ratio—not a 70% fatality rate or a forecast for modern care—and treating it with fatalism sacrifices effective, life-preserving comorbidity management.

exam.q: Three weeks after nursing your unvaccinated dog bare-handed through acute fever, vomiting, and diarrhea—which cleared up after your vet prescribed antibiotics—you develop a high fever, severe muscle aches, and diarrhea. Your dog looks completely healthy today. What is the safest immediate move?

options.label: Have your vet run a urine PCR on your recovered dog first; if the dog’s urine PCR comes back negative today, you can safely rule out leptospirosis and treat your fever at home.
options.why: In Nakashiro et al. (2024), the recovered dog’s post-antibiotic urine PCR was completely negative even though canine MAT titers stood at 800—a negative test weeks after antimicrobials never rules out earlier urinary shedding.

options.label: Seek human medical care promptly, tell the clinician up front about your dog’s prior illness and bare-handed urine/vomit contact, and authorize your doctor and veterinarian to share clinical summaries.
options.why: Survived Tuesday! CDC guidance stresses immediate medical evaluation without waiting for shock vitals or pet test results, and bridging the human and veterinary records unlocked the life-saving diagnosis in Nakashiro et al.’s case.

options.label: Skip the zoonotic history if you live in a dry suburban desert neighborhood and your dog only visits an indoor doggy daycare, since Leptospira requires tropical floodwaters to spread.
options.why: Iverson et al.’s 2021 Maricopa County investigation documented 71 confirmed or probable canine leptospirosis cases across arid Phoenix suburbs, with strong epidemiological clustering around congregate dog daycare and boarding settings.
